Experiments are performed on MNIST, CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 and show that the method has the potential to perform better than standard dropout and at the level of Monte Carlo Dropout (the standard method to compute the real dropout outputs consistently with the training assumption of an ensemble, of course quite expensive computationally) The study gives a very interesting theoretical model for dropout as a latent variable model where standard dropout is then a monte carlo approximation. This is very probably widely applicable to further studies of dropout. The framework for the study of the inference gap is interesting although maybe somewhat less widely applicable. The proposed model is convincing although 1. it is tested on simple datasets 2. the gains are relatively small and 3. there is an increased computational cost during training because a new hyper-parameter is introduced. p6 line 8 typo: expecatation

title: HyperNetworks | OpenReview
abstract: Abstract:###This work explores hypernetworks: an approach of using one network, also known as a hypernetwork, to generate the weights for another network. We apply hypernetworks to generate adaptive weights for recurrent networks. In this case, hypernetworks can be viewed as a relaxed form of weight-sharing across layers. In our implementation, hypernetworks are are trained jointly with the main network in an end-to-end fashion. Our main result is that hypernetworks can generate non-shared weights for LSTM and achieve state-of-the-art results on a variety of sequence modelling tasks including character-level language modelling, handwriting generation and neural machine translation, challenging the weight-sharing paradigm for recurrent networks.
review: A well known limitation in deep neural networks is that the same parameters are typically used for all examples, even though different examples have very different characteristics. For example, recognizing animals will likely require different features than categorizing flowers. Using different parameters for different types of examples has the potential to greatly reduce underfitting. This can be seen in recent results with generative models, where image quality is much better for less diverse datasets. However, it is difficult to use different parameters for different examples because we typically train using minibatches, which relies on using the same parameters for all examples in a minibatch (i.e. doing matrix multiplies in a fully-connected network). The hypernetworks paper cleverly proposes to get around this problem by adapting different *parameters* for different time steps in recurrent networks and different. The basic insight is that a minibatch will always include many different examples from the same time step or spatial position, so there is no computational issue involved with using different *parameters*. In this paper, the *parameters* are modified for different positions based on the output from a hypernetwork which conditions on the time step. Hypothetically, this hypernetwork could also condition on other features that are shared by all sequences in the minibatch. I expect this method to become standard for training RNNs, especially where the length of the sequences is the same during the training and testing phases. Penn Treebank is a highly competitive baseline, so the SOTA result reported here is impressive. The experiments on convolutional networks are less experimentally impressive. I suspect that the authors were aiming to achieve state of the art results here but settled with achieving a reduction in the number of parameters. It might even be worthwhile to consider a synthetic experiment where two completely different types of image are appended (i.e. birds on the left and flowers on the right) and show that the hypernetwork helps in this situation. It may be the case that for convnets, the cases where hypernetworks help are very specific. For RNNs, it seems to be the case that explicitly changing the nature of the computation depending on the position in the sequence greatly improves generalization. While a usual RNN could learn to store a counter (indicating the position in the sequence), the hypernetwork could be a more efficient way to add capacity. Applications to time series forecasting and modeling could be an interesting area for future work.

title: A Learned Representation For Artistic Style | OpenReview
abstract: Abstract:###The diversity of painting styles represents a rich visual vocabulary for the construction of an image. The degree to which one may learn and parsimoniously capture this visual vocabulary measures our understanding of the higher level features of paintings, if not images in general. In this work we investigate the construction of a single, scalable deep network that can parsimoniously capture the artistic style of a diversity of paintings. We demonstrate that such a network generalizes across a diversity of artistic styles by reducing a painting to a point in an embedding space. Importantly, this model permits a user to explore new painting styles by arbitrarily combining the styles learned from individual paintings. We hope that this work provides a useful step towards building rich models of paintings and offers a window on to the structure of the learned representation of artistic style.
review: This paper addresses the problem of efficient neural stylization. Instead of training a separate network for N different styles (as is done, e.g., in Johnson et al.), this paper extends the instance normalization work of Ulyanov et al. to train a single network and learn a smaller set â€œconditional instance normalizationâ€ parameters dependent on the desired output style. The conditional instance normalization applies a learnt affine transformation on normalized feature maps at each layer in the network. Qualitative results are shown. I have not worked in this area, but Iâ€™m generally aware of the main issues in transferring artistic style. The paper addresses a known challenge of incorporating different styles into the same net, which have a number of practical benefits. As far as I can tell the results look compelling. As Iâ€™m less confident in my expertise in this area, Iâ€™m happy to support another reviewer who is willing to champion this paper. My main comments are on the paper writing. As far as I understand, the main novelty of the approach starts in Section 2.2, and before that is review of prior art. If this is indeed the case, one suggestion is to remove the subsection heading for 2.1 so itâ€™s grouped with the first part of Section 2, and to cite related work for the feedforward network (e.g., Johnson et al.) in the text and in Fig 2 so itâ€™s clear. In fact, Iâ€™m wondering if Figs 2 and 3 can be combined somehow so that the contribution is clearer in the figures. I was at first confused by Eq (5) as x and z are not defined anywhere. Also, it may be helpful to write out everything explicitly as is done in the instance normalization paper. In Eq (4), perhaps you could write T_s to emphasize that there are separate networks for different styles. Fig 5 left: Iâ€™m assuming the different colors correspond to the different styles. If so, perhaps mention this in the caption. Also, this figure is hard to read. Maybe instead show single curves with error bars that are averages over the loss curves for N-styles and individual styles. Typos: Page 1: Shouldnâ€™t it be â€œVGG-16â€ network (not *VGG-19â€)? Page 2: â€œnewtorkâ€ => â€œnetworkâ€. Paragraph after Eq. (5): â€œmuch lessâ€ => â€œfewerâ€.

title: Hadamard Product for Low-rank Bilinear Pooling | OpenReview
abstract: Abstract:###Bilinear models provide rich representations compared with linear models. They have been applied in various visual tasks, such as object recognition, segmentation, and visual question-answering, to get state-of-the-art performances taking advantage of the expanded representations. However, bilinear representations tend to be high-dimensional, limiting the applicability to computationally complex tasks. We propose low-rank bilinear pooling using Hadamard product for an efficient attention mechanism of multimodal learning. We show that our model outperforms compact bilinear pooling in visual question-answering tasks with the state-of-the-art results on the VQA dataset, having a better parsimonious property.
review: Summary: The paper presents low-rank bilinear pooling that uses Hadamard product (commonly known as element-wise multiplication). The paper implements low-rank bilinear pooling on an existing model (Kim et al., 2016b) and builds a model for Visual Question Answering (VQA) that outperforms the current state-of-art by 0.42%. The paper presents various ablation studies of the new VQA model they built. Strengths: 1. The paper presents new insights into element-wise multiplication operation which has been previously used in VQA literature (such as Antol et al., ICCV 2015) without insights on why it should work. 2. The paper presents a new model for the task of VQA that beats the current state-of-art by 0.42%. However, I have concerns about the statistical significance of the performance (see weaknesses below). 3. The various design choices made in model development have been experimentally verified. Weaknesses/Suggestions: 1. When authors explicitly (keeping rest of the model architecture same) compared low-rank bilinear pooling with compact bilinear pooling, they found that low-rank bilinear pooling performs worse. Hence, it could not be experimentally verified that low-rank bilinear pooling is better in performance than compact bilinear pooling (at least for the task of VQA). 2. The authors argue that low-rank bilinear pooling uses 25% less parameters than compact bilinear pooling. So, could the authors please explain how does the reduction in number of parameters help experimentally? Does the training time of the model reduce significantly? Can we train the model with less data? 3. One of the contributions of the paper is that the proposed model outperforms the current state-of-art on VQA by 0.42%. However, I am skeptical that the performance of the proposed model is statistically significantly better than the current state-of-art. 4. I would like the authors to explicitly mention the differences between MRN, MARN and MLB. It is not very clear from reading the paper. 5. In the caption for Table 1, fix the following: â€œhave notâ€ -> â€œhave noâ€ Review Summary: I like the insights about low-rank bilinear pooling using Hadamard product (element-wise multiplication) presented in the paper. However, it could not be justified that low-rank bilinear pooling leads to better performance than compact biliear pooling. It does lead to reduction in number of parameters but it is not clear how much that helps experimentally. So, to be more convinced I would like the authors to provide experimental justification of why low-rank bilinear pooling is better than other forms of pooling.

title: Learning Continuous Semantic Representations of Symbolic Expressions | OpenReview
abstract: Abstract:###The question of how procedural knowledge is represented and inferred is a fundamental problem in machine learning and artificial intelligence. Recent work on program induction has proposed neural architectures, based on abstractions like stacks, Turing machines, and interpreters, that operate on abstract computational machines or on execution traces. But the recursive abstraction that is central to procedural knowledge is perhaps most naturally represented by symbolic representations that have syntactic structure, such as logical expressions and source code. Combining abstract, symbolic reasoning with continuous neural reasoning is a grand challenge of representation learning. As a step in this direction, we propose a new architecture, called neural equivalence networks, for the problem of learning continuous semantic representations of mathematical and logical expressions. These networks are trained to represent semantic equivalence, even of expressions that are syntactically very different. The challenge is that semantic representations must be computed in a syntax-directed manner, because semantics is compositional, but at the same time, small changes in syntax can lead to very large changes in semantics, which can be difficult for continuous neural architectures. We perform an exhaustive evaluation on the task of checking equivalence on a highly diverse class of symbolic algebraic and boolean expression types, showing that our model significantly outperforms existing architectures.
review: The authors propose a new model to learn symbolic expression representations. They do a reasonably extensive evaluation with similar approaches and motivate their approach well. As expressed in the preliminary questions, I think the authors could improve the motivation for their subexpforce loss. At the top of page 6 the authors mention that they compare to two-layer MLP w/o residual connections. I think having a direct comparison between a model with and w/o the subexpforce loss would be helpful too and should be included (i.e. keep the residual connections and normalization). My main concern is the evaluation *score*. It appears to be precision on a per query basis. I believe a more standard metric, precision-recall or roc would be more informative. In particular the chosen metric is expected to perform better when the equivalence classes are larger, since this isn*t taken into account in the denominator, but the likelihood of a random expression matching the query increases.

title: Discovering objects and their relations from entangled scene representations | OpenReview
abstract: Abstract:###Our world can be succinctly and compactly described as structured scenes of objects and relations. A typical room, for example, contains salient objects such as tables, chairs and books, and these objects typically relate to each other by virtue of their correlated features, such as position, function and shape. Humans exploit knowledge of objects and their relations for learning a wide spectrum of tasks, and more generally when learning the structure underlying observed data. In this work, we introduce relation networks (RNs) - a general purpose neural network architecture for object-relation reasoning. We show that RNs are capable of learning object relations from scene description data. Furthermore, we show that RNs can act as a bottleneck that induces the factorization of objects from entangled scene description inputs, and from distributed deep representations of scene images provided by a variational autoencoder. The model can also be used in conjunction with differentiable memory mechanisms for implicit relation discovery in one-shot learning tasks. Our results suggest that relation networks are a powerful architecture for solving a variety of problems that require object relation reasoning.
review: + Understanding relations between objects is an important task in domains like vision, language and robotics. However, models trained on real-life datasets can often exploit simple object properties (not relation-based) to identify relations (eg: animals of bigger size are typically predators and small-size animals are preys). Such models can predict relations without necessarily understanding them. Given the difficulty of the task, a controlled setting is required to investigate if neural networks can be designed to actually understand pairwise object relations. The current paper takes a significant step in answering this question through a controlled dataset. Also, multiple experiments are presented to validate the *relation learning* ability of proposed Relation Networks (RN). + The dataset proposed in the paper ensures that relation classification models can succeed only by learning the relations between objects and not by exploiting *predator-prey* like object properties. + The paper presents very thorough experiments to validate the claim that *RNs* truly learn the relation between objects. 1. In particular, the ability of the RN to force a simple linear layer to disentangle scene description from VAE latent space and permuted description is very interesting. This clearly demonstrates that the RN learns object relations. 2. The one-shot experiments again demonstrate this ability in a convincing manner. This requires the model to understand relations in each run, represent them through an abstract label and assign the label to future samples from the relationship graph. Some suggestions: - Is g_{psi}(.) permutation invariant as well. Since it works on pairs of objects, how did you ensure that the MLP is invariant to the order of the objects in the pair? - The RNs need to operate over pairs of objects in order to identify pairwise interactions. However, in practical applications there are more complicated group interactions. (eg. ternary interaction: *person* riding a *bike* wears *helmet*). Would this require g(.) of RN to not just operate on pairs but on every possible subset of objects in the scene? More generally, is such a pairwise edge-based approach scalable to larger number of objects? - The authors mention that * a deep network with a sufficiently large number of parameters and a large enough training set should be capable of matching the performance of a RN*. This is an interesting point, and could be true in practice. Have the authors investigated this effect by trying to identify the minimum model capacity and/or training examples required by a MLP to match the performance of RN for the provided setup? This would help in quantifying the significance of RN for practical applications with limited examples. In other words, the task in Sec. 5.1 could benefit from another plot: the performance of MLP and RN at different amounts of training samples. - While the simulation setup in the current paper is a great first-step towards analyzing the *relation-learning* ability of RNs, it is still not clear if this would transfer to real-life datasets. I strongly encourage the authors to experiment on real-life datasets like Coco, visual genome or HICO as stated in the pre-review stage. - Minor: Some terminologies in the paper such as *objects* and *scene descriptions* used to refer to abstract entities can be misleading for readers from the object detection domain in computer vision. This could be clarified early on in the introduction. - Minor: Some results like Fig. 8 which shows the ability of RN to generalize to unseen categories are quite interesting and could be moved to the main draft for completeness. The paper proposes a network which is capable of understanding relationships between objects in a scene. This ability of the RN is thoroughly investigated through a series of experiments on a controlled dataset. While, the model is currently evaluated only on a simulated dataset, the results are quite promising and could translate to real-life datasets as well.

title: Making Neural Programming Architectures Generalize via Recursion
abstract: Abstract:###Empirically, neural networks that attempt to learn programs from data have exhibited poor generalizability. Moreover, it has traditionally been difficult to reason about the behavior of these models beyond a certain level of input complexity. In order to address these issues, we propose augmenting neural architectures with a key abstraction: recursion. As an application, we implement recursion in the Neural Programmer-Interpreter framework on four tasks: grade-school addition, bubble sort, topological sort, and quicksort. We demonstrate superior generalizability and interpretability with small amounts of training data. Recursion divides the problem into smaller pieces and drastically reduces the domain of each neural network component, making it tractable to prove guarantees about the overall systemâ€™s behavior. Our experience suggests that in order for neural architectures to robustly learn program semantics, it is necessary to incorporate a concept like recursion.
review:
This paper addresses poor generalization in neural program induction by augmenting the Neural Programmer-Interpreter with recursion. The authors reformulate training traces for grade-school addition, bubble sort, topological sort, and quicksort to include recursive calls, showing 100% accuracy on longer inputs from tiny training sets. They also propose a verification procedure over base cases and reduction rules, claiming provable perfect generalization. The core idea is valuable and timely: recursion reduces hidden-state dependence on input length and enables finite verification. Empirical results are compelling, especially for quicksort and topological sort.

However, several concerns remain. First, recursion is not learned; it is injected through hand-designed recursive traces. The central claim that neural architectures must incorporate recursion is therefore demonstrated only under strong supervision. Second, “provable” generalization relies on manually constructed verification sets; completeness arguments are informal, and the procedure may not scale to continuous or large-state tasks. Third, experiments use small tasks and a reimplementation of NPI; comparisons with non-recursive variants are informative but limited. The bubble-sort verification variant changes the encoder, complicating comparison. Finally, the paper does not analyze failure modes or sensitivity to trace indentation and tail-call choices.

Questions: How robust is verification-set construction? Can recursion be induced from non-recursive traces? What is the computational overhead? Overall, this is an important contribution with strong empirical evidence, but claims should be tempered. Recommend acceptance with revisions clarifying supervision and verification limitations.

title: End-to-end Optimized Image Compression
abstract: Abstract:###We describe an image compression method, consisting of a nonlinear analysis transformation, a uniform quantizer, and a nonlinear synthesis transformation. The transforms are constructed in three successive stages of convolutional linear filters and nonlinear activation functions. Unlike most convolutional neural networks, the joint nonlinearity is chosen to implement a form of local gain control, inspired by those used to model biological neurons. Using a variant of stochastic gradient descent, we jointly optimize the entire model for rate-distortion performance over a database of training images, introducing a continuous proxy for the discontinuous loss function arising from the quantizer. Under certain conditions, the relaxed loss function may be interpreted as the log likelihood of a generative model, as implemented by a variational autoencoder. Unlike these models, however, the compression model must operate at any given point along the rate-distortion curve, as specified by a trade-off parameter. Across an independent set of test images, we find that the optimized method generally exhibits better rate-distortion performance than the standard JPEG and JPEG 2000 compression methods. More importantly, we observe a dramatic improvement in visual quality for all images at all bit rates, which is supported by objective quality estimates using MS-SSIM.
review:
This paper presents an end-to-end optimized nonlinear transform coding framework for image compression. It combines cascaded convolutional transforms with generalized divisive normalization (GDN), uniform quantization, and a continuous relaxation via additive uniform noise to enable gradient-based rate–distortion optimization. The authors train separate models for different λ values, implement a CABAC-based entropy coder, and report actual bit rates. Comparisons on Kodak and other images show competitive or better PSNR than JPEG/JPEG 2000 and consistent MS-SSIM improvements, with notably fewer blocking/ringing artifacts.

Strengths: The formulation is clean and principled; the additive-noise relaxation is well motivated and linked to variational autoencoders; using actual entropy-coded bit rates rather than differential entropy estimates strengthens the empirical claims; and the biologically inspired GDN nonlinearity is a sensible, effective design.

Weaknesses: The architecture and training choices are largely ad hoc, with no systematic ablation isolating the contribution of GDN versus capacity or depth. Separate transforms must be trained for each rate point, limiting practicality. The entropy coder exploits little spatial context, and comparisons are restricted to older codecs and a modest test set. Visual-quality claims rely heavily on MS-SSIM and selected examples; broader perceptual studies would help. The paper also does not clearly analyze computational cost or robustness across image types.

Overall, this is a strong and influential proof of concept for learned image compression, though further ablation, efficiency analysis, and broader evaluation would strengthen it.

title: Optimization as a Model for Few-Shot Learning
abstract: Abstract:###Though deep neural networks have shown great success in the large data domain, they generally perform poorly on few-shot learning tasks, where a model has to quickly generalize after seeing very few examples from each class. The general belief is that gradient-based optimization in high capacity models requires many iterative steps over many examples to perform well. Here, we propose an LSTM-based meta-learner model to learn the exact optimization algorithm used to train another learner neural network in the few-shot regime. The parametrization of our model allows it to learn appropriate parameter updates specifically for the scenario where a set amount of updates will be made, while also learning a general initialization of the learner network that allows for quick convergence of training. We demonstrate that this meta-learning model is competitive with deep metric-learning techniques for few-shot learning.
review:
This paper frames few-shot learning as meta-learning an optimization algorithm. An LSTM meta-learner receives learner gradients and losses and outputs parameter updates, while its initial cell state learns a shared initialization. The meta-learner is trained end-to-end on episodes to minimize post-update test loss, with parameter sharing and preprocessing. Experiments on Mini-ImageNet show gains over nearest-neighbor and fine-tuning baselines and performance competitive with Matching Networks.

Strengths: The idea is elegant and well motivated by the analogy between gradient descent and LSTM cell updates. Learning both initialization and update rule is sensible, and matching meta-training to meta-test conditions is important. The gate visualizations offer useful insight, and the method is clearly described.

Weaknesses: Evaluation is narrow: only Mini-ImageNet with custom class splits and self-implemented Matching Networks, making comparisons hard to contextualize. There is no systematic ablation isolating the contributions of learned initialization, input/forget gates, and gradient preprocessing. The gradient-independence approximation is convenient but unjustified empirically. Separate meta-learners are trained for each shot/update setting, limiting generality. Meta-training cost and sensitivity to hyperparameters are not analyzed. Batch-normalization handling is reasonable but ad hoc. The method is also not compared with stronger contemporary few-shot baselines.

Overall, this is an influential and well-presented proof of concept, but broader evaluation and ablations would strengthen the claims.

title: Learning End-to-End Goal-Oriented Dialog
abstract: Abstract:###Traditional dialog systems used in goal-oriented applications require a lot of domain-specific handcrafting, which hinders scaling up to new domains. End- to-end dialog systems, in which all components are trained from the dialogs themselves, escape this limitation. But the encouraging success recently obtained in chit-chat dialog may not carry over to goal-oriented settings. This paper proposes a testbed to break down the strengths and shortcomings of end-to-end dialog systems in goal-oriented applications. Set in the context of restaurant reservation, our tasks require manipulating sentences and symbols, so as to properly conduct conversations, issue API calls and use the outputs of such calls. We show that an end-to-end dialog system based on Memory Networks can reach promising, yet imperfect, performance and learn to perform non-trivial operations. We confirm those results by comparing our system to a hand-crafted slot-filling baseline on data from the second Dialog State Tracking Challenge (Henderson et al., 2014a). We show similar result patterns on data extracted from an online concierge service.
review:
This paper introduces a benchmark and task suite for end-to-end goal-oriented dialog, centered on restaurant reservation. Five simulated tasks isolate dialog management, API-call generation and updating, option ranking, and use of knowledge-base facts; a DSTC2-derived task and a proprietary concierge dataset test realism. The authors compare rule-based, IR, supervised embedding, and Memory Network models, including match-type features for out-of-vocabulary entities. Results show Memory Networks outperform baselines and handle several nontrivial operations, but per-dialog success remains poor on tasks requiring interpretation of API outputs, such as sorting options by rating.

Strengths: The task decomposition is thoughtful and diagnostic, and the inclusion of OOV test sets is valuable. Releasing simulated data and confirming relative method rankings on real dialogs strengthens reproducibility and external validity. The analysis of failures, especially attention and entity handling, is useful.

Weaknesses: The benchmark relies on templated synthetic language, so conclusions about natural dialog may be limited. Candidate-ranking evaluation avoids generation and may overstate deployability. Only Memory Networks are explored as end-to-end models, with no ablations isolating architectural choices beyond match-type features. The proprietary concierge set is not reproducible, and DSTC2 conversion differs from standard evaluation, limiting comparability. Rule-based baselines are reasonable but not tuned equally across tasks.

Overall, this is a well-motivated and useful diagnostic benchmark, though broader model coverage and more naturalistic data would strengthen its impact.

title: Towards Principled Methods for Training Generative Adversarial Networks
abstract: Abstract:###The goal of this paper is not to introduce a single algorithm or method, but to make theoretical steps towards fully understanding the training dynamics of gen- erative adversarial networks. In order to substantiate our theoretical analysis, we perform targeted experiments to verify our assumptions, illustrate our claims, and quantify the phenomena. This paper is divided into three sections. The first sec- tion introduces the problem at hand. The second section is dedicated to studying and proving rigorously the problems including instability and saturation that arize when training generative adversarial networks. The third section examines a prac- tical and theoretically grounded direction towards solving these problems, while introducing new tools to study them.
review:
This paper provides a theoretical analysis of GAN training instability. It argues that when data and generator distributions lie on low-dimensional manifolds with disjoint or non-aligned supports, an optimal discriminator exists that is perfect and locally constant, yielding zero gradients almost everywhere. The authors prove that the original minimax generator loss suffers vanishing gradients as the discriminator improves, while the alternative −log D loss corresponds to an inverted KL minus JSD objective and produces high-variance, potentially Cauchy-distributed updates. They then propose adding continuous noise to discriminator inputs, relate the noisy objective to JSD, and motivate Wasserstein distance as a smoother measure.

Strengths: The paper is rigorous, well organized, and addresses an important practical problem. The manifold argument is insightful, and the targeted DCGAN experiments support the theoretical predictions. The analysis of the −log D objective helps explain mode dropping and instability. The noisy-input discussion provides a principled direction and useful tools for future work.

Weaknesses: The theory relies on idealized assumptions, including near-optimal discriminators and independent noise in D and ∇D; the latter is acknowledged as too strong. The proposed noise injection is not developed into a complete, evaluated algorithm, and annealing schedules remain unspecified. Experiments are illustrative rather than quantitative, using a single architecture and limited datasets. The connection to practical stabilization is suggestive but not fully validated. The Wasserstein discussion is promising but largely motivational.

Overall, this is a valuable conceptual contribution that clarifies GAN training pathologies and points toward principled remedies, though practical validation remains limited.

title: Reinforcement Learning with Unsupervised Auxiliary Tasks
abstract: Abstract:###Deep reinforcement learning agents have achieved state-of-the-art results by directly maximising cumulative reward. However, environments contain a much wider variety of possible training signals. In this paper, we introduce an agent that also maximises many other pseudo-reward functions simultaneously by reinforcement learning. All of these tasks share a common representation that, like unsupervised learning, continues to develop in the absence of extrinsic rewards. We also introduce a novel mechanism for focusing this representation upon extrinsic rewards, so that learning can rapidly adapt to the most relevant aspects of the actual task. Our agent significantly outperforms the previous state-of-the-art on Atari, averaging 880\% expert human performance, and a challenging suite of first-person, three-dimensional emph{Labyrinth} tasks leading to a mean speedup in learning of 10 and averaging 87\% expert human performance on Labyrinth.
review:
This paper introduces UNREAL, an A3C-based agent augmented with unsupervised auxiliary tasks: pixel control, reward prediction, and value-function replay. These tasks share the CNN-LSTM representation and are trained off-policy from a small replay buffer. Experiments on 13 Labyrinth levels and 57 Atari games show large gains over A3C in data efficiency, final performance, and robustness to learning-rate and entropy hyperparameters.

Strengths: The approach is practical and clearly motivated, combining auxiliary control and prediction without extra environment supervision. The ablation studies are informative, showing each component contributes, and the comparison against reconstruction and change-prediction baselines is useful. Results are strong: 87% versus 54% human-normalized score on Labyrinth and roughly 10× faster learning. The method also improves Atari performance and hyperparameter robustness, which is valuable for deep RL reproducibility.

Weaknesses: The paper adds several loss terms and task-specific design choices—pixel-grid resolution, replay buffer size, loss weights, and skewed reward replay—without much theoretical justification or sensitivity analysis. The claim that skewed reward prediction does not bias the policy is plausible but insufficiently examined. Computational overhead and memory costs are not quantified. Atari gains are reported mainly in aggregate, with limited per-game analysis. Feature control is only preliminary. The pseudo-reward tasks are somewhat ad hoc, and it is unclear which are essential in other domains.

Overall, this is a strong empirical contribution demonstrating that auxiliary control and prediction tasks substantially improve deep RL, though more analysis of design choices and generality would strengthen it.

title: Multi-Agent Cooperation and the Emergence of (Natural) Language
abstract: Abstract:###The current mainstream approach to train natural language systems is to expose them to large amounts of text. This passive learning is problematic if we are in- terested in developing interactive machines, such as conversational agents. We propose a framework for language learning that relies on multi-agent communi- cation. We study this learning in the context of referential games. In these games, a sender and a receiver see a pair of images. The sender is told one of them is the target and is allowed to send a message to the receiver, while the receiver must rely on it to identify the target. Thus, the agents develop their own language interactively out of the need to communicate. We show that two networks with simple configurations are able to learn to coordinate in the referential game. We further explore whether the â€œword meaningsâ€ induced in the game reflect intuitive semantic properties of the objects depicted in the image, and we present a simple strategy for grounding the agentsâ€™ code into natural language, a necessary step in developing machines that should eventually be able to communicate with humans.
review:
This paper studies the emergence of communication in a two-agent referential game, where a sender and receiver must coordinate over pairs of natural images using a discrete, initially meaningless vocabulary. Agents are trained with REINFORCE on communication success alone. The authors show that simple feed-forward agents reliably converge to near-perfect coordination, that an “informed” sender using pairwise convolutions converges faster and uses more symbols, and that emergent symbol usage has above-chance purity with respect to human-defined object categories. They further show that class-level targets increase semantic alignment, and that mixing the game with supervised image labeling yields symbols that are partially interpretable by humans, including in a ReferItGame transfer experiment.

Strengths: The setup is clean and well motivated, connecting game-theoretic signaling, emergent communication, and practical AI. The purity and t-SNE analyses provide useful evidence that emergent codes capture conceptual rather than purely low-level visual properties. The grounding experiment and crowdsourced human evaluation are valuable steps toward human-interpretable emergent language.

Weaknesses: The game is highly simplified: two images, one symbol, small vocabularies, and no syntax or compositional structure. Purity is a coarse semantic measure and could be confounded by visual similarity. Hyperparameters appear fixed without sensitivity analysis, and only REINFORCE is used. There are no comparisons to alternative emergent-communication methods or stronger baselines. The human evaluation is limited in scale and uses metonymic interpretations that may not generalize. The paper also does not analyze convergence stability or equilibrium selection theoretically.

Overall, this is an interesting and well-presented initial study, but stronger baselines, richer communication protocols, and more rigorous semantic evaluation are needed.

title: Understanding deep learning requires rethinking generalization
abstract: Abstract:###Despite their massive size, successful deep artificial neural networks can exhibit a remarkably small difference between training and test performance. Conventional wisdom attributes small generalization error either to properties of the model family, or to the regularization techniques used during training. Through extensive systematic experiments, we show how these traditional approaches fail to explain why large neural networks generalize well in practice. Specifically, our experiments establish that state-of-the-art convolutional networks for image classification trained with stochastic gradient methods easily fit a random labeling of the training data. This phenomenon is qualitatively unaffected by explicit regularization, and occurs even if we replace the true images by completely unstructured random noise. We corroborate these experimental findings with a theoretical construction showing that simple depth two neural networks already have perfect finite sample expressivity as soon as the number of parameters exceeds the number of data points as it usually does in practice. We interpret our experimental findings by comparison with traditional models.
review:
This paper challenges classical statistical-learning explanations of generalization in deep networks. Through randomization tests on CIFAR10 and ImageNet, the authors show that standard CNN/MLP architectures trained with SGD can perfectly fit random labels, shuffled pixels, and Gaussian noise, with training time increasing only modestly. They further show that explicit regularization—weight decay, dropout, data augmentation—is neither necessary nor sufficient for good generalization, although it often helps. A finite-sample expressivity theorem demonstrates that a two-layer ReLU network with O(n+d) parameters can represent any labeling of n points. The paper concludes that VC dimension, Rademacher complexity, and uniform stability fail to distinguish networks that generalize from those that memorize, and that implicit regularization from SGD deserves attention.

Strengths: The experiments are simple, systematic, and convincing; the randomization test is a powerful diagnostic. The regularization ablations are informative, and the finite-sample result is a useful corrective to population-level expressivity analyses. The paper is clearly written and has had substantial impact by reframing generalization as an open theoretical problem.

Weaknesses: The work is primarily diagnostic and offers no complete alternative theory. The finite-sample construction is existential and does not explain trained networks. The linear/kernel analysis is suggestive but limited. Random-label fitting does not by itself invalidate data-dependent capacity measures or norm-based bounds. Experiments cover limited architectures and hyperparameter choices, and optimization ease is conflated with generalization. Broader architectures, training algorithms, and datasets would strengthen the claims.

Overall, an important and influential empirical critique, though it raises more questions than it resolves.

title: Neural Architecture Search with Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Abstract:###Neural networks are powerful and flexible models that work well for many difficult learning tasks in image, speech and natural language understanding. Despite their success, neural networks are still hard to design. In this paper, we use a recurrent network to generate the model descriptions of neural networks and train this RNN with reinforcement learning to maximize the expected accuracy of the generated architectures on a validation set. On the CIFAR-10 dataset, our method, starting from scratch, can design a novel network architecture that rivals the best human-invented architecture in terms of test set accuracy. Our CIFAR-10 model achieves a test error rate of 3.65, which is 0.09 percent better and 1.05x faster than the previous state-of-the-art model that used a similar architectural scheme. On the Penn Treebank dataset, our model can compose a novel recurrent cell that outperforms the widely-used LSTM cell, and other state-of-the-art baselines. Our cell achieves a test set perplexity of 62.4 on the Penn Treebank, which is 3.6 perplexity better than the previous state-of-the-art model. The cell can also be transferred to the character language modeling task on PTB and achieves a state-of-the-art perplexity of 1.214.
review:
This paper proposes Neural Architecture Search, using an RNN controller trained with REINFORCE to generate architecture descriptions, with validation accuracy as reward. It searches convolutional architectures for CIFAR-10 and recurrent cells for Penn Treebank, including skip connections and tree-structured cell predictions. Results match or outperform strong hand-designed models, e.g., 3.65% CIFAR-10 error and 62.4 PTB perplexity, with transfer to character language modeling and GNMT.

Strengths: The formulation is simple and general; tokenizing architectures lets one controller search variable-length spaces, and set-selection attention for skip connections is effective. Experiments are extensive for the era: CIFAR-10 and PTB, ablations with strides and pooling, a random-search control, and transfer. Discovering a cell that improves GNMT without tuning is notable.

Weaknesses: Search cost is enormous—hundreds of GPUs or CPUs and thousands of child trainings—limiting reproducibility and access. The reward uses short 50/35-epoch training and validation accuracy, which may favor cheap architectures over final performance; post-search grid search also confounds the contribution. The search space is manually constrained and misses modern operations. The random-search comparison is useful but limited. Statistical variability, seed effects, and compute-matched comparisons are underreported.

Overall, this is an influential proof of concept for RL-based architecture search, but efficiency and fair evaluation remain open.

title: Q-Prop: Sample-Efficient Policy Gradient with An Off-Policy Critic
abstract: Abstract:###Model-free deep reinforcement learning (RL) methods have been successful in a wide variety of simulated domains. However, a major obstacle facing deep RL in the real world is their high sample complexity. Batch policy gradient methods offer stable learning, but at the cost of high variance, which often requires large batches. TD-style methods, such as off-policy actor-critic and Q-learning, are more sample-efficient but biased, and often require costly hyperparameter sweeps to stabilize. In this work, we aim to develop methods that combine the stability of policy gradients with the efficiency of off-policy RL. We present Q-Prop, a policy gradient method that uses a Taylor expansion of the off-policy critic as a control variate. Q-Prop is both sample efficient and stable, and effectively combines the benefits of on-policy and off-policy methods. We analyze the connection between Q-Prop and existing model-free algorithms, and use control variate theory to derive two variants of Q-Prop with conservative and aggressive adaptation. We show that conservative Q-Prop provides substantial gains in sample efficiency over trust region policy optimization (TRPO) with generalized advantage estimation (GAE), and improves stability over deep deterministic policy gradient (DDPG), the state-of-the-art on-policy and off-policy methods, on OpenAI Gym*s MuJoCo continuous control environments.
review:
This paper proposes Q-Prop, a policy-gradient method that uses a first-order Taylor expansion of an off-policy critic as a control variate. The resulting estimator combines an analytic critic gradient with a residual REINFORCE term, preserving the on-policy policy-gradient structure while exploiting off-policy critic training. The authors derive a control-variate variance analysis and introduce adaptive, conservative, and aggressive variants. Experiments on MuJoCo continuous-control tasks show improved sample efficiency over TRPO-GAE and better stability than DDPG, with notable gains on Humanoid.

Strengths: The formulation is clean and well motivated, and the connection to actor-critic and compatible feature approximation is insightful. The control-variate perspective gives a principled way to reduce variance without introducing bias, and conservative Q-Prop is a practical, robust choice. Empirical results are promising and cover multiple tasks and batch sizes.

Weaknesses: Performance depends on the critic being correlated with the true advantage; the single-sample covariance estimate used for adaptation is noisy, and the conservative/aggressive rules are heuristic. The method adds critic-training overhead and several hyperparameters, complicating reproducibility. Experiments are limited to MuJoCo locomotion, with fairness concerns around DDPG reward scaling and baseline tuning. No convergence guarantees are provided, and the bias-variance trade-off under function approximation is not fully characterized.

Overall, this is a solid and useful contribution that bridges policy gradients and off-policy actor-critic learning, though broader evaluation and more robust adaptive schemes would strengthen it.

title: Learning to Act by Predicting the Future
abstract: Abstract:###We present an approach to sensorimotor control in immersive environments. Our approach utilizes a high-dimensional sensory stream and a lower-dimensional measurement stream. The cotemporal structure of these streams provides a rich supervisory signal, which enables training a sensorimotor control model by interacting with the environment. The model is trained using supervised learning techniques, but without extraneous supervision. It learns to act based on raw sensory input from a complex three-dimensional environment. The presented formulation enables learning without a fixed goal at training time, and pursuing dynamically changing goals at test time. We conduct extensive experiments in three-dimensional simulations based on the classical first-person game Doom. The results demonstrate that the presented approach outperforms sophisticated prior formulations, particularly on challenging tasks. The results also show that trained models successfully generalize across environments and goals. A model trained using the presented approach won the Full Deathmatch track of the Visual Doom AI Competition, which was held in previously unseen environments.
review:
This paper proposes Direct Future Prediction (DFP), a supervised approach to sensorimotor control that predicts future measurement changes conditioned on sensory input, current measurements, and a goal vector. Actions are selected by maximizing the goal-weighted predicted outcome. DFP is evaluated in ViZDoom across four scenarios, generalization environments, goal-agnostic training, and a competition, outperforming DQN, A3C, and DSR.

Strengths: the formulation is simple and well motivated; it replaces scalar reward with dense multidimensional measurements, supports goal-conditioned control, and trains without human demonstrations. Experiments are extensive for the domain, and results are strong, especially on complex Battle scenarios and unseen competition environments. The expectation/action-stream architecture and normalization are sensible. The paper is clearly written.

Weaknesses: evaluation is confined to Doom, so generality to other embodied tasks is unclear. Comparisons use a single architecture family and may be sensitive to hyperparameter tuning; DSR is only partially evaluated. The paper lacks detailed ablations isolating the expectation/action streams, temporal offsets, and measurement choice. Goal-agnostic results are promising but limited. Claims of outperforming state-of-the-art deep RL would be stronger with tuned baselines and more environments. Some design choices, such as experience memory and update schedule, are under-analyzed.

Overall, this is a strong empirical contribution with a clean, practical formulation. I recommend acceptance, with clarifications on ablations, baseline tuning, and generality.

title: On Large-Batch Training for Deep Learning: Generalization Gap and Sharp Minima
abstract: Abstract:###The stochastic gradient descent (SGD) method and its variants are algorithms of choice for many Deep Learning tasks. These methods operate in a small-batch regime wherein a fraction of the training data, say -- data points, is sampled to compute an approximation to the gradient. It has been observed in practice that when using a larger batch there is a degradation in the quality of the model, as measured by its ability to generalize. We investigate the cause for this generalization drop in the large-batch regime and present numerical evidence that supports the view that large-batch methods tend to converge to sharp minimizers of the training and testing functions---and as is well known, sharp minima lead to poorer generalization. In contrast, small-batch methods consistently converge to flat minimizers, and our experiments support a commonly held view that this is due to the inherent noise in the gradient estimation. We discuss several strategies to attempt to help large-batch methods eliminate this generalization gap.
review:
This paper studies why large-batch training harms generalization. It argues that large-batch (LB) methods converge to sharp minimizers, while small-batch methods find flatter minima. Evidence includes six MLP/CNN configurations on MNIST, TIMIT, and CIFAR-10/100; linear and curved parametric plots; a box-constrained sharpness metric in full space and random 100-D subspaces; batch-size sweeps; and warm-start experiments. Results consistently show much greater sharpness for LB solutions and a testing-accuracy gap, supporting the sharp/flat-minima hypothesis.

Strengths: the question is important for scalable training; experiments span multiple architectures and datasets; the sharpness metric is practical; warm-starting gives useful insight into when LB training can recover generalization; and the paper is clearly written.

Weaknesses: evidence is mostly correlational, not causal. The sharpness metric is heuristic and sensitive to epsilon, subspace dimension, and approximate L-BFGS maximization; no Hessian spectra or formal statistical tests are reported. Main comparisons use ADAM with fixed hyperparameters across batch sizes, so optimizer and learning-rate effects may confound results. The datasets and architectures are dated, limiting generality. Claims that LB methods remain near initialization are plausible but not conclusively demonstrated. Proposed remedies are preliminary and do not close the gap.

Overall, this is a valuable exploratory study with compelling empirical support but incomplete causal analysis. I recommend acceptance with revisions to clarify measurement choices, control hyperparameters, and broaden validation.

title: Semi-supervised Knowledge Transfer for Deep Learning from Private Training Data
abstract: Abstract:###Some machine learning applications involve training data that is sensitive, such as the medical histories of patients in a clinical trial. A model may inadvertently and implicitly store some of its training data; careful analysis of the model may therefore reveal sensitive information. To address this problem, we demonstrate a generally applicable approach to providing strong privacy guarantees for training data: Private Aggregation of Teacher Ensembles (PATE). The approach combines, in a black-box fashion, multiple models trained with disjoint datasets, such as records from different subsets of users. Because they rely directly on sensitive data, these models are not published, but instead used as **teachers** for a **student** model. The student learns to predict an output chosen by noisy voting among all of the teachers, and cannot directly access an individual teacher or the underlying data or parameters. The student*s privacy properties can be understood both intuitively (since no single teacher and thus no single dataset dictates the student*s training) and formally, in terms of differential privacy. These properties hold even if an adversary can not only query the student but also inspect its internal workings. Compared with previous work, the approach imposes only weak assumptions on how teachers are trained: it applies to any model, including non-convex models like DNNs. We achieve state-of-the-art privacy/utility trade-offs on MNIST and SVHN thanks to an improved privacy analysis and semi-supervised learning.
review:
This paper proposes PATE, a privacy-preserving knowledge-transfer framework in which an ensemble of teachers is trained on disjoint sensitive data partitions, and a student is trained on public unlabeled data labeled by noisy teacher voting. Combined with semi-supervised GAN training (PATE-G) and a moments-accountant privacy analysis, PATE achieves strong reported DP/utility trade-offs on MNIST and SVHN.

Strengths: the approach is clean, model-agnostic, and black-box with respect to teacher/student training. The privacy intuition is compelling, and the formal analysis, including data-dependent bounds for strong quorums, is a meaningful contribution. Results improve on prior DP deep learning baselines, and the semi-supervised component substantially reduces teacher queries. The paper is well written and includes useful ablations on ensemble size, noise, and vote gaps.

Weaknesses: evaluation is limited to MNIST and SVHN; generality to other modalities and non-i.i.d. sensitive data is untested. PATE assumes access to a suitable public unlabeled dataset, which may not hold in practice. Training 250 teachers is computationally expensive, and partitioning may hurt teachers on smaller datasets. The reported ε values are data-dependent, and the paper explicitly ignores the noise added for privately releasing ε; this overhead should be integrated or more carefully bounded. Comparisons to prior DP methods are not fully apples-to-apples. Strong-quorum dependence means utility may degrade on harder tasks. Teacher training privacy is not protected, only the deployed student.

Overall, this is a strong and influential contribution. I recommend acceptance with revisions clarifying assumptions, computational costs, and end-to-end privacy accounting.

title: Amortised MAP Inference for Image Super-resolution
abstract: Abstract:###Image super-resolution (SR) is an underdetermined inverse problem, where a large number of plausible high resolution images can explain the same downsampled image. Most current single image SR methods use empirical risk minimisation, often with a pixel-wise mean squared error (MSE) loss. However, the outputs from such methods tend to be blurry, over-smoothed and generally appear implausible. A more desirable approach would employ Maximum a Posteriori (MAP) inference, preferring solutions that always have a high probability under the image prior, and thus appear more plausible. Direct MAP estimation for SR is non-trivial, as it requires us to build a model for the image prior from samples. Here we introduce new methods for emph{amortised MAP inference} whereby we calculate the MAP estimate directly using a convolutional neural network. We first introduce a novel neural network architecture that performs a projection to the affine subspace of valid SR solutions ensuring that the high resolution output of the network is always consistent with the low resolution input. We show that, using this architecture, the amortised MAP inference problem reduces to minimising the cross-entropy between two distributions, similar to training generative models. We propose three methods to solve this optimisation problem: (1) Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN) (2) denoiser-guided SR which backpropagates gradient-estimates from denoising to train the network, and (3) a baseline method using a maximum-likelihood-trained image prior. Our experiments show that the GAN based approach performs best on real image data. Lastly, we establish a connection between GANs and amortised variational inference as in e.g. variational autoencoders.
review:
This paper formulates single-image super-resolution as amortised MAP inference, arguing that MSE/MAE training yields blurry, low-prior-probability outputs. The key idea is an affine projection layer that enforces exact consistency between the low-resolution input and the downsampled high-resolution output. This reduces MAP inference to minimizing cross-entropy between the model output distribution and the natural image prior. The authors propose AffGAN, denoiser-guided AffDG, and density-guided AffLL, plus an instance-noise trick for GAN stability.

Strengths: the formulation is clean and well motivated; the affine projection is simple, architecture-agnostic, and empirically improves consistency and optimization. The Swiss-roll experiment provides useful insight into why MSE/MAE fail and supports the MAP objective. AffGAN produces visibly sharper, more plausible results on grass textures and faces. The connection between GANs and amortised variational inference is interesting, and instance noise is a practical contribution.

Weaknesses: evaluation is largely qualitative, with no human perceptual study and limited quantitative metrics beyond MSE/SSIM and cross-entropy. AffDG and AffLL underperform and are not thoroughly analyzed. Comparisons are mostly to MSE/MAE baselines and soft-constrained variants, not to strong perceptual-loss SR methods. The GAN training stability and sensitivity to instance-noise schedules are under-discussed. The claim that AffGAN minimizes KL rather than cross-entropy is acknowledged but may weaken the MAP interpretation. Experiments are limited in scale and datasets.

Overall, this is a valuable conceptual and practical contribution. I recommend acceptance with more rigorous perceptual evaluation and analysis of the underperforming methods.

title: Learning Graphical State Transitions
abstract: Abstract:###Graph-structured data is important in modeling relationships between multiple entities, and can be used to represent states of the world as well as many data structures. Li et al. (2016) describe a model known as a Gated Graph Sequence Neural Network (GGS-NN) that produces sequences from graph-structured input. In this work I introduce the Gated Graph Transformer Neural Network (GGT-NN), an extension of GGS-NNs that uses graph-structured data as an intermediate representation. The model can learn to construct and modify graphs in sophisticated ways based on textual input, and also to use the graphs to produce a variety of outputs. For example, the model successfully learns to solve almost all of the bAbI tasks (Weston et al., 2016), and also discovers the rules governing graphical formulations of a simple cellular automaton and a family of Turing machines.
review:
This paper introduces Gated Graph Transformer Neural Networks (GGT-NN), extending GGS-NNs with differentiable graph transformations that can construct and modify graph-structured intermediate states. The model is evaluated on bAbI, a cellular automaton, and Turing-machine tasks. The main contribution is a flexible, composable set of transformations—node addition, state update, edge update, propagation, and attention-based aggregation—that support graph-to-graph and text-to-graph processing.

Strengths: the formulation is clearly presented, the transformations are modular, and the differentiable graph encoding with node strengths and soft connectivity is sensible. Results on bAbI are strong: with direct reference, the model solves most tasks with few examples and reaches 100% on eleven. Demonstrating learned update rules for cellular automata and Turing machines is interesting and supports the claim that the model can learn complex state transitions.

Weaknesses: the paper relies heavily on task-specific supervision of intermediate graphs, which limits claims of learning latent graph structure from text alone. The direct-reference mechanism injects substantial prior knowledge about node types and is not ablated thoroughly. bAbI is a narrow, synthetic benchmark, and comparisons with prior work are not fully controlled in architecture or training budget. The cellular automaton and Turing-machine experiments are only briefly described in the main text. The single-author scope leaves several design choices and failure modes, notably task 17, underexplored, and no code or statistical variability is reported.

Overall, this is a promising and clearly written contribution with strong synthetic results, but broader validation and cleaner ablations are needed. I recommend acceptance with revisions.

title: Maximum Entropy Flow Networks
abstract: Abstract:###Maximum entropy modeling is a flexible and popular framework for formulating statistical models given partial knowledge. In this paper, rather than the traditional method of optimizing over the continuous density directly, we learn a smooth and invertible transformation that maps a simple distribution to the desired maximum entropy distribution. Doing so is nontrivial in that the objective being maximized (entropy) is a function of the density itself. By exploiting recent developments in normalizing flow networks, we cast the maximum entropy problem into a finite-dimensional constrained optimization, and solve the problem by combining stochastic optimization with the augmented Lagrangian method. Simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, and applications to finance and computer vision show the flexibility and accuracy of using maximum entropy flow networks.
review:
This paper introduces Maximum Entropy Flow Networks (MEFN), which reformulate continuous maximum-entropy modeling as learning a normalizing flow that maps a simple Gaussian to a distribution satisfying moment constraints while maximizing entropy. The constrained problem is solved with an augmented Lagrangian method and stochastic optimization, enabling tractable density evaluation and iid sampling.

Strengths: the formulation is clean and well motivated; it directly addresses key weaknesses of Gibbs-distribution approaches—normalizing constants, sampling, and entropy estimation. The Dirichlet ground-truth experiment is convincing, including MMD comparisons and the useful demonstration that moment matching alone yields poor diversity. The texture-synthesis application is compelling: MEFN matches texture cost while producing higher entropy and more varied RGB statistics than a texture-network baseline. The method is practical and broadly applicable.

Weaknesses: convergence of the augmented Lagrangian is not rigorously established for neural-network parameterizations, and the paper acknowledges this. Empirical validation is somewhat limited: the finance application is relegated to an appendix, and texture synthesis uses a single texture with mostly qualitative or indirect metrics. The entropy estimator’s bias and variance, sensitivity to flow architecture and penalty schedule, and behavior under high-dimensional or poorly specified supports are underexplored. Comparisons to alternative ME solvers are limited, and finite network capacity means the true ME distribution is only approximated.

Overall, this is an original and useful contribution with strong conceptual grounding. I recommend acceptance with revisions expanding quantitative evaluation and analysis of convergence and robustness.

title: Topology and Geometry of Half-Rectified Network Optimization
abstract: Abstract:###The loss surface of deep neural networks has recently attracted interest in the optimization and machine learning communities as a prime example of high-dimensional non-convex problem. Some insights were recently gained using spin glass models and mean-field approximations, but at the expense of strongly simplifying the nonlinear nature of the model. In this work, we do not make any such approximation and study conditions on the data distribution and model architecture that prevent the existence of bad local minima. Our theoretical work quantifies and formalizes two important folklore facts: (i) the landscape of deep linear networks has a radically different topology from that of deep half-rectified ones, and (ii) that the energy landscape in the non-linear case is fundamentally controlled by the interplay between the smoothness of the data distribution and model over-parametrization. Our main theoretical contribution is to prove that half-rectified single layer networks are asymptotically connected, and we provide explicit bounds that reveal the aforementioned interplay. The conditioning of gradient descent is the next challenge we address. We study this question through the geometry of the level sets, and we introduce an algorithm to efficiently estimate the regularity of such sets on large-scale networks. Our empirical results show that these level sets remain connected throughout all the learning phase, suggesting a near convex behavior, but they become exponentially more curvy as the energy level decays, in accordance to what is observed in practice with very low curvature attractors.
review:
This paper studies the topology and geometry of loss surfaces in half-rectified networks. The theoretical contribution is to characterize connectedness of level sets, showing that deep linear networks have connected level sets, while half-rectified networks are generally disconnected but become asymptotically connected under overparameterization. The paper also introduces Dynamic String Sampling, a dynamic-programming heuristic for approximating geodesics between trained models and estimating the regularity of level sets empirically on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Penn Treebank.

Strengths: the paper addresses an important question with a useful mix of theory and experiment. The linear-case results are clean, and the half-rectified analysis gives explicit bounds linking data smoothness and overparameterization. The counterexample clarifying why universal connectedness cannot hold without assumptions is valuable. The empirical finding that level sets remain connected but become more elongated as loss decreases is interesting and consistent with practice.

Weaknesses: the main connectedness result is asymptotic and relies on a mixed l1/l2 regularization that the authors acknowledge is a proof artifact. The bounds are likely pessimistic and do not yield practical finite-sample guarantees. Dynamic String Sampling is heuristic and cannot certify disconnection; its runtime and stopping criteria are not fully analyzed. Experiments are limited to mid-scale architectures, and the geodesic estimates are indirect. The connection between level-set geometry and optimization conditioning remains suggestive rather than conclusive.

Overall, this is a solid theoretical and empirical contribution. I recommend acceptance with revisions clarifying assumptions, limitations, and algorithm reliability.

title: Paying More Attention to Attention: Improving the Performance of Convolutional Neural Networks via Attention Transfer
abstract: Abstract:###Attention plays a critical role in human visual experience. Furthermore, it has recently been demonstrated that attention can also play an important role in the context of applying artificial neural networks to a variety of tasks from fields such as computer vision and NLP. In this work we show that, by properly defining attention for convolutional neural networks, we can actually use this type of information in order to significantly improve the performance of a student CNN network by forcing it to mimic the attention maps of a powerful teacher network. To that end, we propose several novel methods of transferring attention, showing consistent improvement across a variety of datasets and convolutional neural network architectures.
review:
This paper proposes attention transfer (AT), a teacher-student training method that encourages a student CNN to mimic a stronger teacher’s spatial attention maps. It defines activation-based attention via channel statistics of feature tensors and gradient-based attention via input gradients, adding normalized attention-matching losses to the standard classification objective. Experiments on CIFAR-10 with NIN and Wide ResNet architectures show consistent improvements over student baselines, with AT combined with knowledge distillation performing best. The paper also reports that transferring attention maps outperforms transferring full activations, and studies several mapping functions and gradient-based variants.

Strengths: the idea is simple, intuitive, and computationally lightweight for activation-based AT. Results are consistent across teacher-student pairs and architectures, and ablations on attention mapping functions and full-activation transfer are useful. The gradient-based formulation and symmetry regularization are interesting extensions.

Weaknesses: attention maps are heuristic, with no theoretical justification for why they transfer better than full activations. Gradient-based AT is evaluated only on a thin NIN/CIFAR-10 setting with single runs and no batch normalization, limiting conclusions. Large-scale ImageNet results are only partially presented in the excerpt. Hyperparameter sensitivity, especially β and normalization, is under-analyzed. Comparisons focus on KD and baselines rather than other hint-based distillation methods.

Overall, this is a practical, well-supported contribution with clear empirical gains. I recommend acceptance, with revisions clarifying limitations and large-scale validation.

title: Learning Visual Servoing with Deep Features and Fitted Q-Iteration
abstract: Abstract:###Visual servoing involves choosing actions that move a robot in response to observations from a camera, in order to reach a goal configuration in the world. Standard visual servoing approaches typically rely on manually designed features and analytical dynamics models, which limits their generalization capability and often requires extensive application-specific feature and model engineering. In this work, we study how learned visual features, learned predictive dynamics models, and reinforcement learning can be combined to learn visual servoing mechanisms. We focus on target following, with the goal of designing algorithms that can learn a visual servo using low amounts of data of the target in question, to enable quick adaptation to new targets. Our approach is based on servoing the camera in the space of learned visual features, rather than image pixels or manually-designed keypoints. We demonstrate that standard deep features, in our case taken from a model trained for object classification, can be used together with a bilinear predictive model to learn an effective visual servo that is robust to visual variation, changes in viewing angle and appearance, and occlusions. A key component of our approach is to use a sample-efficient fitted Q-iteration algorithm to learn which features are best suited for the task at hand. We show that we can learn an effective visual servo on a complex synthetic car following benchmark using just 20 training trajectory samples for reinforcement learning. We demonstrate substantial improvement over a conventional approach based on image pixels or hand-designed keypoints, and we show an improvement in sample-efficiency of more than two orders of magnitude over standard model-free deep reinforcement learning algorithms. Videos are available at http://rll.berkeley.edu/visual_servoing.
review:
This paper presents a visual servoing method that combines pretrained VGG features, a multiscale bilinear dynamics model, and fitted Q-iteration (FQI) to learn feature weights. The servoing policy greedily minimizes weighted predicted feature error, and FQI learns weights efficiently by exploiting the quadratic structure of the policy. Experiments on a synthetic car-following benchmark show strong performance with only 20 training trajectories, large gains over pixel/keypoint baselines, and more than two orders of magnitude better sample efficiency than model-free deep RL.

Strengths: the approach is well motivated and cleanly combines pretrained perception with simple predictive dynamics, avoiding expensive end-to-end RL. The multiscale dilated VGG representation is sensible for preserving spatial information, and the FQI formulation is sample-efficient and analytically tractable. Ablations across VGG layers, pixel baselines, and TRPO/CEM comparisons are informative. Generalization to novel cars is demonstrated.

Weaknesses: evaluation is limited to a synthetic CitySim3D benchmark, with no real-robot validation. The bilinear and locally connected dynamics assumptions may not hold under complex camera motion, occlusion, or lighting. Dynamics training uses a hand-coded exploration policy, which may limit applicability. Comparisons with TRPO and CEM are somewhat affected by differing sample budgets and implementation choices. The method’s sensitivity to feature standardization, scale selection, and FQI hyperparameters is underexplored. The core components are largely existing, though their combination is effective.

Overall, this is a solid, practical contribution with compelling sample-efficiency results. I recommend acceptance with revisions expanding real-world validation and robustness analysis.

title: Stochastic Neural Networks for Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Abstract:###Deep reinforcement learning has achieved many impressive results in recent years. However, tasks with sparse rewards or long horizons continue to pose significant challenges. To tackle these important problems, we propose a general framework that first learns useful skills in a pre-training environment, and then leverages the acquired skills for learning faster in downstream tasks. Our approach brings together some of the strengths of intrinsic motivation and hierarchical methods: the learning of useful skill is guided by a single proxy reward, the design of which requires very minimal domain knowledge about the downstream tasks. Then a high-level policy is trained on top of these skills, providing a significant improvement of the exploration and allowing to tackle sparse rewards in the downstream tasks. To efficiently pre-train a large span of skills, we use Stochastic Neural Networks combined with an information-theoretic regularizer. Our experiments show that this combination is effective in learning a wide span of interpretable skills in a sample-efficient way, and can significantly boost the learning performance uniformly across a wide range of downstream tasks.
review:
This paper proposes a hierarchical RL framework that pre-trains a diverse skill set using stochastic neural networks (SNNs) with a mutual-information regularizer, then trains a high-level manager over frozen skills for downstream sparse-reward tasks. Skills are learned in a simple pre-training environment using only a generic proxy reward. Experiments on Swimmer maze and Gather tasks show improved exploration and sample efficiency, with interpretable skills as the latent code varies.

Strengths: the framework is general and requires minimal downstream domain knowledge. Combining SNNs, bilinear latent integration, and an MI bonus is well motivated and empirically effective for producing diverse skills. The manager design is simple, and using TRPO for both phases avoids extensive tuning. Skill-visitation visualizations and ablations are useful, and gains are shown across several sparse-reward tasks.

Weaknesses: evaluation is limited mainly to MuJoCo Swimmer tasks and a few mazes/Gather, so generality to higher-dimensional robots, manipulation, and real-world settings is unclear. The proxy reward still encodes task-relevant prior knowledge, and the MI regularizer relies on discretized center-of-mass coordinates, which may not scale. Low-level skills are frozen downstream, leaving joint adaptation unexplored. Comparisons focus on exploration baselines rather than strong hierarchical RL alternatives, and sensitivity to number of skills, commitment horizon, and MI coefficient is under-analyzed.

Overall, this is a solid, practical contribution with promising results. I recommend acceptance with revisions expanding evaluation and robustness/scalability analysis.

title: Nonparametric Neural Networks
