abstract: Abstract:###Automatically determining the optimal size of a neural network for a given task without prior information currently requires an expensive global search and training many networks from scratch. In this paper, we address the problem of automatically finding a good network size during a single training cycle. We introduce {it nonparametric neural networks}, a non-probabilistic framework for conducting optimization over all possible network sizes and prove its soundness when network growth is limited via an penalty. We train networks under this framework by continuously adding new units while eliminating redundant units via an penalty. We employ a novel optimization algorithm, which we term ``Adaptive Radial-Angular Gradient Descent** or {it AdaRad}, and obtain promising results.
review:
This paper introduces nonparametric neural networks, a framework for selecting network width during a single training run by growing and pruning hidden units. It proves that fan-in or fan-out ℓp regularization yields a finite global training-error minimum, and proposes AdaRad, a radial-angular optimizer, plus CapNorm to make shrinkage compatible with normalization. Experiments on MNIST, rectangles, and convex datasets compare nonparametric networks against parametric baselines of similar size and tuned parametric networks.

Strengths: the formulation is clean and theoretically grounded; the proof provides a useful justification for bounded growth under ℓp penalties. The training scheme—adding zero units and eliminating redundant ones via ℓ2 shrinkage—is simple and practical. AdaRad is a novel and reasonably motivated optimizer that separates radial shrinkage from angular learning. Results on MNIST and rectangles are promising, showing competitive or better accuracy with fewer parameters.

Weaknesses: empirical evaluation is limited to small datasets and shallow networks with two hidden layers, so scalability to deep convolutional or large-scale models is untested. Performance on the convex dataset is poor, revealing sensitivity to task structure. Results depend heavily on λ, step sizes, and unit-addition schedules, and the reported representative runs weaken statistical conclusions. CapNorm falls outside the theoretical assumptions, and comparisons to modern pruning or NAS methods are absent. The computational overhead of repeated unit addition/removal is also not fully analyzed.

Overall, this is an interesting proof-of-concept with a solid theoretical core. I recommend acceptance with revisions expanding experiments, ablations, and scalability analysis.

title: Distributed Second-Order Optimization using Kronecker-Factored Approximations
abstract: Abstract:###As more computational resources become available, machine learning researchers train ever larger neural networks on millions of data points using stochastic gradient descent (SGD). Although SGD scales well in terms of both the size of dataset and the number of parameters of the model, it has rapidly diminishing returns as parallel computing resources increase. Second-order optimization methods have an affinity for well-estimated gradients and large mini-batches, and can therefore benefit much more from parallel computation in principle. Unfortunately, they often employ severe approximations to the curvature matrix in order to scale to large models with millions of parameters, limiting their effectiveness in practice versus well-tuned SGD with momentum. The recently proposed K-FAC method(Martens and Grosse, 2015) uses a stronger and more sophisticated curvature approximation, and has been shown to make much more per-iteration progress than SGD, while only introducing a modest overhead. In this paper, we develop a version of K-FAC that distributes the computation of gradients and additional quantities required by K-FAC across multiple machines, thereby taking advantage of methodâ€™s superior scaling to large mini-batches and mitigating its additional overheads. We provide a Tensorflow implementation of our approach which is easy to use and can be applied to many existing codebases without modification. Additionally, we develop several algorithmic enhancements to K-FAC which can improve its computational performance for very large models. Finally, we show that our distributed K-FAC method speeds up training of various state-of-the-art ImageNet classification models by a factor of two compared to Batch Normalization(Ioffe and Szegedy, 2015).
review:
This paper presents a distributed asynchronous implementation of K-FAC for large-scale neural network training. It distributes gradient computation, Fisher statistics, and inverse computation across workers, and introduces a doubly-factored Kronecker approximation for large convolutional/fully connected layers, plus generalized factored Tikhonov damping and a Fisher-norm trust-region step-size rule. A TensorFlow implementation is provided. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet report faster wall-clock training and roughly 2x speedup over improved Batch Normalization for several ImageNet models.

Strengths: the system design is practical and well motivated; asynchronously computing Fisher inverses and statistics addresses key K-FAC overheads. The doubly-factored approximation extends K-FAC to layers with very large input feature maps, and the damping generalization is useful. Experiments demonstrate real wall-clock gains and provide implementation details likely valuable to practitioners.

Weaknesses: distributed experiments are simulated on a single 8-GPU server, so multi-machine scalability and communication costs are not validated. Asynchronous staleness is not theoretically or empirically characterized. Meta-parameters were hand-tuned per method, and comparisons are limited to classification and a few architectures. The doubly-factored rank-1 approximation lacks error analysis, and wall-clock results are implementation-dependent. No convergence guarantees are provided.

Overall, this is a strong systems-oriented contribution with convincing practical speedups. I recommend acceptance, with revisions clarifying scalability, staleness effects, and approximation error.

title: Pruning Filters for Efficient ConvNets
abstract: Abstract:###The success of CNNs in various applications is accompanied by a significant increase in the computation and parameter storage costs. Recent efforts toward reducing these overheads involve pruning and compressing the weights of various layers without hurting original accuracy. However, magnitude-based pruning of weights reduces a significant number of parameters from the fully connected layers and may not adequately reduce the computation costs in the convolutional layers due to irregular sparsity in the pruned networks. We present an acceleration method for CNNs, where we prune filters from CNNs that are identified as having a small effect on the output accuracy. By removing whole filters in the network together with their connecting feature maps, the computation costs are reduced significantly. In contrast to pruning weights, this approach does not result in sparse connectivity patterns. Hence, it does not need the support of sparse convolution libraries and can work with existing efficient BLAS libraries for dense matrix multiplications. We show that even simple filter pruning techniques can reduce inference costs for VGG-16 by up to 34% and ResNet-110 by up to 38% on CIFAR10 while regaining close to the original accuracy by retraining the networks.
review:
This paper proposes structured filter pruning for efficient CNNs. Filters with small ℓ1 norm are removed together with their feature maps and corresponding kernels in the next layer, yielding dense, accelerated networks without sparse libraries. The authors describe single-layer sensitivity analysis, independent and greedy multi-layer pruning, ResNet shortcut handling, and one-shot/iterative retraining. Experiments on VGG-16 and ResNet-56/110 on CIFAR-10 and ResNet-34 on ImageNet report FLOP reductions of roughly 10–38% with near-original accuracy.

Strengths: the method is simple, practical, and directly reduces computation rather than only parameter count. The ℓ1 criterion is data-free and easy to implement. Handling residual shortcut constraints is useful, and comparisons against random, largest-filter, and activation-based pruning support the chosen criterion. The one-shot retraining strategy is appealing for deep networks.

Weaknesses: evaluation is limited to older architectures and small-scale CIFAR/ImageNet settings, with no measured wall-clock latency or energy. The ℓ1 heuristic is weakly justified theoretically, and sensitivity analysis still requires per-layer or per-stage pruning ratios. Comparisons to modern structured-pruning and regularization-based methods are absent. The paper notes that training pruned models from scratch performs worse, but does not analyze why or whether iterative pruning would close the gap. Sensitivity to retraining budget and hyperparameters is also underexplored.

Overall, this is a solid, practical contribution with clear empirical benefits. I recommend acceptance, with revisions adding latency measurements, broader baselines, and more analysis of pruning criteria and retraining.

title: Learning to Generate Samples from Noise through Infusion Training
abstract: Abstract:###In this work, we investigate a novel training procedure to learn a generative model as the transition operator of a Markov chain, such that, when applied repeatedly on an unstructured random noise sample, it will denoise it into a sample that matches the target distribution from the training set. The novel training procedure to learn this progressive denoising operation involves sampling from a slightly different chain than the model chain used for generation in the absence of a denoising target. In the training chain we infuse information from the training target example that we would like the chains to reach with a high probability. The thus learned transition operator is able to produce quality and varied samples in a small number of steps. Experiments show competitive results compared to the samples generated with a basic Generative Adversarial Net.
review:
This paper proposes infusion training for generative modeling: learn a Markov transition operator that progressively denoises unstructured input-space noise into data samples. During training, an auxiliary infusion chain slightly biases samples toward a target training example, producing useful denoising inputs without requiring an explicit inference network. The model is evaluated on MNIST, TFD, CIFAR-10, and CelebA, with qualitative samples, Parzen-window estimates, likelihood bounds, and Inception scores.

Strengths: the method is conceptually clean and avoids latent-space inference, using input-space transitions and a simple heuristic proposal. The infusion-chain idea is novel and well motivated, and the connection to denoising autoencoders, GSNs, and diffusion is clearly discussed. The paper provides likelihood lower-bound and importance-sampling estimates, and the sampling procedure is efficient with few steps. Qualitative samples are sharp, and CIFAR-10 Inception scores are competitive with an unsupervised GAN baseline.

Weaknesses: quantitative evaluation is limited, with Parzen-window estimates known to be unreliable and Inception scores below semi-supervised GAN baselines. Comparisons to modern diffusion, VAE, and strong GAN baselines are absent. The likelihood bounds appear loose, and no variance analysis is reported. Infusion rate, number of steps, and sampling-step mismatch are tuned per dataset without ablation. The chain’s theoretical properties and mode coverage are underexplored.

Overall, this is an interesting and promising contribution. I recommend acceptance with revisions strengthening quantitative comparisons, ablations, and analysis of mode coverage.

title: FILTER SHAPING FOR CONVOLUTIONAL NEURAL NETWORKS
abstract: Abstract:###Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are powerful tools for classification of visual inputs. An important property of CNN is its restriction to local connections and sharing of local weights among different locations. In this paper, we consider the definition of appropriate local neighborhoods in CNN. We provide a theoretical analysis that justifies the traditional square filter used in CNN for analyzing natural images. The analysis also provides a principle for designing customized filter shapes for application domains that do not resemble natural images. We propose an approach that automatically designs multiple layers of different customized filter shapes by repeatedly solving lasso problems. It is applied to customize the filter shape for both bioacoustic applications and gene sequence analysis applications. In those domains with small sample sizes we demonstrate that the customized filters achieve superior classification accuracy, improved convergence behavior in training and reduced sensitivity to hyperparameters.
review:
This paper proposes data-driven filter shaping for CNNs in domains unlike natural images. It uses correlation analysis and a Gaussian-complexity bound to justify square filters for images, then solves LASSO/group-LASSO problems to derive layer-specific filter shapes for spectrograms and gene sequences. Experiments on hummingbird wingbeats, bird songs, and rSNP prediction show accuracy gains, faster convergence, and reduced hyperparameter sensitivity in small-sample settings.

Strengths: the motivation is clear and timely; extending CNNs beyond natural images is valuable. The correlation-based principle is intuitive, and the Gaussian-complexity argument provides useful justification. The method is simple to implement, and the discrete-data group-LASSO extension is sensible. Empirical results on bioacoustic and genomic tasks are promising, with gains especially for wingbeats and under reduced training data.

Weaknesses: theoretical support is limited to two-layer networks and does not establish guarantees for deep CNNs. The LASSO-derived shapes are heuristic, and selection depends on DFMax/threshold choices. Evaluation covers only three small datasets and limited baselines; comparisons to modern architectures, data augmentation, transfer learning, and alternative structured filters are absent. Gains on rSNP are modest, and statistical significance is not reported. The average-pooling approximation for max-pooling is also weakly justified. Overall, this is a useful and practical contribution, but broader validation and stronger theory are needed. I recommend acceptance with revisions.

title: Normalizing the Normalizers: Comparing and Extending Network Normalization Schemes
abstract: Abstract:###Normalization techniques have only recently begun to be exploited in supervised learning tasks. Batch normalization exploits mini-batch statistics to normalize the activations. This was shown to speed up training and result in better models. However its success has been very limited when dealing with recurrent neural networks. On the other hand, layer normalization normalizes the activations across all activities within a layer. This was shown to work well in the recurrent setting. In this paper we propose a unified view of normalization techniques, as forms of divisive normalization, which includes layer and batch normalization as special cases. Our second contribution is the finding that a small modification to these normalization schemes, in conjunction with a sparse regularizer on the activations, leads to significant benefits over standard normalization techniques. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our unified divisive normalization framework in the context of convolutional neural nets and recurrent neural networks, showing improvements over baselines in image classification, language modeling as well as super-resolution.
review:
This paper presents a unified view of normalization methods as divisive normalization, with batch and layer normalization as special cases defined by different summation/suppression fields. It proposes two simple extensions: a smoothing term σ in the denominator and an L1 regularizer on centered pre-normalization activations. These modifications are applied to BN, LN, and local divisive normalization (DN), and evaluated on CIFAR-10/100 classification, Penn Treebank language modeling, and image super-resolution.

Strengths: the unification is clean and conceptually useful, clarifying how normalization schemes differ mainly in their statistics range and smoothing. The σ term is well motivated and empirically helpful; the L1 activation regularizer consistently improves all variants. DN avoids batch statistics and performs comparably to BN on CIFAR while outperforming LN, and the ResNet analysis showing learned σ decreasing with depth is interesting. The paper covers CNNs, RNNs, and super-resolution, demonstrating breadth.

Weaknesses: empirical gains are modest in places, and DN underperforms BN in ResNet experiments, limiting claims of superiority. Evaluation uses relatively small datasets and older architectures, with limited comparisons to recent normalization methods. The L1 regularizer’s decorrelation explanation is plausible but not rigorously established. DN’s local-window computation and extra hyperparameters may add overhead and tuning burden. Statistical variability is not fully reported, and RNN/super-resolution results are less thoroughly analyzed in the main text.

Overall, this is a useful conceptual and practical contribution. I recommend acceptance with revisions strengthening large-scale comparisons, overhead analysis, and theoretical justification.

title: Multilayer Recurrent Network Models of Primate Retinal Ganglion Cell Responses
abstract: Abstract:###Developing accurate predictive models of sensory neurons is vital to understanding sensory processing and brain computations. The current standard approach to modeling neurons is to start with simple models and to incrementally add interpretable features. An alternative approach is to start with a more complex model that captures responses accurately, and then probe the fitted model structure to understand the neural computations. Here, we show that a multitask recurrent neural network (RNN) framework provides the flexibility necessary to model complex computations of neurons that cannot be captured by previous methods. Specifically, multilayer recurrent neural networks that share features across neurons outperform generalized linear models (GLMs) in predicting the spiking responses of parasol ganglion cells in the primate retina to natural images. The networks achieve good predictive performance given surprisingly small amounts of experimental training data. Additionally, we present a novel GLM-RNN hybrid model with separate spatial and temporal processing components which provides insights into the aspects of retinal processing better captured by the recurrent neural networks.
review:
This paper models primate retinal ganglion cell responses to natural movies using multilayer recurrent neural networks with shared feature representations across neurons. The authors compare against LN and GLM baselines, analyze a GLM-RNN hybrid to separate spatial and temporal nonlinearities, and show good predictive performance with modest training data and multitask sharing.

Strengths: the application is compelling and the empirical results are clear. Shared two-layer RNNs outperform GLMs/LNs for both ON and OFF parasol cells across two experiments, with gains across almost all neurons. The multitask comparison is well motivated, and the hybrid model provides useful insight that temporal nonlinearities account for much of the improvement. The data-efficiency analysis is practically important for neuroscience experiments. The paper is generally well written and appropriately cautious about interpretability.

Weaknesses: evaluation is limited to two retinas and parasol cells, with a small criteria-passing subset used for reported metrics. Neuron-to-neuron correlations and population coding are not modeled. Training uses MSE rather than a Poisson likelihood, which is somewhat mismatched to spiking data. Architecture and hyperparameter search are limited, and the RNN remains largely black-box. Comparisons to other nonlinear neural models are modest. Statistical variability across animals and recording conditions is not fully characterized.

Overall, this is a valuable and well-executed contribution at the neuroscience–ML interface. I recommend acceptance with revisions clarifying population generalization, likelihood-based training, and interpretability.

title: Improving Generative Adversarial Networks with Denoising Feature Matching
abstract: Abstract:###We propose an augmented training procedure for generative adversarial networks designed to address shortcomings of the original by directing the generator towards probable configurations of abstract discriminator features. We estimate and track the distribution of these features, as computed from data, with a denoising auto-encoder, and use it to propose high-level targets for the generator. We combine this new loss with the original and evaluate the hybrid criterion on the task of unsupervised image synthesis from datasets comprising a diverse set of visual categories, noting a qualitative and quantitative improvement in the ``objectness** of the resulting samples.
review:
This paper proposes denoising feature matching, an auxiliary GAN generator objective. A denoising autoencoder is trained online on discriminator features from real data, and its reconstruction of generator features provides a high-probability target for the generator. Combined with the standard adversarial loss, this yields better unsupervised samples on CIFAR-10, STL-10, and ImageNet at low resolution, with Inception scores improving over unsupervised baselines (e.g., 7.72 on CIFAR-10 versus 4.36 for the unsupervised improved GAN) and apparent robustness to collapse.

Strengths: the idea is simple, well motivated, and orthogonal to many GAN extensions. The connection to score estimation via denoising autoencoders is clearly explained, and the invertible-feature analysis, while idealized, provides useful intuition. Experiments span three datasets of increasing diversity, and gains on STL-10 and ImageNet are demonstrated against matched baselines. The method does not require labels, addressing an important limitation of semi-supervised GAN improvements.

Weaknesses: the approach remains largely heuristic. The denoiser is trained on a non-stationary feature distribution, so targets are stale and theoretical guarantees do not apply. Sensitivity to corruption noise, λ_denoise, denoiser depth, and architecture is under-analyzed. Evaluation relies heavily on the Inception score, which is imperfect and does not directly measure mode coverage or likelihood. Comparisons are limited, and CIFAR-10 still trails semi-supervised GANs. Experiments are low-resolution and computationally unspecified. No mode-collapse metrics or ablation of the adversarial term are reported.

Overall, this is a useful and empirically promising contribution. I recommend acceptance with revisions strengthening ablations, evaluation, and analysis of non-stationarity.

title: Efficient Vector Representation for Documents through Corruption
abstract: Abstract:###We present an efficient document representation learning framework, Document Vector through Corruption (Doc2VecC). Doc2VecC represents each document as a simple average of word embeddings. It ensures a representation generated as such captures the semantic meanings of the document during learning. A corruption model is included, which introduces a data-dependent regularization that favors informative or rare words while forcing the embeddings of common and non-discriminative ones to be close to zero. Doc2VecC produces significantly better word embeddings than Word2Vec. We compare Doc2VecC with several state-of-the-art document representation learning algorithms. The simple model architecture introduced by Doc2VecC matches or out-performs the state-of-the-art in generating high-quality document representations for sentiment analysis, document classification as well as semantic relatedness tasks. The simplicity of the model enables training on billions of words per hour on a single machine. At the same time, the model is very efficient in generating representations of unseen documents at test time.
review:
This paper proposes Doc2VecC, an efficient document representation framework that represents a document as the average of learned word embeddings. During training, a document-level context is formed from a randomly corrupted bag-of-words, with unbiased mask-out corruption scaled by 1/(1−q). The model predicts target words from local context plus this global corrupted document context, using negative sampling. The authors show that corruption acts as a data-dependent regularizer favoring informative or rare words while suppressing common non-discriminative words, and that document vectors can be generated at test time by simple averaging. Experiments on IMDB sentiment analysis, document classification, and semantic relatedness show competitive or better accuracy than bag-of-words, denoising autoencoders, Word2Vec averaging/IDF, Paragraph Vectors, and Skip-thought vectors, while training and inference are much faster than Paragraph Vectors.

Strengths: the model is simple, scalable, and test-time efficient; the corruption-based regularization is well motivated and supported by both analysis and qualitative word-embedding inspection. Results are competitive and training time is attractive.

Weaknesses: evaluation is somewhat narrow, relying on linear classifiers and limited datasets. The second-order Taylor approximation justifying the regularizer is heuristic, and sensitivity to corruption rate, negative sampling, and vocabulary cutoff is only briefly examined. Comparisons to Paragraph Vectors and Skip-thought are not fully controlled in dimensionality or training data. The paper lacks ablation isolating local versus global context and deeper error analysis. Statistical significance is not reported.

Overall, this is a useful and practical contribution with clear efficiency benefits. I recommend acceptance with revisions expanding ablations, datasets, and analysis.

title: Learning Invariant Feature Spaces to Transfer Skills with Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Abstract:###People can learn a wide range of tasks from their own experience, but can also learn from observing other creatures. This can accelerate acquisition of new skills even when the observed agent differs substantially from the learning agent in terms of morphology. In this paper, we examine how reinforcement learning algorithms can transfer knowledge between morphologically different agents (e.g., different robots). We introduce a problem formulation where twp agents are tasked with learning multiple skills by sharing information. Our method uses the skills that were learned by both agents to train invariant feature spaces that can then be used to transfer other skills from one agent to another. The process of learning these invariant feature spaces can be viewed as a kind of ``analogy making,** or implicit learning of partial correspondences between two distinct domains. We evaluate our transfer learning algorithm in two simulated robotic manipulation skills, and illustrate that we can transfer knowledge between simulated robotic arms with different numbers of links, as well as simulated arms with different actuation mechanisms, where one robot is torque-driven while the other is tendon-driven.
review:
This paper studies transfer between morphologically different agents by learning a shared invariant feature space from previously acquired proxy skills. Each agent’s state is mapped through a separate encoder, trained with a contrastive pairing loss plus reconstruction decoders to avoid degenerate embeddings. Correspondences are obtained by time alignment or DTW-based alternating optimization, and transfer is implemented as reward shaping that matches target trajectories to source trajectories in the shared space. Experiments in MuJoCo show transfer from a 3-link to a 4-link arm and across torque- versus tendon-driven actuation, outperforming no-transfer, random projection, CCA, KCCA, UMA, and direct state-mapping baselines in sparse-reward manipulation tasks.

Strengths: the problem is important and well motivated; avoiding direct state-to-state mappings is sensible for morphological differences. The contrastive-plus-autoencoder objective is simple and helps prevent collapse, and the sparse-reward button-pressing setting makes the transfer benefit convincing. Comparisons to linear and kernel alignment methods are useful, as is the use of multiple proxy tasks.

Weaknesses: evaluation is limited to two simulated robot pairs and a few tasks, with no real-robot validation. The method assumes access to source optimal trajectories and reasonable proxy-task correspondences; DTW and time alignment may fail under different speeds or task executions. Sensitivity to the transfer-reward weight, decay schedule, encoder capacity, and number/choice of proxy tasks is underexplored. Theoretical claims are informal, and reconstruction does not guarantee informative or invertible embeddings. Baseline tuning is not fully specified.

Overall, this is a promising and clearly presented contribution. I recommend acceptance with revisions expanding ablations, robustness analysis, and real-world or more diverse simulated validation.

title: Transfer of View-manifold Learning to Similarity Perception of Novel Objects
abstract: Abstract:###We develop a model of perceptual similarity judgment based on re-training a deep convolution neural network (DCNN) that learns to associate different views of each 3D object to capture the notion of object persistence and continuity in our visual experience. The re-training process effectively performs distance metric learning under the object persistency constraints, to modify the view-manifold of object representations. It reduces the effective distance between the representations of different views of the same object without compromising the distance between those of the views of different objects, resulting in the untangling of the view-manifolds between individual objects within the same category and across categories. This untangling enables the model to discriminate and recognize objects within the same category, independent of viewpoints. We found that this ability is not limited to the trained objects, but transfers to novel objects in both trained and untrained categories, as well as to a variety of completely novel artificial synthetic objects. This transfer in learning suggests the modification of distance metrics in view- manifolds is more general and abstract, likely at the levels of parts, and independent of the specific objects or categories experienced during training. Interestingly, the resulting transformation of feature representation in the deep networks is found to significantly better match human perceptual similarity judgment than AlexNet, suggesting that object persistence could be an important constraint in the development of perceptual similarity judgment in biological neural networks.
review:
This paper investigates whether object-persistence constraints can shape perceptual similarity representations. The authors fine-tune AlexNet with a Siamese triplet loss on multi-view renders of ShapeNet objects, encouraging different views of the same object to cluster while separating different objects. The resulting OPnet is evaluated on instance and category retrieval across novel instances, novel categories, synthetic objects, Pokemon models, and a human-labeled object set. OPnet substantially outperforms AlexNet, classification-fine-tuned AlexNet, HoG, and a joint-embedding baseline on most instance-retrieval tasks, and shows higher correlation with human similarity judgments (Spearman 0.659 versus 0.460). The view-manifold visualizations support the intended untangling effect.

Strengths: the question is interesting; the training signal is simple and well motivated by object persistence; transfer to untrained categories and synthetic objects is a compelling result; and the human-correlation analysis adds value beyond retrieval metrics.

Weaknesses: training uses only 200 rendered objects from 29 categories, so scale is limited. Images are grayscale, background-free renders, which may not reflect natural visual conditions. Evaluation relies heavily on retrieval mAP and proxy similarity assumptions, with only a small direct human-judgment comparison. Baselines are dated and lack modern metric-learning, 3D-aware, or self-supervised comparisons. Hyperparameter and ablation analysis is limited, and fine-tuning all layers on a small dataset raises overfitting concerns. The claim that object persistence is important in human development remains suggestive rather than established. Overall, this is a promising and clearly presented contribution, but broader validation and stronger baselines are needed.

title: What does it take to generate natural textures?
abstract: Abstract:###Natural image generation is currently one of the most actively explored fields in Deep Learning. Many approaches, e.g. for state-of-the-art artistic style transfer or natural texture synthesis, rely on the statistics of hierarchical representations in supervisedly trained deep neural networks. It is, however, unclear what aspects of this feature representation are crucial for natural image generation: is it the depth, the pooling or the training of the features on natural images? We here address this question for the task of natural texture synthesis and show that none of the above aspects are indispensable. Instead, we demonstrate that natural textures of high perceptual quality can be generated from networks with only a single layer, no pooling and random filters.
review:
This paper asks which ingredients of deep texture synthesis are truly necessary. The authors show that a single convolutional layer with random filters, no pooling, and a multi-scale filter bank can synthesize textures that often rival the VGG-based Gatys et al. model. They compare random, Fourier, PCA, k-means, and hand-crafted filters, examine filter size, multi-scale combination, and ReLU nonlinearity, and introduce a VGG-based reconstruction loss as a quantitative proxy for perceptual quality. The central finding—that depth and supervised feature learning are not indispensable for natural texture synthesis—is provocative and clearly demonstrated.

Strengths: the ablations are well controlled, the minimal baseline is simple and reproducible, and the multi-scale analysis convincingly shows the importance of combining receptive-field sizes. The VGG-loss offers a useful alternative to purely qualitative inspection, and the discussion of maximum-entropy modeling and finite-image effects is insightful.

Weaknesses: evaluation relies heavily on the VGG-loss, which is itself derived from the model being challenged, and no human perceptual study is reported. The number of reference textures is limited, and hyperparameter/optimization tuning strongly affects sample quality. The large-filter multi-scale model is computationally inefficient, and comparisons to state-of-the-art methods are qualitative. The claim that random filters perform on par with learned filters is nuanced and may depend on optimization and stopping criteria. Variability versus similarity is discussed but not measured.

Overall, this is a valuable and thought-provoking contribution. I recommend acceptance with revisions adding human evaluation, broader texture sets, and quantitative variability analysis.

title: Emergence of foveal image sampling from learning to attend in visual scenes
abstract: Abstract:###We describe a neural attention model with a learnable retinal sampling lattice. The model is trained on a visual search task requiring the classification of an object embedded in a visual scene amidst background distractors using the smallest number of fixations. We explore the tiling properties that emerge in the model*s retinal sampling lattice after training. Specifically, we show that this lattice resembles the eccentricity dependent sampling lattice of the primate retina, with a high resolution region in the fovea surrounded by a low resolution periphery. Furthermore, we find conditions where these emergent properties are amplified or eliminated providing clues to their function.
review:
This paper introduces a differentiable recurrent attention model whose retinal sampling lattice is learned end-to-end on cluttered MNIST visual search. The main finding is that when the lattice can translate but not zoom, training produces an eccentricity-dependent layout resembling the primate fovea: a high-acuity center surrounded by a lower-acuity periphery. When zoom is allowed, the lattice becomes more uniform, suggesting that foveal sampling and zoom serve similar functional roles. The paper is well motivated, connects to biological vision, and the ablations across fixed lattice, translation-only, and translation-plus-zoom are informative. The quantitative results show that learning the lattice improves classification error, and the variable-sized-digit dataset strengthens the eccentricity–resolution relationship.

Weaknesses: the experiments are limited to synthetic cluttered MNIST scenes, so generality to natural images and more complex tasks is unclear. The model uses Gaussian kernels and a simple RNN, and the biological analogy remains suggestive rather than definitive. Training and evaluation details are sparse in places, and there is no statistical variability across seeds. The claim that foveal sampling emerges as optimal is supported only within this constrained task family. Comparisons to alternative attention mechanisms and non-learned sampling baselines are limited.

Overall, this is an interesting and well-executed proof-of-concept at the intersection of attention and biological vision. I recommend acceptance with revisions expanding task diversity, reporting variability, and clarifying limitations of the biological interpretation.

title: An Information-Theoretic Framework for Fast and Robust Unsupervised Learning via Neural Population Infomax
abstract: Abstract:###A framework is presented for unsupervised learning of representations based on infomax principle for large-scale neural populations. We use an asymptotic approximation to the Shannon*s mutual information for a large neural population to demonstrate that a good initial approximation to the global information-theoretic optimum can be obtained by a hierarchical infomax method. Starting from the initial solution, an efficient algorithm based on gradient descent of the final objective function is proposed to learn representations from the input datasets, and the method works for complete, overcomplete, and undercomplete bases. As confirmed by numerical experiments, our method is robust and highly efficient for extracting salient features from input datasets. Compared with the main existing methods, our algorithm has a distinct advantage in both the training speed and the robustness of unsupervised representation learning. Furthermore, the proposed method is easily extended to the supervised or unsupervised model for training deep structure networks.
review:
This paper proposes an information-theoretic unsupervised representation-learning framework based on an asymptotic mutual-information approximation for large neural populations. The approach combines hierarchical infomax for initialization with gradient descent on a final objective, supports complete, overcomplete, and undercomplete bases, and uses Poisson neuron models. Experiments on natural-image patches and MNIST report Gabor-like filters and faster convergence than IICA, FastICA, and sparse RBM.

Strengths: the population-level MI approximation is well motivated and makes large output populations tractable. The hierarchical initialization is a sensible way to address nonconvexity, and the derivation connecting membrane noise, Markov-chain bounds, and the final objective is substantial. The method’s ability to handle N >> K and overcomplete bases is a genuine advantage over standard ICA-style approaches. The empirical comparisons show clear speed gains and reasonable filter quality.

Weaknesses: the asymptotic approximation requires large populations and independent noise, and its accuracy for finite N is not thoroughly quantified. The theory and algorithm are dense, with much critical detail relegated to appendices, limiting reproducibility. Experiments are limited to small patches and MNIST, with no modern deep-learning baselines or downstream classification evaluations. Hyperparameter sensitivity, convergence guarantees, and robustness to model misspecification are underexplored. Claims of robustness and efficiency need more systematic statistical comparison.

Overall, this is a promising and theoretically rich contribution, but broader empirical validation and clearer presentation are needed. I recommend acceptance with revisions.

title: PixelCNN++: Improving the PixelCNN with Discretized Logistic Mixture Likelihood and Other Modifications
abstract: Abstract:###PixelCNNs are a recently proposed class of powerful generative models with tractable likelihood. Here we discuss our implementation of PixelCNNs which we make available at https://github.com/openai/pixel-cnn. Our implementation contains a number of modifications to the original model that both simplify its structure and improve its performance. 1) We use a discretized logistic mixture likelihood on the pixels, rather than a 256-way softmax, which we find to speed up training. 2) We condition on whole pixels, rather than R/G/B sub-pixels, simplifying the model structure. 3) We use downsampling to efficiently capture structure at multiple resolutions. 4) We introduce additional short-cut connections to further speed up optimization. 5) We regularize the model using dropout. Finally, we present state-of-the-art log likelihood results on CIFAR-10 to demonstrate the usefulness of these modifications.
review:
This paper presents PixelCNN++, an improved autoregressive image model with several practical modifications: a discretized logistic mixture likelihood instead of a 256-way softmax, joint conditioning on whole pixels with linear cross-channel dependencies, downsampling with long-range shortcut connections, and dropout regularization. The authors report state-of-the-art CIFAR-10 log-likelihood (2.92 bits/sub-pixel) and provide code, with ablations supporting each change.

Strengths: The modifications are clearly motivated, mostly simple, and computationally beneficial. The discretized mixture likelihood addresses sparse gradients and memory costs while naturally handling edge values. Whole-pixel conditioning simplifies the architecture without evident loss. The shortcut design makes downsampling viable, and ablations show its necessity. Dropout is shown to be important for test likelihood and sample quality. The code release and implementation details are valuable.

Weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to CIFAR-10, with no additional datasets or downstream applications, so generality is unclear. Comparisons to prior PixelCNN variants are not fully controlled for architecture, capacity, and tuning, and run-to-run variability is not reported. The downsampling-versus-dilated-convolution claim is supported only by similar performance, not a systematic comparison. Sample quality remains qualitative, with no quantitative perceptual metric or human evaluation. Interactions between modifications are only partially isolated. Sampling cost and practical deployment are not discussed.

Overall, this is a useful, well-executed engineering contribution with strong likelihood results. I recommend acceptance, with revisions adding broader validation, controlled baselines, and statistical reporting.

title: Mode Regularized Generative Adversarial Networks
abstract: Abstract:###Although Generative Adversarial Networks achieve state-of-the-art results on a variety of generative tasks, they are regarded as highly unstable and prone to miss modes. We argue that these bad behaviors of GANs are due to the very particular functional shape of the trained discriminators in high dimensional spaces, which can easily make training stuck or push probability mass in the wrong direction, towards that of higher concentration than that of the data generating distribution. We introduce several ways of regularizing the objective, which can dramatically stabilize the training of GAN models. We also show that our regularizers can help the fair distribution of probability mass across the modes of the data generating distribution during the early phases of training, thus providing a unified solution to the missing modes problem.
review:
This paper addresses GAN training instability and missing modes by regularizing the generator objective. The authors argue that discriminator gradients in high-dimensional space can be poorly shaped and fail to penalize absent modes. They propose a geometric metric regularizer using a jointly trained encoder and reconstruction distance, a mode regularizer that encourages G∘E(x) toward high discriminator values, and a manifold-diffusion training scheme (MDGAN) that separates manifold matching from probability-mass diffusion. They also introduce a MODE score and a noisy third-party discriminator for mode-missing evaluation. Experiments on MNIST grid search and compositional MNIST, plus CelebA, show substantial reductions in missed modes and improved stability over DCGAN baselines.

Strengths: the diagnosis is well motivated, and the regularizers are simple and broadly applicable. The compositional MNIST evaluation is particularly convincing, and the proposed mode-estimation metrics are useful practical contributions. MDGAN performs strongly on CelebA.

Weaknesses: the method introduces an encoder and several sensitive hyperparameters (λ1, λ2), with limited tuning guidance. The MODE score depends on an external classifier, and the noisy third-party discriminator is only a heuristic estimate of missing mass. Theoretical claims remain informal. Evaluation is limited to MNIST and CelebA, with no FID or human study, and MDGAN adds complexity and extra discriminators. Comparisons to recent mode-collapse remedies are limited.

Overall, this is a valuable contribution with strong empirical evidence. I recommend acceptance with revisions clarifying hyperparameter sensitivity, metric validity, and broader quantitative evaluation.

title: Highway and Residual Networks learn Unrolled Iterative Estimation
abstract: Abstract:###The past year saw the introduction of new architectures such as Highway networks and Residual networks which, for the first time, enabled the training of feedforward networks with dozens to hundreds of layers using simple gradient descent. While depth of representation has been posited as a primary reason for their success, there are indications that these architectures defy a popular view of deep learning as a hierarchical computation of increasingly abstract features at each layer. In this report, we argue that this view is incomplete and does not adequately explain several recent findings. We propose an alternative viewpoint based on unrolled iterative estimation---a group of successive layers iteratively refine their estimates of the same features instead of computing an entirely new representation. We demonstrate that this viewpoint directly leads to the construction of highway and residual networks. Finally we provide preliminary experiments to discuss the similarities and differences between the two architectures.
review:
This paper proposes an “unrolled iterative estimation” interpretation of Highway and Residual networks: blocks within a stage refine the same representation rather than computing new abstraction levels, with representation changes at dimensionality-changing stages. The authors use this view to derive residual and highway update forms, present empirical evidence that estimation error stays near zero within stages of a 50-layer ResNet, and discuss lesioning and shuffling findings. Comparative case studies examine Highway versus Residual variants on language modeling and ImageNet.

Strengths: The perspective is clear, timely, and reconciles several puzzling observations about very deep networks. The derivation is intuitive, and the zero-mean estimation-error experiment plus feature visualization provide useful corroboration. The comparison of Highway and Residual variants with and without batch normalization is informative.

Weaknesses: The argument is largely interpretive and relies on idealized assumptions, notably zero-mean residuals and unbiased estimators, which are not rigorously guaranteed. Empirical support is preliminary: one ResNet for the central prediction, limited architectures, and modest comparative studies. The stage definition depends on dimensionality changes, leaving within-stage behavior and stage boundaries under-analyzed. Batch normalization’s role is acknowledged but not fully integrated into the theory. Lesioning and shuffling evidence is discussed rather than newly tested. No causal test distinguishes iterative refinement from ensemble-like explanations.

Overall, this is a thought-provoking conceptual contribution with suggestive evidence, but stronger theory and broader experiments are needed. I recommend acceptance with revisions.

title: Improving Neural Language Models with a Continuous Cache
abstract: Abstract:###We propose an extension to neural network language models to adapt their prediction to the recent history. Our model is a simplified version of memory augmented networks, which stores past hidden activations as memory and accesses them through a dot product with the current hidden activation. This mechanism is very efficient and scales to very large memory sizes. We also draw a link between the use of external memory in neural network and cache models used with count based language models. We demonstrate on several language model datasets that our approach performs significantly better than recent memory augmented networks.
review:
This paper proposes a Neural Cache Model that augments pretrained neural language models with a lightweight external memory of recent hidden activations. Cache probabilities are computed by dot-product similarity between the current hidden state and stored states, then interpolated with vocabulary predictions. The method requires no cache-specific training, scales to thousands of entries, and is evaluated on Penn Treebank, WikiText-2/103, text8, and LAMBADA.

Strengths: the approach is simple, efficient, and easy to apply to existing models. The connection to classical count-based cache models is well explained, and avoiding a learned memory-access mechanism enables much larger caches than memory-augmented networks. Results are strong: substantial perplexity reductions on WikiText-2, text8, and LAMBADA, with particularly large gains when the target word appears in recent context. The analysis of linear interpolation versus global normalization is useful.

Weaknesses: the cache is applied only at test time, so the model cannot learn to write or read memory adaptively. It primarily exploits lexical repetition, which explains large LAMBADA gains but may not transfer to tasks requiring semantic or syntactic memory. Hyperparameters θ, λ/α are tuned per dataset on validation, and no sensitivity or statistical variability is reported. Comparisons to memory-augmented networks are not fully controlled for base model, cache size, or training budget. The paper lacks ablations on hidden-state choice and cache recency/weighting.

Overall, this is a practical and effective contribution with clear gains, though deeper analysis and broader task validation are needed. I recommend acceptance with revisions.

title: Unsupervised Cross-Domain Image Generation
abstract: Abstract:###We study the problem of transferring a sample in one domain to an analog sample in another domain. Given two related domains, S and T, we would like to learn a generative function G that maps an input sample from S to the domain T, such that the output of a given representation function f, which accepts inputs in either domains, would remain unchanged. Other than f, the training data is unsupervised and consist of a set of samples from each domain, without any mapping between them. The Domain Transfer Network (DTN) we present employs a compound loss function that includes a multiclass GAN loss, an f preserving component, and a regularizing component that encourages G to map samples from T to themselves. We apply our method to visual domains including digits and face images and demonstrate its ability to generate convincing novel images of previously unseen entities, while preserving their identity.
review:
This paper proposes a Domain Transfer Network (DTN) for unsupervised cross-domain image generation. Given source and target samples and a function f, DTN learns G = g∘f so that f(G(x)) ≈ f(x), while a ternary GAN loss encourages target-domain realism and an identity regularizer keeps G(x) ≈ x on target samples. Experiments transfer SVHN to MNIST and face photos to emoji, with ablations and a domain-adaptation comparison.

Strengths: the formulation is clear, and the f-constancy plus target-identity regularization are sensible for preserving content while changing style. The baseline comparison and component ablations are informative, especially the large drop when f is removed from G or when both constancy and identity losses are removed. The SVHN→MNIST quantitative evaluation and the human-annotator emoji comparison are useful. The method applies to pretrained f and requires no paired data.

Weaknesses: evaluation is limited to two visual domains and a single forward mapping. The method depends heavily on f being meaningful on both domains; performance may degrade when f is weak or biased. Hyperparameters α, β, γ are tuned per task, and sensitivity is under-reported. Image quality is assessed largely qualitatively; no FID, precision/recall, or human perceptual study beyond the small emoji set. Identity preservation is indirectly measured via retrieval. The ternary GAN and TID losses lack theoretical analysis. Comparisons to modern domain-translation methods are absent.

Overall, this is a solid and practical contribution with convincing ablations, but broader quantitative validation is needed. I recommend acceptance with revisions.

title: Third Person Imitation Learning
abstract: Abstract:###Reinforcement learning (RL) makes it possible to train agents capable of achieving sophisticated goals in complex and uncertain environments. A key difficulty in reinforcement learning is specifying a reward function for the agent to optimize. Traditionally, imitation learning in RL has been used to overcome this problem. Unfortunately, hitherto imitation learning methods tend to require that demonstrations are supplied in the first-person: the agent is provided with a sequence of states and a specification of the actions that it should have taken. While powerful, this kind of imitation learning is limited by the relatively hard problem of collecting first-person demonstrations. Humans address this problem by learning from third-person demonstrations: they observe other humans perform tasks, infer the task, and accomplish the same task themselves. In this paper, we present a method for unsupervised third-person imitation learning. Here third-person refers to training an agent to correctly achieve a simple goal in a simple environment when it is provided a demonstration of a teacher achieving the same goal but from a different viewpoint; and unsupervised refers to the fact that the agent receives only these third-person demonstrations, and is not provided a correspondence between teacher states and student states. Our methods primary insight is that recent advances from domain confusion can be utilized to yield domain agnostic features which are crucial during the training process. To validate our approach, we report successful experiments on learning from third-person demonstrations in a pointmass domain, a reacher domain, and inverted pendulum.
review:
This paper proposes a Domain Transfer Network (DTN) for unsupervised cross-domain image generation. Given source and target samples and a function f, DTN learns G = g∘f so that f(G(x)) ≈ f(x), while a ternary GAN loss encourages target-domain realism and an identity regularizer keeps G(x) ≈ x on target samples. Experiments transfer SVHN to MNIST and face photos to emoji, with ablations and a domain-adaptation comparison.

Strengths: the formulation is clear, and the f-constancy plus target-identity regularization are sensible for preserving content while changing style. The baseline comparison and component ablations are informative, especially the large drop when f is removed from G or when both constancy and identity losses are removed. The SVHN→MNIST quantitative evaluation and the human-annotator emoji comparison are useful. The method applies to pretrained f and requires no paired data.

Weaknesses: evaluation is limited to two visual domains and a single forward mapping. The method depends heavily on f being meaningful on both domains; performance may degrade when f is weak or biased. Hyperparameters α, β, γ are tuned per task, and sensitivity is under-reported. Image quality is assessed largely qualitatively; no FID, precision/recall, or human perceptual study beyond the small emoji set. Identity preservation is indirectly measured via retrieval. The ternary GAN and TID losses lack theoretical analysis. Comparisons to modern domain-translation methods are absent.

Overall, this is a solid and practical contribution with convincing ablations, but broader quantitative validation is needed. I recommend acceptance with revisions.

title: Variational Recurrent Adversarial Deep Domain Adaptation
abstract: Abstract:###We study the problem of learning domain invariant representations for time series data while transferring the complex temporal latent dependencies between the domains. Our model termed as Variational Recurrent Adversarial Deep Domain Adaptation (VRADA) is built atop a variational recurrent neural network (VRNN) and trains adversarially to capture complex temporal relationships that are domain-invariant. This is (as far as we know) the first to capture and transfer temporal latent dependencies in multivariate time-series data. Through experiments on real-world multivariate healthcare time-series datasets, we empirically demonstrate that learning temporal dependencies helps our model*s ability to create domain-invariant representations, allowing our model to outperform current state-of-the-art deep domain adaptation approaches.
review:
This paper proposes VRADA, a variational recurrent adversarial model for unsupervised domain adaptation of multivariate time series. VRADA combines a VRNN encoder/decoder with a DANN-style domain classifier and gradient reversal to learn latent representations that capture temporal dependencies while being domain-invariant. Experiments on MIMIC-III adult AHRF, pediatric AHRF, and ICD9 prediction tasks compare against logistic regression, AdaBoost, DNNs, DANN, R-DANN, and VFAE, reporting higher target-domain AUC in most source-target pairs and more stable results. The t-SNE visualizations support the claim that temporal modeling improves domain mixing.

Strengths: the problem is important and underexplored; the VRNN plus adversarial adaptation combination is sensible and clearly described; the healthcare domain is appropriate for longitudinal data; and the quantitative comparisons across many age-group transfer pairs are useful. The paper is generally well organized.

Weaknesses: evaluation is limited to healthcare datasets and AUC metrics, with no statistical significance testing or broad ablation of VRNN components, adversarial weight, and latent dimensionality. Domain definitions and source-target pair construction may introduce label and cohort confounds. Comparisons are not fully controlled for capacity and tuning, and no code or reproducibility details are provided. Theoretical claims about transferring temporal latent dependencies are supported mainly by performance and qualitative t-SNE. Calibration and clinical utility are not assessed.

Overall, this is a solid contribution with promising results, but stronger ablations and broader validation are needed. I recommend acceptance with revisions.

title: Program Synthesis for Character Level Language Modeling
abstract: Abstract:###We propose a statistical model applicable to character level language modeling and show that it is a good fit for both, program source code and English text. The model is parameterized by a program from a domain-specific language (DSL) that allows expressing non-trivial data dependencies. Learning is done in two phases: (i) we synthesize a program from the DSL, essentially learning a good representation for the data, and (ii) we learn parameters from the training data - the process is done via counting, as in simple language models such as n-gram. Our experiments show that the precision of our model is comparable to that of neural networks while sharing a number of advantages with n-gram models such as fast query time and the capability to quickly add and remove training data samples. Further, the model is parameterized by a program that can be manually inspected, understood and updated, addressing a major problem of neural networks.
review:
This paper proposes TChar, a domain-specific language for character-level language modeling, and learns a probabilistic model by synthesizing a program from the DSL and then estimating probabilities by counting. TChar supports move/write instructions, switch programs, state programs, and backoff/cache, enabling n-gram-like and context-specialized submodels. Experiments on Linux Kernel source code and Hutter Prize Wikipedia compare against n-grams and LSTMs/other neural models.

Strengths: the approach is novel and interpretable in principle; it combines program synthesis with simple counting, yielding fast training, fast queries, and easy addition/removal of data. On structured code, results are strong, improving both bits-per-character and error rate over n-grams and LSTMs. The DSL design is well motivated, and ablations on cache and backoff are useful.

Weaknesses: synthesis is computationally expensive and relies on extensive search plus manual domain-specific additions, such as the comment/code state program for Linux. The learned program for Linux is very large (thousands of instructions), undercutting interpretability. Evaluation is limited to two datasets and largely reported numbers, without statistical variability or controlled neural-network tuning. Hutter results lack error rate and trail state-of-the-art neural models. The DSL’s restricted expressiveness and sensitivity to synthesis hyperparameters, regularization, and hash collisions are underexplored. Query speed degrades with backoff/cache in the current implementation.

Overall, this is a promising bridge between synthesis and statistical language modeling with strong structured-data results. I recommend acceptance with revisions strengthening comparisons, interpretability analysis, and robustness evaluation.

title: Episodic Exploration for Deep Deterministic Policies for StarCraft Micromanagement
abstract: Abstract:###We consider scenarios from the real-time strategy game StarCraft as benchmarks for reinforcement learning algorithms. We focus on micromanagement, that is, the short-term, low-level control of team members during a battle. We propose several scenarios that are challenging for reinforcement learning algorithms because the state- action space is very large, and there is no obvious feature representation for the value functions. We describe our approach to tackle the micromanagement scenarios with deep neural network controllers from raw state features given by the game engine. We also present a heuristic reinforcement learning algorithm which combines direct exploration in the policy space and backpropagation. This algorithm collects traces for learning using deterministic policies, which appears much more efficient than, e.g., ?-greedy exploration. Experiments show that this algorithm allows to successfully learn non-trivial strategies for scenarios with armies of up to 15 agents, where both Q-learning and REINFORCE struggle.
review:
This paper proposes StarCraft micromanagement scenarios as RL benchmarks and a deep deterministic controller trained with episodic exploration. The main ideas are a greedy-inference MDP for multi-unit action selection, reward normalization by unit count, a permutation-invariant state-action featurization, and a heuristic algorithm that randomizes last-layer policy parameters per episode while using backpropagation for the rest. Experiments show non-trivial strategies for armies up to 15 units, where Q-learning and REINFORCE struggle.

Strengths: The benchmark is relevant and challenging. The greedy MDP reduction is principled and reduces joint-action complexity. Reward normalization and pooled unit features are sensible. The episodic parameter-space exploration is well motivated for multi-agent control, where action randomization disorganizes units. The paper is clearly written and provides useful feature/model details.

Weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to a few small scenarios against built-in AI, with no human-level comparison, few seeds, and limited statistical reporting. The exploration algorithm is heuristic, with no convergence analysis and several sensitive hyperparameters. Baselines are not tuned extensively, and comparisons to other parameter-space or hierarchical RL methods are absent. The feature representation still encodes domain structure, and results may not scale to larger armies or full games. Reproducibility is limited by missing implementation and compute details.

Overall, this is a solid benchmark and algorithmic contribution with promising results, but stronger empirical validation and analysis are needed. I recommend acceptance with revisions.

title: Soft Weight-Sharing for Neural Network Compression
abstract: Abstract:###The success of deep learning in numerous application domains created the desire to run and train them on mobile devices. This however, conflicts with their computationally, memory and energy intense nature, leading to a growing interest in compression. Recent work by Han et al. (2016) propose a pipeline that involves retraining, pruning and quantization of neural network weights, obtaining state-of-the-art compression rates. In this paper, we show that competitive compression rates can be achieved by using a version of *soft weight-sharing* (Nowlan & Hinton, 1991). Our method achieves both quantization and pruning in one simple (re-)training procedure. This point of view also exposes the relation between compression and the minimum description length (MDL) principle.
review:
This paper revisits soft weight-sharing for neural network compression, framing it through MDL and variational inference. A Gaussian mixture prior is learned jointly with network weights, encouraging clustering around means and pruning via a fixed zero component; post-processing quantizes weights to responsible components. Experiments on LeNet-300-100, LeNet-5-Caffe, and a light ResNet report competitive compression rates, including state-of-the-art results on the LeNet models, with modest accuracy loss.

Strengths: the MDL/variational framing is clean and connects compression to empirical Bayes. The method combines pruning and quantization in one retraining procedure, avoiding the fixed post-hoc assignments of Han et al. The zero-component mechanism and mixture-merging post-processing are sensible. Results on MNIST networks are strong, and the ResNet experiment, while weaker, shows applicability beyond small models.

Weaknesses: evaluation is limited and inconsistent. The ResNet compression incurs a 2% accuracy drop, and the paper admits the method is too slow for large networks such as VGG. Hyperparameter tuning relies on a 13-dimensional Bayesian optimization search with only 40 epochs, and the authors note unclear relationships among good settings. The procedure is sensitive to learning rates and mixture collapse, requiring hyperpriors. Comparisons are not fully controlled, and no wall-clock or memory measurements are reported. Theoretical ties to bits-back coding are not operationalized in the actual storage scheme. Reproducibility of the compression-rate accounting is limited.

Overall, this is a principled and promising compression method with strong small-model results, but scalability and robustness require more work. I recommend acceptance with revisions.

title: Neural Program Lattices
abstract: Abstract:###We propose the Neural Program Lattice (NPL), a neural network that learns to perform complex tasks by composing low-level programs to express high-level programs. Our starting point is the recent work on Neural Programmer-Interpreters (NPI), which can only learn from strong supervision that contains the whole hierarchy of low-level and high-level programs. NPLs remove this limitation by providing the ability to learn from weak supervision consisting only of sequences of low-level operations. We demonstrate the capability of NPL to learn to perform long-hand addition and arrange blocks in a grid-world environment. Experiments show that it performs on par with NPI while using weak supervision in place of most of the strong supervision, thus indicating its ability to infer the high-level program structure from examples containing only the low-level operations.
review:
This paper introduces Neural Program Lattices (NPL), a framework for training Neural Programmer-Interpreter-like models from weak supervision consisting mainly of flat sequences of elementary operations and world states. The key technical ideas are reformulating NPI with explicit call stacks, adapting CTC-style dynamic programming to marginalize over program alignments, using a differentiable StackRNN-style call stack, and introducing a lattice approximation that trades computation for a closer approximation of the marginal likelihood. Experiments on long-hand addition and a grid-world block-arrangement task show NPL performs comparably to NPI while requiring only a few fully supervised traces.

Strengths: the problem is important, and relaxing NPI’s strong hierarchy supervision is a meaningful step. The CTC/StackRNN connection is well motivated, and the lattice formulation is a sensible way to interpolate between exact path enumeration and a single blurred execution. The paper is generally clear and provides useful conceptual framing.

Weaknesses: the method still requires some strongly supervised traces, so the claim of weak supervision is qualified. Evaluation is limited to two synthetic, noiseless tasks, with small-scale experiments and limited statistical reporting. The marginal-likelihood approximation and differentiable stack lack theoretical guarantees, and error propagation from soft stack operations is not analyzed. Comparisons to alternative latent-program induction methods are limited. Scalability to longer programs and noisier domains is untested.

Overall, this is a promising contribution with a clear technical idea and encouraging results. I recommend acceptance with revisions expanding empirical validation and analysis of approximation error.

title: Tracking the World State with Recurrent Entity Networks
abstract: Abstract:###We introduce a new model, the Recurrent Entity Network (EntNet). It is equipped with a dynamic long-term memory which allows it to maintain and update a rep- resentation of the state of the world as it receives new data. For language under- standing tasks, it can reason on-the-fly as it reads text, not just when it is required to answer a question or respond as is the case for a Memory Network (Sukhbaatar et al., 2015). Like a Neural Turing Machine or Differentiable Neural Computer (Graves et al., 2014; 2016) it maintains a fixed size memory and can learn to perform location and content-based read and write operations. However, unlike those models it has a simple parallel architecture in which several memory loca- tions can be updated simultaneously. The EntNet sets a new state-of-the-art on the bAbI tasks, and is the first method to solve all the tasks in the 10k training examples setting. We also demonstrate that it can solve a reasoning task which requires a large number of supporting facts, which other methods are not able to solve, and can generalize past its training horizon. It can also be practically used on large scale datasets such as Childrenâ€™s Book Test, where it obtains competitive performance, reading the story in a single pass.
review:
This paper introduces the Recurrent Entity Network (EntNet), a memory-augmented model with fixed key-value memory slots updated by parallel gated recurrent processors. Each slot is gated by content and location terms, and unit normalization provides a forgetting mechanism. The model is evaluated on a synthetic world-model task, all 20 bAbI tasks with 10k examples, and the Children’s Book Test.

Strengths: the architecture is simple, parallel, and well motivated. The independent per-slot gating avoids a central controller and allows simultaneous updates. Results on bAbI are strong—all tasks solved with 0.5% mean error—and the world-model experiment convincingly shows generalization beyond the training horizon. The tied-key interpretability analysis is a useful addition, and single-pass CBT performance is competitive.

Weaknesses: evaluation relies heavily on synthetic tasks, with limited real-world validation. The fixed number of memory slots and lack of inter-slot communication may limit complex relational reasoning. The normalization-based forgetting rule is heuristic and not thoroughly analyzed. bAbI results use best-of-10 runs selected on validation, and comparisons are not fully controlled for tuning or capacity. CBT experiments use a simplified variant, and multi-pass comparisons are limited. Scalability to larger stories and noisy natural language remains unclear.

Overall, this is a strong and practical contribution with compelling benchmark results. I recommend acceptance with revisions clarifying limitations, memory scaling, and robustness.

title: Steerable CNNs
abstract: Abstract:###It has long been recognized that the invariance and equivariance properties of a representation are critically important for success in many vision tasks. In this paper we present Steerable Convolutional Neural Networks, an efficient and flexible class of equivariant convolutional networks. We show that steerable CNNs achieve state of the art results on the CIFAR image classification benchmark. The mathematical theory of steerable representations reveals a type system in which any steerable representation is a composition of elementary feature types, each one associated with a particular kind of symmetry. We show how the parameter cost of a steerable filter bank depends on the types of the input and output features, and show how to use this knowledge to construct CNNs that utilize parameters effectively.
review:
This paper introduces Steerable CNNs, a representation-theoretic framework for equivariant convolutional networks. The authors model feature spaces as fibers carrying group representations, characterize equivariant filter banks as intertwiners, and use induced representations to obtain steerability for the full group from fiber-level equivariance. Character theory is used to define feature types, compute parameter cost, and assess parameter utilization. The paper also discusses admissible nonlinearities/capsules and a blockwise implementation that keeps computation practical.

Strengths: The framework is elegant and substantially more general than prior equivariant CNNs restricted to small discrete groups. Decoupling parameter cost from group size is important, and the type system gives principled guidance for architecture design. The exposition of intertwiners, induced representations, and capsule compatibility is technically sound and potentially useful beyond this specific model.

Weaknesses: The paper is mathematically dense; intuitive examples and implementation pseudocode would improve accessibility. Empirical validation needs to be more convincing: the reported CIFAR results should be accompanied by detailed ablations on capsule types, multiplicities, nonlinearities, parameter utilization, and wall-clock/memory costs. The choice of capsule catalogue remains somewhat heuristic, and admissibility of nonlinearities is only partially explored. Comparisons to concurrent equivariant CNN methods should be strengthened. Reproducibility would benefit from released code and exact hyperparameters.

Overall, this is a strong theoretical contribution with practical promise. I recommend acceptance with minor revisions clarifying empirical evidence and limitations.

title: Learning to Query, Reason, and Answer Questions On Ambiguous Texts
abstract: Abstract:###A key goal of research in conversational systems is to train an interactive agent to help a user with a task. Human conversation, however, is notoriously incomplete, ambiguous, and full of extraneous detail. To operate effectively, the agent must not only understand what was explicitly conveyed but also be able to reason in the presence of missing or unclear information. When unable to resolve ambiguities on its own, the agent must be able to ask the user for the necessary clarifications and incorporate the response in its reasoning. Motivated by this problem we introduce QRAQ (*crack*; Query, Reason, and Answer Questions), a new synthetic domain, in which a User gives an Agent a short story and asks a challenge question. These problems are designed to test the reasoning and interaction capabilities of a learning-based Agent in a setting that requires multiple conversational turns. A good Agent should ask only non-deducible, relevant questions until it has enough information to correctly answer the User*s question. We use standard and improved reinforcement learning based memory-network architectures to solve QRAQ problems in the difficult setting where the reward signal only tells the Agent if its final answer to the challenge question is correct or not. To provide an upper-bound to the RL results we also train the same architectures using supervised information that tells the Agent during training which variables to query and the answer to the challenge question. We evaluate our architectures on four QRAQ dataset types, and scale the complexity for each along multiple dimensions.
review:
This paper introduces QRAQ, a synthetic multi-turn domain where an agent must reason over short stories containing ambiguous variables, decide whether enough information is available, query only relevant non-deducible variables, and answer a challenge question. The authors propose two memory-network RL agents—baseRL and impRL—and compare them with supervised upper bounds across four dataset variants that scale vocabulary, sentence count, variables, and reasoning depth.
