Weaknesses: Conclusions rely heavily on massive hyperparameter tuning, so practical relevance under limited tuning budgets is unclear. Capacity is measured mainly on synthetic memorization tasks, and the five-bits-per-parameter estimate is approximate. Trainability results are task-specific, and +RNN cannot be used at depth one. No theoretical guarantees accompany the empirical trends, and variance across tuner runs is not fully reported.

Questions: How robust are conclusions to smaller tuning budgets? Do they hold for large-scale language modeling? How sensitive is capacity to nonlinearity and unrolling length?

Overall: A valuable, thought-provoking empirical study. I recommend acceptance, with claims qualified by the tuning regime.

title: Learning to Perform Physics Experiments via Deep Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Abstract:###When encountering novel objects, humans are able to infer a wide range of physical properties such as mass, friction and deformability by interacting with them in a goal driven way. This process of active interaction is in the same spirit as a scientist performing experiments to discover hidden facts. Recent advances in artificial intelligence have yielded machines that can achieve superhuman performance in Go, Atari, natural language processing, and complex control problems; however, it is not clear that these systems can rival the scientific intuition of even a young child. In this work we introduce a basic set of tasks that require agents to estimate properties such as mass and cohesion of objects in an interactive simulated environment where they can manipulate the objects and observe the consequences. We found that deep reinforcement learning methods can learn to perform the experiments necessary to discover such hidden properties. By systematically manipulating the problem difficulty and the cost incurred by the agent for performing experiments, we found that agents learn different strategies that balance the cost of gathering information against the cost of making mistakes in different situations. We also compare our learned experimentation policies to randomized baselines and show that the learned policies lead to better predictions.
review:
This paper investigates whether deep reinforcement learning agents can learn active experimentation to infer hidden physical properties. Two simulated tasks are introduced: Which is Heavier, where blocks’ masses are randomized independently of appearance, and Towers, where agents must infer how many rigid bodies compose a tower by knocking it down. Agents use A3C with LSTM policies from features or pixels, and the paper compares learned interaction policies with randomized baselines while varying task difficulty and discount factor.

Strengths: The problem framing is interesting and well motivated. Randomizing hidden properties ensures the tasks require interaction rather than visual shortcuts. The experiments show agents learn to balance information gathering against answering, adapt behavior to instance difficulty, and outperform randomized interaction. The Towers timing analysis usefully argues against fixed-step strategies. The paper is candid that it introduces no new algorithm.

Weaknesses: The technical contribution is limited; the core methods are standard and the environments are simple, low-dimensional, and synthetic. Results rely on qualitative strategy interpretation, with few quantitative comparisons, no variance across seeds in many analyses, and no ablation of architecture or reward design. Baseline comparisons are weak: random interaction is not a strong experimental-design baseline. Claims about “scientific intuition” are speculative. Pixel experiments show narrow hyperparameter robustness, which is underdiscussed.

Questions: How robust are learned strategies across seeds and hyperparameters? How do they compare with bandit-inspired or information-gain baselines? Do results scale to richer 3D scenes?

Overall: A thought-provoking proof-of-concept, but limited methodological novelty and empirical depth. Borderline accept.

title: Improving Policy Gradient by Exploring Under-appreciated Rewards
abstract: Abstract:###This paper presents a novel form of policy gradient for model-free reinforcement learning (RL) with improved exploration properties. Current policy-based methods use entropy regularization to encourage undirected exploration of the reward landscape, which is ineffective in high dimensional spaces with sparse rewards. We propose a more directed exploration strategy that promotes exploration of under-appreciated reward regions. An action sequence is considered under-appreciated if its log-probability under the current policy under-estimates its resulting reward. The proposed exploration strategy is easy to implement, requiring only small modifications to the standard REINFORCE algorithm. We evaluate the approach on a set of algorithmic tasks that have long challenged RL methods. We find that our approach reduces hyper-parameter sensitivity and demonstrates significant improvements over baseline methods. Notably, the approach is able to solve a benchmark multi-digit addition task. To our knowledge, this is the first time that a pure RL method has solved addition using only reward feedback.
review:
This paper introduces UREX, a policy-gradient objective that augments expected reward with a RAML-style mean-seeking term approximated via self-normalized importance weights. Intuitively, action sequences whose reward is under-estimated by the current policy receive extra reinforcement, yielding directed exploration in sparse-reward settings. The derivation connecting entropy-regularized REINFORCE, KL directions, and importance sampling is clear, and the modification to REINFORCE is simple. Experiments on six algorithmic tasks, including multi-digit addition and binary search, show substantial gains over entropy-regularized REINFORCE and Q-learning, with better hyperparameter robustness. The reported generalization of addition policies to much longer sequences is striking.

Weaknesses: The importance weights are treated as constants in the gradient, so the optimized objective is only approximated; variance and bias are not analyzed. Early-training instability is acknowledged but only heuristically addressed. Baselines are limited, and comparisons lack variance across seeds in several places. The tasks are small synthetic domains, so scalability to high-dimensional control or language is unclear. The claim of solving addition via pure RL is compelling, but the mechanism and failure cases need deeper ablation, e.g., separating the mean-seeking term from reward scaling and sampling.

Questions: How sensitive is UREX to temperature τ and K? Does it scale to continuous or long-horizon tasks? How often does it fail?

Overall: promising and clearly motivated, but theoretical and empirical analysis should be strengthened. Borderline accept.

title: Deep Learning with Dynamic Computation Graphs
abstract: Abstract:###Neural networks that compute over graph structures are a natural fit for problems in a variety of domains, including natural language (parse trees) and cheminformatics (molecular graphs). However, since the computation graph has a different shape and size for every input, such networks do not directly support batched training or inference. They are also difficult to implement in popular deep learning libraries, which are based on static data-flow graphs. We introduce a technique called dynamic batching, which not only batches together operations between different input graphs of dissimilar shape, but also between different nodes within a single input graph. The technique allows us to create static graphs, using popular libraries, that emulate dynamic computation graphs of arbitrary shape and size. We further present a high-level library of compositional blocks that simplifies the creation of dynamic graph models. Using the library, we demonstrate concise and batch-wise parallel implementations for a variety of models from the literature.
review:
This paper introduces dynamic batching for neural networks over input-specific computation graphs, plus TensorFlow Fold combinators. It schedules same-depth operations across heterogeneous graphs into a static TensorFlow `while_loop` with gather/concat, enabling batched training and inference for TreeRNNs and graph models. Benchmarks show large speedups versus batch-size-1 execution and modest overhead versus manual same-shape batching. Tree-LSTM sentiment and graph-convolution examples demonstrate practical expressiveness and concise implementations.

Strengths: clear systems contribution; it solves a real batching obstacle; implementation detail is useful; speed benchmarks are informative; the combinator abstraction is reusable; examples validate utility.

Weaknesses: primarily engineering rather than a new learning method; benchmarks are synthetic TreeRNN inference with limited end-to-end training/runtime comparisons; overhead is reported mostly for same-shape best cases, while “full dynamic” uses random trees rather than diverse real parses; memory costs are not analyzed; lines-of-code comparison is informal; Tree-LSTM accuracy gains rely on hyperparameters and ensembling, so dynamic batching’s contribution to accuracy is indirect; limitations and debugging are underdiscussed.

Questions: How does overhead scale with graph depth, type diversity, and real batch heterogeneity? What are memory costs? Can it handle recursive/cyclic structures beyond DAGs? How does it compare with SPINN on varied tree sizes?

Overall: a solid systems/tooling paper with clear practical value, but it should be framed as enabling infrastructure rather than a modeling advance. Accept.

title: Calibrating Energy-based Generative Adversarial Networks
abstract: Abstract:###In this paper, we propose to equip Generative Adversarial Networks with the ability to produce direct energy estimates for samples. Specifically, we propose a flexible adversarial training framework, and prove this framework not only ensures the generator converges to the true data distribution, but also enables the discriminator to retain the density information at the global optimal. We derive the analytic form of the induced solution, and analyze the properties. In order to make the proposed framework trainable in practice, we introduce two effective approximation techniques. Empirically, the experiment results closely match our theoretical analysis, verifying the discriminator is able to recover the energy of data distribution.
review:
This paper proposes calibrating energy-based GANs by adding a convex regularizer K(p_gen) to the adversarial objective, yielding a minimax formulation whose optimum matches data while the discriminator retains density/energy information. The authors derive KKT-based forms for the optimal discriminator under negative entropy and L2 regularization, and introduce nearest-neighbor and variational approximations for entropy. Synthetic 2D experiments show EGAN-Ent recovers non-flat energy contours, unlike GAN and constant-regularized EBGAN; NIST ranking supports higher-dimensional relative density.

Strengths: clear theoretical motivation, elegant dual/KKT analysis, and useful connection to EBGAN/imitation learning. The distinction between generator stationarity and discriminator calibration is well explained. Both entropy approximations are practical and the synthetic visualizations are convincing.

Weaknesses: theory is nonparametric and assumes strong convexity/feasibility; parametric transfer is asserted rather than proven. The NN entropy approximation uses Euclidean kNN, unreliable in high dimensions, and scale normalization introduces an arbitrary α. The VI approximation fails on biased mixtures, showing instability. Experiments are limited (synthetic plus NIST ranking), with no quantitative comparison to density estimators or likelihood-based models, no variance across seeds, and little discussion of training cost or hyperparameter sensitivity.

Questions: How robust is EGAN-Ent to k, α, and batch size? Can the discriminator serve as a reliable high-dimensional energy estimator? How does it compare with explicit density models?

Overall: theoretically interesting and promising, but empirical evidence is preliminary. Borderline accept.

title: Pruning Convolutional Neural Networks for Resource Efficient Inference
abstract: Abstract:###We propose a new formulation for pruning convolutional kernels in neural networks to enable efficient inference. We interleave greedy criteria-based pruning with fine-tuning by backpropagation-a computationally efficient procedure that maintains good generalization in the pruned network. We propose a new criterion based on Taylor expansion that approximates the change in the cost function induced by pruning network parameters. We focus on transfer learning, where large pretrained networks are adapted to specialized tasks. The proposed criterion demonstrates superior performance compared to other criteria, e.g. the norm of kernel weights or feature map activation, for pruning large CNNs after adaptation to fine-grained classification tasks (Birds-200 and Flowers-102) relaying only on the first order gradient information. We also show that pruning can lead to more than 10x theoretical reduction in adapted 3D-convolutional filters with a small drop in accuracy in a recurrent gesture classifier. Finally, we show results for the large-scale ImageNet dataset to emphasize the flexibility of our approach.
review:
This paper proposes pruning convolutional feature maps via greedy Taylor-based saliency interleaved with fine-tuning. The saliency criterion approximates loss change by |∂C/∂h · h|, avoiding Hessian computation, and is compared with weight magnitude, activation statistics, APoZ, mutual information, and OBD. The authors characterize oracle rankings on transfer-learning tasks, show Taylor ranking correlates best with oracle after layer-wise normalization, and demonstrate pruning on Birds-200, Flowers-102, a 3D gesture model, and ImageNet.

Strengths: The method is simple, practical, and compatible with standard backpropagation. The oracle analysis is useful, and the FLOPs-aware regularization plus global rescaling address cross-layer comparability. Empirical results support the criterion’s advantage over common heuristics.

Weaknesses: The first-order Taylor approximation neglects the remainder and assumes parameter independence; the justification via ReLU is heuristic. Evaluation prunes one feature map per iteration, so runtime and scalability are not fully analyzed. Comparisons are mostly against heuristic criteria rather than strong structured-pruning baselines, and theoretical FLOP reduction is not translated into measured hardware speedups. Oracle experiments use a single iteration and do not track how rankings change after pruning. Variance across runs, hyperparameter sensitivity (λ, pruning schedule), and behavior under aggressive compression are underreported. The transfer-learning focus limits generality.

Questions: How sensitive are results to λ and batch size? Does Taylor remain accurate after many pruning iterations? Are measured latency gains realized on GPUs?

Overall: A solid, practical pruning method with useful empirical evidence, but stronger baselines and runtime analysis are needed. Borderline accept.

title: Query-Reduction Networks for Question Answering
abstract: Abstract:###In this paper, we study the problem of question answering when reasoning over multiple facts is required. We propose Query-Reduction Network (QRN), a variant of Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) that effectively handles both short-term (local) and long-term (global) sequential dependencies to reason over multiple facts. QRN considers the context sentences as a sequence of state-changing triggers, and reduces the original query to a more informed query as it observes each trigger (context sentence) through time. Our experiments show that QRN produces the state-of-the-art results in bAbI QA and dialog tasks, and in a real goal-oriented dialog dataset. In addition, QRN formulation allows parallelization on RNN*s time axis, saving an order of magnitude in time complexity for training and inference.
review:
The paper proposes Query-Reduction Network (QRN), a recurrent unit for multi-hop question answering that treats context sentences as triggers and reduces the query locally via an update gate and candidate-query function. QRN avoids dependence of candidate state on previous hidden state, enabling time-axis parallelization via matrix formulation. Experiments report state-of-the-art results on bAbI story QA, bAbI dialog, and transformed DSTC2.

Strengths: The model is simple and well motivated; local sigmoid attention differs usefully from global softmax memory access. The parallelization derivation is elegant and potentially impactful. Ablations/extensions (reset/vector gates, bidirectionality) are discussed, and code is released.

Weaknesses: Evaluation is dominated by synthetic bAbI tasks; only DSTC2 is real, and it is transformed, limiting claims of general QA utility. The paper should include stronger real-domain multi-hop QA benchmarks and error analysis. The O(T^2) parallelization memory cost and behavior on very long stories are not analyzed. Claims about avoiding vanishing gradients and overfitting are plausible but not empirically isolated. Comparisons to N2N/DMN+ would benefit from matched parameter counts, training regimes, and statistical significance. Interpretability examples are qualitative. Some equations and gate descriptions need clearer notation.

Overall, QRN is a clean, novel recurrent design with strong synthetic results and a useful parallelization trick. I recommend acceptance, conditional on expanded real-data evaluation and clearer empirical justification of the claimed advantages.

title: Designing Neural Network Architectures using Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Abstract:###At present, designing convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures requires both human expertise and labor. New architectures are handcrafted by careful experimentation or modified from a handful of existing networks. We introduce MetaQNN, a meta-modeling algorithm based on reinforcement learning to automatically generate high-performing CNN architectures for a given learning task. The learning agent is trained to sequentially choose CNN layers using -learning with an -greedy exploration strategy and experience replay. The agent explores a large but finite space of possible architectures and iteratively discovers designs with improved performance on the learning task. On image classification benchmarks, the agent-designed networks (consisting of only standard convolution, pooling, and fully-connected layers) beat existing networks designed with the same layer types and are competitive against the state-of-the-art methods that use more complex layer types. We also outperform existing meta-modeling approaches for network design on image classification tasks.
review:
Review: Designing Neural Network Architectures Using Reinforcement Learning

The paper presents MetaQNN, a Q-learning meta-model for CNN architecture search. States encode layer type/parameters and depth; actions add layers or terminate; epsilon-greedy exploration and experience replay train a Q-table from validation accuracy. On CIFAR-10/100, SVHN, and MNIST, discovered networks using standard layers outperform comparable hand-crafted and prior meta-modeling baselines, and are competitive with more complex architectures.

Strengths: The formulation is clear and well grounded in Q-learning. Restricting the state-action graph to a DAG with representation-size constraints makes search tractable. The progressive epsilon schedule and replay dictionary are sensible. Results demonstrate that automatically discovered standard-layer CNNs can be strong, and ensembling/transfer experiments add useful evidence.

Weaknesses: Search cost is very high (8–10 days on 10 GPUs per dataset), and the proxy training scheme (20 epochs) may poorly rank architectures later finetuned with different schedules. Comparisons mix ensembles, top models, augmentation, and finetuning, complicating claims. The architecture space excludes residual, batch-norm, and modern activation choices, limiting relevance. Reward uses validation accuracy only, with no explicit parameter/FLOP penalty. R-size binning creates stochastic transitions whose impact is not analyzed. Variance across Q-learning runs appears only in appendix, and the CIFAR-10 ensemble underperforming the best model suggests insufficient exploration. Also, transfer finetuning underperforms scratch training, which deserves discussion.

Overall, this is a solid, early demonstration of RL-based architecture search. I recommend acceptance, with clearer cost-aware comparisons and limitations.

title: Machine Comprehension Using Match-LSTM and Answer Pointer
abstract: Abstract:###Machine comprehension of text is an important problem in natural language processing. A recently released dataset, the Stanford Question Answering Dataset (SQuAD), offers a large number of real questions and their answers created by humans through crowdsourcing. SQuAD provides a challenging testbed for evaluating machine comprehension algorithms, partly because compared with previous datasets, in SQuAD the answers do not come from a small set of candidate answers and they have variable lengths. We propose an end-to-end neural architecture for the task. The architecture is based on match-LSTM, a model we proposed previously for textual entailment, and Pointer Net, a sequence-to-sequence model proposed by Vinyals et al. (2015) to constrain the output tokens to be from the input sequences. We propose two ways of using Pointer Net for our tasks. Our experiments show that both of our two models substantially outperform the best results obtained by Rajpurkar et al. (2016) using logistic regression and manually crafted features. Besides, our boundary model also achieves the best performance on the MSMARCO dataset (Nguyen et al. 2016).
review:
The paper presents two end-to-end neural models for SQuAD machine comprehension, combining match-LSTM with Pointer Net. The sequence model predicts answer tokens individually; the boundary model predicts start/end indices and optionally searches spans up to 15 tokens. The boundary model substantially outperforms the logistic-regression baseline and is competitive with contemporary neural systems; attention visualizations and question-type analyses add useful insight.

Strengths: The formulation is clear and well motivated. Repurposing match-LSTM for passage-question matching is sensible, and using Pointer Net to copy spans addresses SQuAD's variable-length extractive answers. The boundary model is simple and effective, and the span-search extension is a practical inference improvement. Ablations on bi-directional preprocessing, Ans-Ptr, dimension, and ensemble are informative.

Weaknesses: The method is largely an application/combination of prior components, so novelty is moderate. The sequence model is under-motivated and under-analyzed; its failure modes versus boundary prediction deserve more discussion. The 15-token search cap is heuristic and may bias evaluation, especially for long answers. The ensemble and search results mix inference-time heuristics with model changes, making comparisons less clean. The paper lacks statistical significance and detailed error analysis beyond length/question-type strata. Attention visualizations are qualitative. Comparisons to concurrent work are limited, and test-set improvements are modest.

Overall, this is a solid, useful contribution with strong empirical results for its time. I recommend acceptance, with clearer separation of model versus inference gains and more error analysis.

title: DeepDSL: A Compilation-based Domain-Specific Language for Deep Learning
abstract: Abstract:###In recent years, Deep Learning (DL) has found great success in domains such as multimedia understanding. However, the complex nature of multimedia data makes it difficult to develop DL-based software. The state-of-the-art tools, such as Caffe, TensorFlow, Torch7, and CNTK, while are successful in their applicable domains, are programming libraries with fixed user interface, internal representation, and execution environment. This makes it difficult to implement portable and customized DL applications. In this paper, we present DeepDSL, a domain specific language (DSL) embedded in Scala, that compiles deep networks written in DeepDSL to Java source code. Deep DSL provides (1) intuitive constructs to support compact encoding of deep networks; (2) symbolic gradient derivation of the networks; (3) static analysis for memory consumption and error detection; and (4) DSL-level optimization to improve memory and runtime efficiency. DeepDSL programs are compiled into compact, efficient, customizable, and portable Java source code, which operates the CUDA and CUDNN interfaces running on NVIDIA GPU via a Java Native Interface (JNI) library. We evaluated DeepDSL with a number of popular DL networks. Our experiments show that the compiled programs have very competitive runtime performance and memory efficiency compared to the existing libraries.
review:
The paper presents DeepDSL, a Scala-embedded DSL compiling deep network definitions to portable Java source invoking CUDA/cuDNN via JCuda. Contributions include compact tensor-function composition, symbolic gradients, static dimension/memory analysis, SSA-based optimization, memory scheduling/reuse, and generated-code customization/persistency. It is evaluated on LeNet, AlexNet, Overfeat, GoogLeNet, VGG, and ResNet against Caffe/TensorFlow.

Strengths: Clear motivation; exposing tensors as indexed scalar expressions enables compiler optimizations and static analysis. Memory scheduling/reuse is practically valuable, evidenced by running ResNet batch 64 where Caffe/TensorFlow OOM. Generated Java portability and readability are appealing, and runtime/memory comparisons are useful.

Weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to one K40c GPU and older CUDA/cuDNN versions; no CPU or multi-GPU scalability. Comparisons are not fully apples-to-apples: TensorFlow uses synthetic data, GoogLeNet main branch only, and different workspace/algorithm choices. Compiler implementation, optimization correctness, and symbolic-gradient validation are underdescribed. Memory accounting excludes some parameter/workspace details and lacks end-to-end training convergence/accuracy comparisons. No ablation isolates gains from SSA, code motion, or memory reuse. DSL expressiveness is demonstrated only on standard feed-forward/ResNet/GoogLeNet; recurrent/dynamic control flow is not addressed. Portability claims rely on JVM plus CUDA availability. Although the memory-efficiency claims are compelling, they are demonstrated mostly through peak-memory snapshots rather than sustained training throughput. The paper would benefit from an explicit artifact/availability statement and convergence plots.

Overall, a solid systems/PL contribution with promising memory efficiency, but evaluation and reproducibility need strengthening. Recommend acceptance with revisions.

title: Bidirectional Attention Flow for Machine Comprehension
abstract: Abstract:###Machine comprehension (MC), answering a query about a given context paragraph, requires modeling complex interactions between the context and the query. Recently, attention mechanisms have been successfully extended to MC. Typically these methods use attention to focus on a small portion of the context and summarize it with a fixed-size vector, couple attentions temporally, and/or often form a uni-directional attention. In this paper we introduce the Bi-Directional Attention Flow (BIDAF) network, a multi-stage hierarchical process that represents the context at different levels of granularity and uses bi-directional attention flow mechanism to obtain a query-aware context representation without early summarization. Our experimental evaluations show that our model achieves the state-of-the-art results in Stanford Question Answering Dataset (SQuAD) and CNN/DailyMail cloze test.
review:
The paper introduces BiDAF, a hierarchical machine comprehension model combining character-level CNNs, pretrained word embeddings, contextual LSTM embeddings, bidirectional attention flow (context-to-query and query-to-context), memory-less attention, and a start/end pointer output layer. It reports state-of-the-art SQuAD and CNN/DailyMail results, with ablations highlighting the importance of C2Q attention and static attention flow.

Strengths: The architecture is clearly motivated and well described. Avoiding early summarization and separating attention from modeling are sensible design choices. Bidirectional attention is convincingly supported by ablations, and qualitative analyses—t-SNE plots, nearest-neighbor tables, and attention matrices—help explain model behavior. The modular output layer enables application to different comprehension tasks.

Weaknesses: The model is complex, with many design choices and hyperparameters; improvements over concurrent systems are modest and leaderboard-based. Ensemble results use 12 training runs, while ablations are single runs without variance or significance testing, making small differences difficult to interpret. The memory-less versus dynamic attention comparison changes capacity and optimization, so causal attribution is not fully isolated. Character CNN, similarity-function, and fusion choices lack sufficient sensitivity analysis. Training cost and inference latency are not analyzed, despite requiring roughly 20 hours per run. Error analysis remains largely qualitative.

Overall, BiDAF is a strong and influential contribution with solid empirical support. I recommend acceptance, with more rigorous statistical comparisons and efficiency analysis.

title: Incorporating long-range consistency in CNN-based texture generation
abstract: Abstract:###Gatys et al. (2015) showed that pair-wise products of features in a convolutional network are a very effective representation of image textures. We propose a simple modification to that representation which makes it possible to incorporate long-range structure into image generation, and to render images that satisfy various symmetry constraints. We show how this can greatly improve rendering of regular textures and of images that contain other kinds of symmetric structure. We also present applications to inpainting and season transfer.
review:
The paper proposes a simple modification to Gatys et al.’s CNN texture synthesis: transformed Gram matrices computed between spatially shifted (or flipped) feature maps, enforcing long-range consistency and symmetry. It demonstrates improved regular textures, inpainting, season transfer, and symmetric patterns, with code released.

Strengths: The idea is clear and well motivated. Relating shifted Gramians to gray-level co-occurrence matrices and MRF-like constraints is insightful. The method is easy to implement as an additional loss and generalizes beyond translation to flipping. Qualitative results show clear gains over standard Gram matrices for brick walls, text, flags, and inpainting; using multiple offsets is shown not to harm diversity in examples.

Weaknesses: Evaluation is almost entirely qualitative, with no quantitative metrics, user study, or comparison to nonparametric patch-based methods on regular textures. The offset/layer schedule and weight choices are heuristic; sensitivity and failure cases are underexplored. Adding cross-correlation terms increases runtime by roughly 80%, but cost/quality trade-offs are not analyzed. Inpainting and season transfer results lack baselines and quantitative evaluation. Claims about diversity preservation and symmetry capture are supported only by selected examples. The transformation-based loss may interact unpredictably with content/style weights.

Overall, this is a promising and practical extension with compelling visuals, but stronger quantitative validation is needed. I recommend acceptance with revisions.

title: Dynamic Coattention Networks For Question Answering
abstract: Abstract:###Several deep learning models have been proposed for question answering. How- ever, due to their single-pass nature, they have no way to recover from local maxima corresponding to incorrect answers. To address this problem, we introduce the Dynamic Coattention Network (DCN) for question answering. The DCN first fuses co-dependent representations of the question and the document in order to focus on relevant parts of both. Then a dynamic pointer decoder iterates over potential answer spans. This iterative procedure enables the model to recover from initial local maxima corresponding to incorrect answers. On the Stanford question answering dataset, a single DCN model improves the previous state of the art from 71.0% F1 to 75.9%, while a DCN ensemble obtains 80.4% F1.
review:
The paper introduces Dynamic Coattention Networks (DCN) for SQuAD-style question answering. DCN encodes document and question with LSTMs, applies bidirectional coattention to produce co-dependent representations, then uses a dynamic pointing decoder that iteratively predicts start and end positions via Highway Maxout Networks. A single model reports 75.9 test F1 and an ensemble 80.4, improving over prior published results.

Strengths: The coattention encoder is clearly described and ablation shows a 1.9 F1 gain over standard attention. The iterative decoder is well motivated and ablations (single iteration, MLP vs. HMN, pool size) support its contribution. Figure 5 qualitatively illustrates escaping local maxima, and analysis across document/question/answer lengths is useful. Results are strong and leaderboard comparisons are timely.

Weaknesses: The method is complex, with many hyperparameters and architectural choices that are not fully justified. The iterative decoder can oscillate between plausible spans (as the paper notes), but convergence behavior and stopping criteria are only lightly analyzed. Ablations are single-run without variance or significance tests, so modest differences are hard to interpret. Comparisons to concurrent unpublished leaderboard models are inherently unstable. Training cost and inference latency are not reported. Error analysis by question type is brief.

Overall, DCN is a strong, well-validated contribution with a clear ablation story. I recommend acceptance, with requests for statistical reporting, decoder convergence analysis, and efficiency details.

title: SampleRNN: An Unconditional End-to-End Neural Audio Generation Model
abstract: Abstract:###In this paper we propose a novel model for unconditional audio generation task that generates one audio sample at a time. We show that our model which profits from combining memory-less modules, namely autoregressive multilayer perceptron, and stateful recurrent neural networks in a hierarchical structure is de facto powerful to capture the underlying sources of variations in temporal domain for very long time on three datasets of different nature. Human evaluation on the generated samples indicate that our model is preferred over competing models. We also show how each component of the model contributes to the exhibited performance.
review:
The paper introduces SampleRNN, a hierarchical autoregressive model for raw audio that combines frame-level RNNs operating at coarse temporal resolutions with a sample-level MLP that predicts one quantized sample at a time. Conditioning vectors are upsampled across tiers, and truncated BPTT enables training on short subsequences. Experiments on speech, onomatopoeia, and piano music report improved test NLL over an RNN baseline and a reimplemented WaveNet, plus human preference for 3-tier SampleRNN and informative ablations (embedding, Multi-Softmax, subsequence length, GMM outputs). The memory-span experiment with injected silence is a nice diagnostic.

Strengths: clear architecture, tractable training, strong empirical validation across heterogeneous audio, and useful ablations. The different-clock-rate design is well motivated and flexible.

Weaknesses: the WaveNet comparison is not authoritative because of missing hyperparameters and compute constraints. Human evaluation lacks rater counts, confidence intervals, and inter-rater agreement. NLL comparisons across quantized and GMM variants are not fully commensurate. The 2-tier model wins on Music while 3-tier wins on Blizzard, but guidance for choosing tiers is limited. The speaker-memory result (83%) lacks statistical analysis and uses one dataset. Training cost and sample-generation latency are not reported.

Overall, this is a solid, well-written contribution with convincing audio samples. I recommend acceptance, requesting clearer evaluation statistics, cost reporting, and tempered WaveNet claims.

title: Metacontrol for Adaptive Imagination-Based Optimization
abstract: Abstract:###Many machine learning systems are built to solve the hardest examples of a particular task, which often makes them large and expensive to run---especially with respect to the easier examples, which might require much less computation. For an agent with a limited computational budget, this *one-size-fits-all* approach may result in the agent wasting valuable computation on easy examples, while not spending enough on hard examples. Rather than learning a single, fixed policy for solving all instances of a task, we introduce a metacontroller which learns to optimize a sequence of *imagined* internal simulations over predictive models of the world in order to construct a more informed, and more economical, solution. The metacontroller component is a model-free reinforcement learning agent, which decides both how many iterations of the optimization procedure to run, as well as which model to consult on each iteration. The models (which we call *experts*) can be state transition models, action-value functions, or any other mechanism that provides information useful for solving the task, and can be learned on-policy or off-policy in parallel with the metacontroller. When the metacontroller, controller, and experts were trained with *interaction networks* (Battaglia et al., 2016) as expert models, our approach was able to solve a challenging decision-making problem under complex non-linear dynamics. The metacontroller learned to adapt the amount of computation it performed to the difficulty of the task, and learned how to choose which experts to consult by factoring in both their reliability and individual computational resource costs. This allowed the metacontroller to achieve a lower overall cost (task loss plus computational cost) than more traditional fixed policy approaches. These results demonstrate that our approach is a powerful framework for using rich forward models for efficient model-based reinforcement learning.
review:
The paper introduces a metacontroller that learns when to stop an imagination-based optimization loop and which expert model to consult, jointly trading task loss against computational cost. A manager policy selects ponder/execute and expert choice, while a controller proposes controls and a memory summarizes history. Experiments on a gravitational spaceship task show adaptive per-episode computation, lower total cost than fixed-iteration baselines, and preference for the more reliable interaction-network expert.

Strengths: The framing of adaptive computation as a meta-level MDP is clear and well motivated. The architecture is modular, and the manager’s learned speed–accuracy trade-off is demonstrated across ponder costs. Per-episode difficulty analysis is convincing, and comparisons against reactive/iterative agents are informative. The multi-expert analysis, while mixed, honestly reports limitations.

Weaknesses: Evaluation is confined to one synthetic physics domain and a one-shot control task, limiting generality claims. The multi-expert metacontroller yields only modest gains and is hindered by the entropy term, which the authors acknowledge but do not resolve. Expert and critic training details are largely deferred to appendices, complicating reproducibility. The manager uses REINFORCE, but variance, seeds, and statistical significance are underreported. Computational costs are modeled as fixed per-expert constants rather than measured wall-clock or energy costs. The claim of superiority over gradient-based model-based optimization is speculative and untested.

Overall, this is a promising and clearly presented framework with honest analysis, but broader tasks and stronger multi-expert results are needed. I recommend acceptance with revisions.

title: Exploring Sparsity in Recurrent Neural Networks
abstract: Abstract:###Recurrent neural networks (RNN) are widely used to solve a variety of problems and as the quantity of data and the amount of available compute have increased, so have model sizes. The number of parameters in recent state-of-the-art networks makes them hard to deploy, especially on mobile phones and embedded devices. The challenge is due to both the size of the model and the time it takes to evaluate it. In order to deploy these RNNs efficiently, we propose a technique to reduce the parameters of a network by pruning weights during the initial training of the network. At the end of training, the parameters of the network are sparse while accuracy is still close to the original dense neural network. The network size is reduced by 8Ã— and the time required to train the model remains constant. Additionally, we can prune a larger dense network to achieve better than baseline performance while still reducing the total number of parameters significantly. Pruning RNNs reduces the size of the model and can also help achieve significant inference time speed-up using sparse GEMMs. Benchmarks show that using our technique model size can be reduced by 90% and speed-up is around 2Ã— to 7Ã—.
review:
The paper proposes gradual magnitude pruning during RNN training using binary masks and a monotonically increasing per-layer threshold schedule. On Deep Speech 2-style bidirectional RNNs and GRUs for speech recognition, it reaches ~88–92% sparsity, reducing model size by ~8× without extra retraining, and shows larger sparse models can match or beat dense baselines. Gradual pruning also outperforms hard pruning. Speedups of roughly 2–7× are reported for sparse matrix-vector products.

Strengths: the method is simple, easy to integrate, and avoids costly prune-and-retrain cycles. The comparison against smaller dense models is valuable, as is the analysis of layer-wise pruning. Results are practically relevant for deployment.

Weaknesses: evaluation is limited to one ASR dataset and Deep Speech 2 variants; generalization to language modeling and other RNN tasks is untested. Same-size sparse models lose 10–20% relative accuracy, and the hyperparameter schedule requires a previously trained model to set q, adding tuning burden. Runtime results use cuSPARSE at batch size 1 and fall far short of bandwidth-limited expectations; end-to-end latency, energy, and mobile deployment are not measured. No variance or significance is reported. The claim of constant training time is plausible but not quantified.

Overall, a practical and well-motivated contribution with clear empirical benefits, but broader evaluation and efficiency accounting are needed. I recommend acceptance with revisions.

title: Lossy Image Compression with Compressive Autoencoders
abstract: Abstract:###We propose a new approach to the problem of optimizing autoencoders for lossy image compression. New media formats, changing hardware technology, as well as diverse requirements and content types create a need for compression algorithms which are more flexible than existing codecs. Autoencoders have the potential to address this need, but are difficult to optimize directly due to the inherent non-differentiabilty of the compression loss. We here show that minimal changes to the loss are sufficient to train deep autoencoders competitive with JPEG 2000 and outperforming recently proposed approaches based on RNNs. Our network is furthermore computationally efficient thanks to a sub-pixel architecture, which makes it suitable for high-resolution images. This is in contrast to previous work on autoencoders for compression using coarser approximations, shallower architectures, computationally expensive methods, or focusing on small images.
review:
The paper proposes compressive autoencoders for lossy image compression. It handles non-differentiable rounding by replacing only its backward derivative with identity, approximates entropy rate via a Jensen upper bound, models quantized coefficients with Gaussian scale mixtures, and uses a sub-pixel convolutional architecture for efficient high-resolution decoding. It also introduces scale parameters for variable bit rates and incremental coefficient training. On Kodak, it is competitive with JPEG 2000 and improves over an RNN-based baseline on perceptual metrics.

Strengths: The approach is simple and well motivated. Keeping rounding in the forward pass while using a straight-through gradient avoids the decoder inverting a smooth approximation. The entropy-rate bound and GSM model are sensible. The sub-pixel architecture and variable-rate finetuning are practical contributions. Comparisons use multiple perceptual metrics, and the method supports content- and metric-specific optimization.

Weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to 24 Kodak images and MSE training, with no large-scale or diverse-content study. The comparison to Toderici et al. uses an implementation without entropy coding, which weakens the claimed advantage. Actual bitstream overhead, encoder/decoder runtime, memory, and complexity relative to codecs are not quantified. The ensemble selects the best autoencoder per image, increasing encoding cost. The entropy model is trained separately and may not be jointly optimal. Ablations on quantization-gradient choices are largely qualitative.

Overall, this is a solid and practical contribution with promising results, but broader evaluation and complete rate-distortion accounting are needed. I recommend acceptance with revisions.

title: Structured Attention Networks
abstract: Abstract:###Attention networks have proven to be an effective approach for embedding categorical inference within a deep neural network. However, for many tasks we may want to model richer structural dependencies without abandoning end-to-end training. In this work, we experiment with incorporating richer structural distributions, encoded using graphical models, within deep networks. We show that these structured attention networks are simple extensions of the basic attention procedure, and that they allow for extending attention beyond the standard soft-selection approach, such as attending to partial segmentations or to subtrees. We experiment with two different classes of structured attention networks: a linear-chain conditional random field and a graph-based parsing model, and describe how these models can be practically implemented as neural network layers. Experiments show that this approach is effective for incorporating structural biases, and structured attention networks outperform baseline attention models on a variety of synthetic and real tasks: tree transduction, neural machine translation, question answering, and natural language inference. We further find that models trained in this way learn interesting unsupervised hidden representations that generalize simple attention.
review:
The paper introduces Structured Attention Networks, replacing standard categorical softmax attention with differentiable inference in graphical models: a linear-chain CRF for segmentation/subsequence selection and a graph-based dependency parser for syntactic tree attention. Forward-backward and inside-outside inference are implemented as neural layers, with signed log-space backpropagation, and models are trained end-to-end. Experiments cover synthetic tree transduction, Japanese–English translation, question answering, and natural language inference.

Strengths: The formulation is clean and general, casting attention as expectation under a structured distribution. The synthetic tree-transduction results are striking, and attention visualizations show meaningful learned structure. The implementation notes on numerical stability and inference backpropagation are useful. Applying structured layers as internal attention rather than output layers is a sensible contribution.

Weaknesses: Real-task gains are uneven—translation improvements are modest and possibly insignificant, and the marginal-normalization term in NMT departs from the stated expectation interpretation. The paper lacks statistical significance and systematic ablations on inference approximation, normalization, and runtime. QA and NLI results are referenced but not fully presented in the main text. Training and inference costs of structured layers versus simple attention are not quantified. The synthetic task may overstate benefits.

Overall, this is a well-motivated and technically solid contribution with a convincing synthetic demonstration, but stronger empirical and efficiency analysis on real tasks is needed. I recommend acceptance with revisions.

title: Zoneout: Regularizing RNNs by Randomly Preserving Hidden Activations
abstract: Abstract:###We propose zoneout, a novel method for regularizing RNNs. At each timestep, zoneout stochastically forces some hidden units to maintain their previous values. Like dropout, zoneout uses random noise to train a pseudo-ensemble, improving generalization. But by preserving instead of dropping hidden units, gradient information and state information are more readily propagated through time, as in feedforward stochastic depth networks. We perform an empirical investigation of various RNN regularizers, and find that zoneout gives significant performance improvements across tasks. We achieve competitive results with relatively simple models in character- and word-level language modelling on the Penn Treebank and Text8 datasets, and combining with recurrent batch normalization yields state-of-the-art results on permuted sequential MNIST.
review:
The paper proposes zoneout, a simple RNN regularizer that stochastically preserves hidden units’ previous activations rather than zeroing them as dropout does. It applies identity masks to LSTM cells and hidden states, and is motivated as a pseudo-ensemble method that improves forward information and backward gradient flow. Experiments cover character- and word-level Penn Treebank, Text8, and permuted sequential MNIST, with comparisons to recurrent dropout, weight noise, norm stabilization, and stochastic depth.

Strengths: The idea is clean, general, and easy to implement. The LSTM formulation and relationship to dropout/stochastic depth are clearly explained. Results are competitive: character-level PTB reaches 1.27 BPC, word-level PTB improves perplexity from 78.4 to 77.4 when combined with dropout, and zoneout plus recurrent batch normalization achieves state-of-the-art pMNIST error. The gradient-flow analysis provides useful mechanistic support.

Weaknesses: Gains on word-level PTB are modest, and several baselines are reimplementations rather than directly comparable published systems. Hyperparameter choices for cell versus hidden zoneout are task-specific, and the paper lacks variance estimates or significance tests. The test-time expectation approximation is not analyzed in depth. Evaluation is limited to language modeling and pMNIST; broader sequence tasks would strengthen generality.

Overall, zoneout is a well-motivated and effective regularizer with convincing empirical support. I recommend acceptance, requesting statistical reporting and broader task validation.

title: Deep Probabilistic Programming
abstract: Abstract:###We propose Edward, a Turing-complete probabilistic programming language. Edward defines two compositional representationsâ€”random variables and inference. By treating inference as a first class citizen, on a par with modeling, we show that probabilistic programming can be as flexible and computationally efficient as traditional deep learning. For flexibility, Edward makes it easy to fit the same model using a variety of composable inference methods, ranging from point estimation to variational inference to MCMC. In addition, Edward can reuse the modeling representation as part of inference, facilitating the design of rich variational models and generative adversarial networks. For efficiency, Edward is integrated into TensorFlow, providing significant speedups over existing probabilistic systems. For example, we show on a benchmark logistic regression task that Edward is at least 35x faster than Stan and 6x faster than PyMC3. Further, Edward incurs no runtime overhead: it is as fast as handwritten TensorFlow.
review:
The paper presents Edward, a Turing-complete probabilistic programming language embedded in TensorFlow, with two compositional representations: random variables and inference. Random variables are graph-embedded objects supporting sampling and log densities; inference is a first-class abstraction covering variational inference, Monte Carlo, MAP, GANs, and composed inference such as variational EM. The paper argues this design supports rich variational models, stochastic control flow, data subsampling, and model reuse, while inheriting TensorFlow efficiency.

Strengths: The inference-as-first-class-citizen framing is compelling and well motivated. The examples—VAE, Bayesian RNN, Dirichlet process mixture, GAN—are concise and demonstrate flexibility beyond standard PPLs. Integrating with TensorFlow enables GPU acceleration and distributed execution. The reported speedups over Stan and PyMC3, and parity with handwritten TensorFlow, are practically important. The composition of inference procedures is a valuable conceptual contribution.

Weaknesses: The evaluation section is incomplete in the provided text, with limited empirical detail on accuracy, scalability, and overhead beyond the logistic regression benchmark. Comparisons with Stan/PyMC3 need clearer discussion of sampler settings and hardware fairness. The language’s Turing-completeness claims are not formally developed. Error handling, debugging, and inference correctness are not addressed. Many advanced features (conjugacy detection, exact inference) are described as future work.

Overall, Edward is an influential and well-designed system with strong conceptual and practical merit. I recommend acceptance, requesting fuller empirical validation and clearer comparison protocols.

title: LR-GAN: Layered Recursive Generative Adversarial Networks for Image Generation
abstract: Abstract:###We present LR-GAN: an adversarial image generation model which takes scene structure and context into account. Unlike previous generative adversarial networks (GANs), the proposed GAN learns to generate image background and foregrounds separately and recursively, and stitch the foregrounds on the background in a contextually relevant manner to produce a complete natural image. For each foreground, the model learns to generate its appearance, shape and pose. The whole model is unsupervised, and is trained in an end-to-end manner with conventional gradient descent methods. The experiments demonstrate that LR-GAN can generate more natural images with objects that are more human recognizable than baseline GANs.
review:
The paper proposes LR-GAN, a layered recursive GAN that generates a background and then recurrently composes foreground objects with separate appearance, mask, and affine pose parameters. Foregrounds are warped and alpha-composited onto the canvas, yielding unsupervised foreground-background masks. Experiments cover synthetic MNIST-ONE/TWO, CIFAR-10, and CUB-200, with comparisons to DCGAN and proposed adversarial accuracy/divergence metrics.

Strengths: The inductive bias toward layered scene composition is well motivated and clearly implemented. Factorizing appearance, shape, and pose is sensible and enables unsupervised mask emergence. The recursive LSTM conditioning encourages contextual placement, as shown qualitatively on MNIST-TWO and CUB-200. The controlled relationship to DCGAN at the first timestep is useful.

Weaknesses: The model assumes the number of objects/timesteps is known, limiting generality. The main text emphasizes qualitative results; quantitative tables for Inception score and the proposed metrics are not shown in the provided pages, and ablations are deferred. The proposed metrics require human annotations and separately trained classifiers, raising circularity concerns. Comparisons are mostly to DCGAN, without stronger baselines or statistical reporting. Training stability and failure cases are not analyzed.

Overall, LR-GAN is a promising compositional generative model with a clear structural contribution, but evaluation and generality need strengthening. I recommend acceptance with revisions.

title: Variational Lossy Autoencoder
abstract: Abstract:###Representation learning seeks to expose certain aspects of observed data in a learned representation that*s amenable to downstream tasks like classification. For instance, a good representation for 2D images might be one that describes only global structure and discards information about detailed texture. In this paper, we present a simple but principled method to learn such global representations by combining Variational Autoencoder (VAE) with neural autoregressive models such as RNN, MADE and PixelRNN/CNN. Our proposed VAE model allows us to have control over what the global latent code can learn and , by designing the architecture accordingly, we can force the global latent code to discard irrelevant information such as texture in 2D images, and hence the code only ``autoencodes** data in a lossy fashion. In addition, by leveraging autoregressive models as both prior distribution and decoding distribution , we can greatly improve generative modeling performance of VAEs, achieving new state-of-the-art results on MNIST, OMNIGLOT and Caltech-101 as well as competitive results on CIFAR10.
review:
The paper introduces the Variational Lossy Autoencoder (VLAE), combining VAEs with autoregressive models for both the prior and decoder. Its key insight is a bits-back coding explanation of why powerful autoregressive decoders often ignore latent codes: information that can be modeled locally is encoded locally, leaving only the remainder for the latent variable. The authors exploit this by constraining the PixelCNN decoder’s receptive field, forcing global structure into the latent code while local texture is modeled autoregressively. They also propose an autoregressive-flow prior, shown to be equivalent to an inverse autoregressive-flow posterior along the encoder path but with a deeper, more expressive generator at no additional training cost.

Strengths: The theoretical analysis is clear and practically useful. The lossy-code construction is principled and supported by qualitative decompression examples on MNIST and Omniglot. Density-estimation results on MNIST, Omniglot, and Caltech-101 Silhouettes are strong, and the AF-prior/IAF-posterior equivalence is a neat observation.

Weaknesses: Experiments are limited to small binary images; no natural-image or downstream representation-learning evaluation is presented. The claim that the latent code captures “global” information is demonstrated qualitatively, with acknowledged failures on Omniglot. Comparisons and ablations are partially deferred, and the receptive-field design is task-specific. Training stability and computational costs are not fully quantified.

Overall, this is a well-motivated and theoretically insightful contribution with strong density-estimation results. I recommend acceptance, requesting broader evaluation and more systematic analysis of learned representations.

title: A recurrent neural network without chaos
abstract: Abstract:###We introduce an exceptionally simple gated recurrent neural network (RNN) that achieves performance comparable to well-known gated architectures, such as LSTMs and GRUs, on the word-level language modeling task. We prove that our model has simple, predicable and non-chaotic dynamics. This stands in stark contrast to more standard gated architectures, whose underlying dynamical systems exhibit chaotic behavior.
review:
The paper proposes the Chaos-Free Network (CFN), a simple gated RNN combining forget and input gates with tanh recurrence. It proves relaxation bounds and convergence to the zero state for the input-free dynamics, arguing CFN avoids the chaotic autonomous behavior observed in LSTM/GRU, and compares CFN against LSTM/GRU on Penn Treebank and Text8 word-level language modeling.

Strengths: The architecture is simple, clearly specified, and easy to implement. The dynamical-systems framing is well motivated, and Lemmas 1–2 give interpretable activation/decay behavior plus a multilayer extension. Experiments match parameter counts and show competitive perplexity: CFN reaches 106.3 versus LSTM 105.1 on PTB and 142.0 versus 139.9 on Text8, supporting the claim that chaotic dynamics are not necessary for strong language modeling. The paper is readable and candid about the model’s minimalist dynamics.

Weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to word-level language modeling, so generality is unsupported. The main theoretical guarantee—convergence to zero—is weak and does not rule out complex input-driven transients. The claim that chaos cannot explain RNN success is stronger than the evidence. Novelty relative to existing gated RNNs needs clearer positioning. Hyperparameter search, variance, and significance tests are absent; small perplexity gaps make parity tentative.

Overall, CFN is a clean, well-motivated architecture with interesting theory and competitive but narrow evidence. I recommend acceptance, requesting broader task validation and statistical reporting.

title: Outrageously Large Neural Networks: The Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts Layer
abstract: Abstract:###The capacity of a neural network to absorb information is limited by its number of parameters. Conditional computation, where parts of the network are active on a per-example basis, has been proposed in theory as a way of dramatically increasing model capacity without a proportional increase in computation. In practice, however, there are significant algorithmic and performance challenges. In this work, we address these challenges and finally realize the promise of conditional computation, achieving greater than 1000x improvements in model capacity with only minor losses in computational efficiency on modern GPU clusters. We introduce a Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts layer (MoE), consisting of up to thousands of feed-forward sub-networks. A trainable gating network determines a sparse combination of these experts to use for each example. We apply the MoE to the tasks of language modeling and machine translation, where model capacity is critical for absorbing the vast quantities of knowledge available in the training corpora. We present model architectures in which a MoE with up to 137 billion parameters is applied convolutionally between stacked LSTM layers. On large language modeling and machine translation benchmarks, these models achieve significantly better results than state-of-the-art at lower computational cost.
review:
The paper introduces a Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layer that enables conditional computation at massive scale, with up to 137 billion parameters and only minor computational overhead. A trainable noisy top-k gating network selects a sparse subset of feed-forward experts per example; the layer is applied convolutionally between stacked LSTM layers for language modeling and machine translation. The paper also addresses key systems challenges—shrinking expert batches, network bandwidth, and expert load balancing—through mixed data/model parallelism and auxiliary importance/load losses.

Strengths: The work is ambitious and practically significant, demonstrating that conditional computation can deliver large capacity gains without proportional compute. Empirical results are strong: on the 1B-word benchmark, high-capacity MoE models improve perplexity substantially at lower cost than prior LSTM baselines; on WMT En→Fr/De and a production dataset, MoE models improve BLEU. The systems contributions—convolutional batching, hierarchical MoEs, and balancing losses—are clearly explained and likely useful beyond these tasks.

Weaknesses: The top-k gating is discontinuous and non-differentiable at selection boundaries; the paper acknowledges this but provides little theoretical or stability analysis. Load-balancing and importance losses require hand-tuned weights, and sensitivity is not thoroughly ablated. Results depend on large GPU clusters, limiting reproducibility. Comparisons across training epochs and architectures are somewhat uneven, and expert specialization is mostly qualitative. Broader task validation and variance reporting would strengthen the claims.

Overall, this is an influential and well-executed paper with convincing scale results. I recommend acceptance, requesting more ablation and stability analysis.

title: Tree-structured decoding with doubly-recurrent neural networks
abstract: Abstract:###We propose a neural network architecture for generating tree-structured objects from encoded representations. The core of the method is a doubly-recurrent neural network that models separately the width and depth recurrences across the tree, and combines them inside each cell to generate an output. The topology of the tree is explicitly modeled, allowing the network to predict both content and topology of the tree when decoding. That is, given only an encoded vector representation, the network is able to simultaneously generate a tree from it and predict labels for the nodes. We test this architecture in an encoder-decoder framework, where we train a network to encode a sentence as a vector, and then generate a tree structure from it. The experimental results show the effectiveness of this architecture at recovering latent tree structure in sequences and at mapping sentences to simple functional programs.
review:
The paper proposes a doubly-recurrent neural network (DRNN) for tree-structured decoding from encoded representations. Each node maintains separate ancestral (parent-to-child) and fraternal (sibling-to-sibling) recurrent states, which are combined for label prediction; explicit topology modules predict whether a node has children or a next sibling, avoiding special padding tokens. The model is trained end-to-end with backpropagation through structure and evaluated on synthetic tree recovery, IFTTT sentence-to-program mapping, and a small-scale machine translation setting.

Strengths: The architecture is well motivated and cleanly separates depth and width recurrences, giving a more appropriate inductive bias than sequence decoders for tree generation. Explicit topology prediction is a sensible alternative to stopping tokens, and the formulation is concise. Experiments show the method can recover latent trees and outperforms SEQ2TREE and other baselines on IFTTT, especially with LSTM modules; the qualitative MT study suggests useful structural properties.

Weaknesses: Evaluation is somewhat narrow and preliminary. The synthetic task is toy-scale, and the MT experiment is qualitative with limited data, so general effectiveness is unclear. Teacher forcing creates exposure bias, acknowledged but unresolved. Topology sampling/beam search and loss weighting are not deeply analyzed, and variance/significance are absent. Comparisons on noisy IFTTT data could be strengthened with more controlled ablations. Complexity and scalability to large trees are not discussed.

Overall, DRNN is a novel and promising tree decoder with encouraging results. I recommend acceptance, requesting stronger quantitative MT evaluation and ablation studies.

title: Introspection:Accelerating Neural Network Training By Learning Weight Evolution
abstract: Abstract:###Neural Networks are function approximators that have achieved state-of-the-art accuracy in numerous machine learning tasks. In spite of their great success in terms of accuracy, their large training time makes it difficult to use them for various tasks. In this paper, we explore the idea of learning weight evolution pattern from a simple network for accelerating training of novel neural networks. We use a neural network to learn the training pattern from MNIST classification and utilize it to accelerate training of neural networks used for CIFAR-10 and ImageNet classification. Our method has a low memory footprint and is computationally efficient. This method can also be used with other optimizers to give faster convergence. The results indicate a general trend in the weight evolution during training of neural networks.
review:
The paper proposes Introspection, a method that learns weight-evolution patterns from a simple network trained on MNIST and uses a forecasting network to accelerate training of novel networks on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet. It claims low memory footprint, computational efficiency, parallel layer updates, and compatibility with existing optimizers.

Strengths: The motivation is clear, and the related-work positioning against learned optimizers and synthetic gradients is reasonable. The preliminary histogram analysis suggesting that many weights change little during training is an interesting observation and could motivate a lightweight forecasting approach.

Weaknesses: The submitted content does not specify the forecasting architecture, training objective, update schedule, or how predicted weights are integrated into training. No quantitative results are provided, so claims of faster convergence and cross-dataset/architecture generalization are unsupported. Evidence for a “general trend” is only qualitative histograms, and it is unclear whether MNIST observations transfer to CIFAR-10 or ImageNet. Memory and compute benefits are asserted but not measured. Baselines against Adam/RMSProp and learned-optimizer methods are absent. The method may overfit to MNIST dynamics, and asynchronous invocation could destabilize training.

Overall, the idea is interesting but the paper is incomplete and lacks empirical validation. I recommend rejection in its current form, encouraging full method details, convergence curves, wall-clock comparisons, and ablations across architectures and optimizers.

title: Hyperband: Bandit-Based Configuration Evaluation for Hyperparameter Optimization
abstract: Abstract:###Performance of machine learning algorithms depends critically on identifying a good set of hyperparameters. While recent approaches use Bayesian Optimization to adaptively select configurations, we focus on speeding up random search through adaptive resource allocation. We present Hyperband, a novel algorithm for hyperparameter optimization that is simple, flexible, and theoretically sound. Hyperband is a principled early-stoppping method that adaptively allocates a predefined resource, e.g., iterations, data samples or number of features, to randomly sampled configurations. We compare Hyperband with state-of-the-art Bayesian Optimization methods on several hyperparameter optimization problems. We observe that Hyperband can provide over an order of magnitude speedups over competitors on a variety of neural network and kernel-based learning problems.
review:
The paper introduces Hyperband, a bandit-based hyperparameter optimization method that speeds up random search through adaptive resource allocation. It wraps successive halving in multiple brackets over different exploration/exploitation tradeoffs, addressing the “n versus B/n” problem, and evaluates Hyperband against SMAC, TPE, Spearmint, random search, and SMAC with early stopping on CIFAR-10, MRBI, SVHN, and kernel classification tasks.

Strengths: The algorithm is simple, flexible, and easy to implement, with a clear motivation and useful intuition. The bracket construction is principled, and the theoretical overview explains why adaptive allocation can outperform uniform budgets. Empirical results are strong: Hyperband is often an order of magnitude faster than Bayesian optimization and up to 70× faster than random search, while being less variable across trials. The ablations comparing individual brackets and repeated exploratory brackets are informative, and the paper honestly notes when SMAC with early stopping is competitive.

Weaknesses: Hyperband relies on random configuration sampling, so it may underperform adaptive selection in low-dimensional or highly structured spaces. The analysis assumes resource-performance envelopes behave favorably, and slow-starting configurations can be prematurely discarded. Sensitivity to η and R is discussed but not thoroughly ablated. Comparisons are limited to vision and kernel methods, with no NLP or reinforcement learning tasks. The theoretical treatment is deferred, and the Fabolas comparison is missing due to technical issues.

Overall, Hyperband is a well-motivated, practical, and empirically convincing contribution. I recommend acceptance, requesting more sensitivity analysis and broader task validation.

title: Lie-Access Neural Turing Machines
abstract: Abstract:###External neural memory structures have recently become a popular tool for algorithmic deep learning (Graves et al. 2014; Weston et al. 2014). These models generally utilize differentiable versions of traditional discrete memory-access structures (random access, stacks, tapes) to provide the storage necessary for computational tasks. In this work, we argue that these neural memory systems lack specific structure important for relative indexing, and propose an alternative model, Lie-access memory, that is explicitly designed for the neural setting. In this paradigm, memory is accessed using a continuous head in a key-space manifold. The head is moved via Lie group actions, such as shifts or rotations, generated by a controller, and memory access is performed by linear smoothing in key space. We argue that Lie groups provide a natural generalization of discrete memory structures, such as Turing machines, as they provide inverse and identity operators while maintaining differentiability. To experiment with this approach, we implement a simplified Lie-access neural Turing machine (LANTM) with different Lie groups. We find that this approach is able to perform well on a range of algorithmic tasks.
review:
The paper proposes Lie-access memory for neural Turing machines, arguing that relative indexing in neural memory should satisfy differentiability, identity, invertibility, and associativity. Memory keys live on a manifold, and a continuous read/write head moves via Lie group actions such as shifts or rotations; reads use distance-based linear smoothing. The authors implement LANTM (additive shifts in R²) and SLANTM (SO(3) rotations on S²), and compare against LSTM, random-access memory, and a simplified RAM/tape hybrid on algorithmic tasks including copy, reverse, bigram flip, addition, odd-first, repeat-copy, and priority sort.

Strengths: The Lie-group framing is elegant and well motivated, providing a principled alternative to soft tape shifts that lack true inverses. The architecture is clearly described, and the combination of relative Lie access with random-access interpolation is sensible. Experiments show strong generalization to 2× length examples: inverse-square LANTM and SLANTM achieve over 90% coarse accuracy on most tasks, notably solving odd-first and repeat-copy where baselines fail. Qualitative PCA visualizations revealing learned circular and linear memory structures are compelling.

Weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to small synthetic algorithmic tasks, with no larger-scale or real-world sequence problems. Baselines use simplified NTM variants rather than full NTM/DNC implementations, weakening claims of superiority. Write/erase behavior is rudimentary, and sensitivity to manifold choice, distance metric, and temperature is not thoroughly ablated. Theoretical guarantees beyond group axioms are absent, and scalability to long sequences is unclear.

Overall, this is a novel and well-presented memory architecture with promising algorithmic results. I recommend acceptance, requesting stronger baselines and broader task validation.

title: Quasi-Recurrent Neural Networks
abstract: Abstract:###Recurrent neural networks are a powerful tool for modeling sequential data, but the dependence of each timestepâ€™s computation on the previous timestepâ€™s output limits parallelism and makes RNNs unwieldy for very long sequences. We introduce quasi-recurrent neural networks (QRNNs), an approach to neural sequence modeling that alternates convolutional layers, which apply in parallel across timesteps, and a minimalist recurrent pooling function that applies in parallel across channels. Despite lacking trainable recurrent layers, stacked QRNNs have better predictive accuracy than stacked LSTMs of the same hidden size. Due to their increased parallelism, they are up to 16 times faster at train and test time. Experiments on language modeling, sentiment classification, and character-level neural machine translation demonstrate these advantages and underline the viability of QRNNs as a basic building block for a variety of sequence tasks.
review:
The paper proposes quasi-recurrent neural networks (QRNNs), which alternate masked convolutional layers—parallel across timesteps—with a minimalist recurrent pooling function that operates independently per channel. Variants include f-, fo-, and ifo-pooling, zoneout adapted to the pooling gates, densely connected layers, and an attention-based encoder–decoder. Experiments cover IMDb sentiment classification, Penn Treebank language modeling, and character-level IWSLT German–English translation.

Strengths: The architecture is simple, clearly motivated, and effectively combines CNN parallelism with RNN-style order dependence. Speed results are compelling, with up to 16× faster training/inference than cuDNN LSTMs and large gains on long sequences. Accuracy is competitive or better: IMDb 91.4%, PTB test perplexity 78.3 with zoneout, and character-level MT BLEU 19.41 versus 16.53 for an equal-sized LSTM. The zoneout formulation is elegant, and hidden-state visualizations suggest interpretability.

Weaknesses: The recurrent pooling is highly constrained, which may limit expressivity for tasks requiring complex long-range state updates. PTB gains are modest and not state-of-the-art. MT evaluation is limited to one character-level language pair, and BLEU remains below word-level attention baselines. Some comparisons vary in parameter count and optimization details. Speed claims depend on hardware and library implementations, and no theoretical analysis of representational capacity is provided.

Overall, QRNN is a well-executed, practical architecture with strong speed and competitive accuracy. I recommend acceptance, requesting broader MT validation and expressivity analysis.

title: Recurrent Environment Simulators
abstract: Abstract:###Models that can simulate how environments change in response to actions can be used by agents to plan and act efficiently.
