We improve on previous environment simulators from high-dimensional pixel observations by introducing recurrent neural networks that are able to make temporally and spatially coherent predictions for hundreds of time-steps into the future. We present an in-depth analysis of the factors affecting performance, providing the most extensive attempt to advance the understanding of the properties of these models. We address the issue of computationally inefficiency with a model that does not need to generate a high-dimensional image at each time-step. We show that our approach can be used to improve exploration and is adaptable to many diverse environments, namely 10 Atari games, a 3D car racing environment, and complex 3D mazes.
review:
The paper proposes recurrent environment simulators that predict future observations/state from actions and pixels. It builds on Oh et al. by allowing actions to directly condition state transitions, introducing prediction-independent simulators that avoid decoding an image every step, and extensively analyzing training with observation- versus prediction-dependent transitions. Experiments cover 10 Atari games, 3D mazes, and TORCS, with long-horizon rollouts, interactive simulation, and model-based exploration.

Strengths: The architectural changes are simple and well motivated, and the prediction-independent variant offers clear computational savings. The training-scheme analysis is unusually thorough: the finding that consecutive prediction-dependent transitions improve long-term accuracy while hurting sharpness is useful and well supported. The paper evaluates diverse environments and reports both error curves and qualitative rollouts, and the ablations on warm-up length, prediction length, and truncated BPTT are informative.

Weaknesses: Long-horizon pixel predictions remain blurry and sometimes lose key objects, and MSE curves can mislead about simulator usefulness. Evaluation is largely deterministic and discrete-action; stochastic dynamics are not addressed. Downstream benefits for planning/exploration are asserted but not quantified with control performance. The compute budget and hyperparameter sensitivity limit reproducibility. Some conclusions rely on video inspection rather than systematic metrics.

Overall, this is a strong empirical and conceptual contribution to model-based RL. I recommend acceptance, requesting downstream planning metrics, stochastic-environment tests, and more object-level evaluation.

title: EPOpt: Learning Robust Neural Network Policies Using Model Ensembles
abstract: Abstract:###Sample complexity and safety are major challenges when learning policies with reinforcement learning for real-world tasks, especially when the policies are represented using rich function approximators like deep neural networks. Model-based methods where the real-world target domain is approximated using a simulated source domain provide an avenue to tackle the above challenges by augmenting real data with simulated data. However, discrepancies between the simulated source domain and the target domain pose a challenge for simulated training. We introduce the EPOpt algorithm, which uses an ensemble of simulated source domains and a form of adversarial training to learn policies that are robust and generalize to a broad range of possible target domains, including to unmodeled effects. Further, the probability distribution over source domains in the ensemble can be adapted using data from the target domain and approximate Bayesian methods, to progressively make it a better approximation. Thus, learning on a model ensemble, along with source domain adaptation, provides the benefit of both robustness and learning.
review:
The paper introduces EPOpt, a robust policy-search method that trains neural-network policies on an ensemble of simulated source domains. It samples models from a parameter distribution and uses a CVaR-style adversarial subsampling step to emphasize poorly performing models, then optionally adapts the source distribution via approximate Bayesian updates from target-domain trajectories. Experiments on MuJoCo hopper and half-cheetah compare EPOpt against TRPO and maximum-likelihood training under parametric mismatch and unmodeled effects.

Strengths: The method is simple, well motivated, and compatible with existing batch policy optimizers such as TRPO. The adversarial ensemble objective directly targets robustness, and the results are convincing: EPOpt policies remain stable across wide torso-mass and friction ranges where single-model policies fail, with little loss in average performance. The model-adaptation experiments are particularly useful, showing good target performance from only a handful of target trajectories. Robustness to unmodeled mass variation is also a valuable demonstration.

Weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to two simulated locomotion tasks; no real-world or higher-dimensional manipulation task is included. The source distribution is assumed Gaussian and parametric, which may be restrictive for multimodal or high-dimensional uncertainty. The CVaR subsampling can hurt early exploration, and epsilon sensitivity is mostly relegated to the appendix. Comparisons are limited to TRPO and maximum-likelihood baselines, without other robust RL or ensemble methods. Theoretical guarantees are absent, and the Bayesian adaptation is approximate and simple.

Overall, EPOpt is a practical and well-executed robust RL method with strong simulated evidence. I recommend acceptance, requesting broader baselines, real-world validation, and more analysis of adaptation and epsilon sensitivity.

title: Attend, Adapt and Transfer: Attentive Deep Architecture for Adaptive Transfer from multiple sources in the same domain
abstract: Abstract:###Transferring knowledge from prior source tasks in solving a new target task can be useful in several learning applications. The application of transfer poses two serious challenges which have not been adequately addressed. First, the agent should be able to avoid negative transfer, which happens when the transfer hampers or slows down the learning instead of helping it. Second, the agent should be able to selectively transfer, which is the ability to select and transfer from different and multiple source tasks for different parts of the state space of the target task. We propose A2T (Attend Adapt and Transfer), an attentive deep architecture which adapts and transfers from these source tasks. Our model is generic enough to effect transfer of either policies or value functions. Empirical evaluations on different learning algorithms show that A2T is an effective architecture for transfer by being able to avoid negative transfer while transferring selectively from multiple source tasks in the same domain.
review:
The paper proposes A2T, an attentive deep architecture for adaptive transfer from multiple source tasks in the same domain. A per-state attention network produces soft weights over fixed source-task solutions and a trainable base network; their convex combination forms the target policy or value function. The base network is trained as if its own action were taken, allowing the agent to avoid negative transfer while selectively transferring different sources across the target state space. Experiments cover policy transfer in chain and puddle worlds and value transfer on Atari Pong.

Strengths: The architecture is clean, generic, and applicable to both policies and value functions. State-level soft attention is a sensible way to achieve selective transfer, and the base-network mechanism provides a plausible route to avoiding negative transfer. The paper clearly explains instantiations with REINFORCE, actor-critic, and DQN, and the preliminary experiments support the intended behavior.

Weaknesses: Empirical evaluation is limited and small-scale: two grid worlds and a single Atari game, with no comparison to closely related methods such as Parisotto et al. and Rusu et al. despite being discussed. Claims about avoiding negative transfer are mostly qualitative, without systematic quantification or variance estimates. Training the base network off-policy is not analyzed for stability or convergence. Scalability to many sources, high-dimensional tasks, and continuous actions remains unclear. Ablations on attention design, source quality, and base-network updates are missing.

Overall, A2T is a promising and clearly presented transfer architecture, but the evidence is preliminary. I recommend acceptance with requests for stronger baselines, broader Atari evaluation, statistical reporting, and stability analysis.

title: Multi-view Recurrent Neural Acoustic Word Embeddings
abstract: Abstract:###Recent work has begun exploring neural acoustic word embeddingsâ€“fixed dimensional vector representations of arbitrary-length speech segments corresponding to words. Such embeddings are applicable to speech retrieval and recognition tasks, where reasoning about whole words may make it possible to avoid ambiguous sub-word representations. The main idea is to map acoustic sequences to fixed-dimensional vectors such that examples of the same word are mapped to similar vectors, while different-word examples are mapped to very different vectors. In this work we take a multi-view approach to learning acoustic word embeddings, in which we jointly learn to embed acoustic sequences and their corresponding character sequences. We use deep bidirectional LSTM embedding models and multi-view contrastive losses. We study the effect of different loss variants, including fixed-margin and cost-sensitive losses. Our acoustic word embeddings improve over previous approaches for the task of word discrimination. We also present results on other tasks that are enabled by the multi-view approach, including cross-view word discrimination and word similarity.
review:
The paper proposes multi-view acoustic word embeddings, jointly embedding speech segments and their character sequences with bidirectional LSTM encoders and contrastive losses. It compares fixed-margin objectives and a cost-sensitive margin based on orthographic edit distance, and evaluates acoustic word discrimination, cross-view discrimination, and word similarity on Switchboard data.

Strengths: The multi-view formulation is novel and well motivated, producing comparable acoustic and orthographic embeddings that support both spoken and written queries. The architecture and loss variants are clearly described, and the objective ablation is useful: the symmetrized obj0+obj2 loss achieves the best acoustic discrimination, with test AP 0.806 versus 0.671 for a prior Siamese LSTM. Cross-view AP of 0.892 demonstrates a capability prior acoustic-only embeddings cannot offer. The cost-sensitive loss notably improves rank correlation with edit distance (0.240 versus 0.179), aligning with its intended purpose. Visualizations suggest meaningful clustering and reasonable generalization to unseen words.

Weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to one Switchboard setup with given word boundaries, so downstream search/recognition benefits remain unproven. The data contain few orthographically similar word pairs, weakening word-similarity conclusions. Hyperparameter search is coarse, and variance or significance tests are absent. Comparisons are mostly to older baselines, and the contrastive negative sampling is simple. Scalability to large vocabularies and continuous speech is not addressed.

Overall, this is a solid and clearly presented contribution with strong intrinsic results. I recommend acceptance, requesting downstream task validation, statistical reporting, and broader data evaluation.

title: Learning Features of Music From Scratch
abstract: Abstract:###This paper introduces a new large-scale music dataset, MusicNet, to serve as a source of supervision and evaluation of machine learning methods for music research. MusicNet consists of hundreds of freely-licensed classical music recordings by 10 composers, written for 11 instruments, together with instrument/note annotations resulting in over 1 million temporal labels on 34 hours of chamber music performances under various studio and microphone conditions. The paper defines a multi-label classification task to predict notes in musical recordings, along with an evaluation protocol, and benchmarks several machine learning architectures for this task: i) learning from spectrogram features; ii) end-to-end learning with a neural net; iii) end-to-end learning with a convolutional neural net. These experiments show that end-to-end models trained for note prediction learn frequency selective filters as a low-level representation of audio.
review:
The paper introduces MusicNet, a large freely licensed classical music dataset with 34 hours of audio, 330 recordings by 10 composers, 11 instruments, and over 1.3 million aligned note labels. Labels are obtained by aligning MIDI scores to recordings using DTW against synthesized performances. The paper defines multi-label note prediction and benchmarks spectrogram features, fully connected end-to-end networks, and convolutional end-to-end networks. A central finding is that end-to-end models learn frequency-selective, Gabor-like filters resembling spectrograms, and that large data is necessary for clean features.

Strengths: MusicNet is a valuable community resource, addressing the lack of large labeled data for music informatics. The alignment and annotation protocol are clearly described, and the error analysis is useful. The feature-learning analysis is insightful: learned filters are interpretable, and the ReLUgram connection helps explain why spectrograms work. Experiments show learned features modestly outperform spectrogram features, and the dataset-size ablation convincingly demonstrates the importance of scale.

Weaknesses: Evaluation uses only three held-out recordings, which is small and may not represent the dataset’s skew toward Beethoven and solo piano. The 4% alignment error and MIDI-derived labels are not propagated into the benchmark results. Comparisons are limited to simple MLP/CNN models, without stronger MIR baselines or downstream tasks such as transcription or retrieval. Statistical significance and variance are absent. The dataset’s limited instrument coverage and licensing constraints may restrict broader generalization.

Overall, MusicNet is a significant dataset contribution with useful benchmarking and interpretable findings. I recommend acceptance, requesting expanded evaluation, stronger baselines, and downstream validation.

title: A Baseline for Detecting Misclassified and Out-of-Distribution Examples in Neural Networks
abstract: Abstract:###We consider the two related problems of detecting if an example is misclassified or out-of-distribution. We present a simple baseline that utilizes probabilities from softmax distributions. Correctly classified examples tend to have greater maximum softmax probabilities than erroneously classified and out-of-distribution examples, allowing for their detection. We assess performance by defining several tasks in computer vision, natural language processing, and automatic speech recognition, showing the effectiveness of this baseline across all. We then show the baseline can sometimes be surpassed, demonstrating the room for future research on these underexplored detection tasks.
review:
The paper proposes a simple baseline for detecting misclassified and out-of-distribution (OOD) examples using the maximum softmax probability. Correct predictions tend to have higher confidence than errors and OOD inputs, so thresholding this score yields useful detection. The authors define standardized tasks across computer vision, NLP, and speech recognition, and report AUROC/AUPR for error detection, in-/out-of-distribution detection, and an auxiliary-decoder abnormality module.

Strengths: The baseline is extremely simple, widely applicable, and empirically effective across many architectures and datasets. Establishing common tasks and metrics is a valuable contribution, and the broad evaluation—MNIST/CIFAR, IMDB, Newsgroups/Reuters, POS tagging, and TIMIT—demonstrates generality. The abnormality module shows that learned reconstruction can outperform softmax statistics on some OOD tasks, highlighting room for improvement.

Weaknesses: The method is largely an empirical observation rather than a principled confidence estimator, and softmax probabilities are known to be poorly calibrated. The paper does not compare against strong calibration or detection baselines such as temperature scaling, ensembles, Mahalanobis distance, or ODIN. Several OOD sets are synthetic or near-distribution, and AUPR values are sensitive to base rates. The auxiliary decoder adds complexity without thorough ablation, and no theoretical guarantees are provided. Statistical significance is reported for AUROC but not consistently for AUPR.

Overall, this is an influential, clearly written baseline with broad empirical support. I recommend acceptance, requesting stronger calibration/detection baselines and deeper analysis of the abnormality module.

title: Learning to superoptimize programs
abstract: Abstract:###Code super-optimization is the task of transforming any given program to a more efficient version while preserving its input-output behaviour. In some sense, it is similar to the paraphrase problem from natural language processing where the intention is to change the syntax of an utterance without changing its semantics. Code-optimization has been the subject of years of research that has resulted in the development of rule-based transformation strategies that are used by compilers. More recently, however, a class of stochastic search based methods have been shown to outperform these strategies. This approach involves repeated sampling of modifications to the program from a proposal distribution, which are accepted or rejected based on whether they preserve correctness, and the improvement they achieve. These methods, however, neither learn from past behaviour nor do they try to leverage the semantics of the program under consideration. Motivated by this observation, we present a novel learning based approach for code super-optimization. Intuitively, our method works by learning the proposal distribution using unbiased estimators of the gradient of the expected improvement. Experiments on benchmarks comprising of automatically generated as well as existing (``Hacker*s Delight**) programs show that the proposed method is able to significantly outperform state of the art approaches for code super-optimization.
review:
The paper proposes learning the proposal distribution for stochastic code super-optimization. Building on Stoke’s MCMC sampler, the authors parameterize move proposals with categorical distributions—either an unconditioned bias or an MLP conditioned on bag-of-opcode program features—and train them with REINFORCE using unbiased gradient estimates. Experiments cover Hacker’s Delight programs and automatically generated programs, comparing against Stoke’s uniform proposal.

Strengths: The formulation is clean and well motivated: learning which moves to propose directly addresses a clear weakness of uniform stochastic search. The use of actual programs and symbolic/test-based correctness is appropriate, and the stochastic computation graph and gradient estimator are clearly explained. Empirical gains are substantial: average relative scores improve from 53.71% to 31.82%/31.51% on Hacker’s Delight and from 78.15% to 63.56%/62.27% on generated programs. Learned proposals also reach good solutions in fewer iterations. Overhead is modest because the proposal is evaluated once per program.

Weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to short bit-manipulation programs, with Hacker’s Delight offering little diversity and generated programs lacking structure. The MLP barely improves over the unconditioned bias on Hacker’s Delight, and bag-of-opcodes features ignore temporal program structure. No comparisons are made to other learned-search or enumerative solvers, and variance/significance are not reported. Throughput drops from 60k to 20k MCMC iterations/second, and longer real-world programs remain untested.

Overall, this is a novel, clearly presented, and empirically promising application of learning to stochastic search. I recommend acceptance, requesting broader benchmarks, stronger representations, and variance reporting.

title: Trusting SVM for Piecewise Linear CNNs
abstract: Abstract:###We present a novel layerwise optimization algorithm for the learning objective of Piecewise-Linear Convolutional Neural Networks (PL-CNNs), a large class of convolutional neural networks. Specifically, PL-CNNs employ piecewise linear non-linearities such as the commonly used ReLU and max-pool, and an SVM classifier as the final layer. The key observation of our approach is that the prob- lem corresponding to the parameter estimation of a layer can be formulated as a difference-of-convex (DC) program, which happens to be a latent structured SVM. We optimize the DC program using the concave-convex procedure, which requires us to iteratively solve a structured SVM problem. This allows to design an opti- mization algorithm with an optimal learning rate that does not require any tuning. Using the MNIST, CIFAR and ImageNet data sets, we show that our approach always improves over the state of the art variants of backpropagation and scales to large data and large network settings.
review:
The paper proposes a layerwise optimizer for piecewise-linear CNNs with ReLU/max-pool and an SVM classifier. It shows that per-layer parameter estimation is a difference-of-convex program equivalent to a latent structured SVM, solves it via CCCP and block-coordinate Frank-Wolfe, and introduces trust-region initialization, memory-efficient feature representation, and constraint reduction. Advantages include monotonic objective decrease and no learning-rate tuning.

Strengths: The formulation is novel and principled, connecting PL-CNNs to latent SVMs. The DC/CCCP decomposition is clearly motivated, and the BCFW extensions address practical initialization, memory, and time issues. Avoiding learning-rate tuning is attractive, and latent inference is solved efficiently using forward/backward passes. The approach is reported to scale to MNIST, CIFAR, and ImageNet.

Weaknesses: The layerwise schedule is simple and may be slow; convergence to good local minima is not guaranteed. The latent space grows exponentially with depth, and constraint reduction is approximate. The proximal/trust-region parameter is fixed rather than ablated. Comparisons to adaptive SGD methods need statistical rigor and wall-clock accounting. Generality beyond PL-CNN+SVM—e.g., softmax, batch normalization, residual connections—is unclear. Sensitivity analysis is limited.

Overall, this is a theoretically appealing and practical optimization approach. I recommend acceptance, requesting thorough empirical comparisons, ablations, and broader architecture validation.

title: Sigma Delta Quantized Networks
abstract: Abstract:###Deep neural networks can be obscenely wasteful. When processing video, a convolutional network expends a fixed amount of computation for each frame with no regard to the similarity between neighbouring frames. As a result, it ends up repeatedly doing very similar computations. To put an end to such waste, we introduce Sigma-Delta networks. With each new input, each layer in this network sends a discretized form of its change in activation to the next layer. Thus the amount of computation that the network does scales with the amount of change in the input and layer activations, rather than the size of the network. We introduce an optimization method for converting any pre-trained deep network into an optimally efficient Sigma-Delta network, and show that our algorithm, if run on the appropriate hardware, could cut at least an order of magnitude from the computational cost of processing video data.
review:
The paper introduces Sigma-Delta networks, which communicate quantized temporal differences between layers so computation scales with input change rather than network size. Temporal-difference and integration modules make the transformation exact, herding discretizes changes into sparse integer spikes, and sparse dot products become additions. The authors propose optimizing layer-wise scales in pretrained networks to trade error against computation, and evaluate on a toy network, Temporal-MNIST, and preliminary VGG-19 video processing.

Strengths: The core idea is novel and clearly presented. The equivalence between the Sigma-Delta and rounding networks is elegant, and the sparse dot-product formulation gives a concrete route to energy savings. Scale optimization via a straight-through estimator is simple and shows sensible Pareto frontiers. Temporal-MNIST demonstrates the expected benefit of temporal redundancy, and the VGG experiment suggests roughly 4–11× computation reductions on video with modest accuracy loss. The paper is candid about preliminary results and hardware assumptions.

Weaknesses: The method is inference-only and relies on pretrained networks; training Sigma-Delta networks from scratch is not explored. Evaluation is limited to toy data and a small, qualitative video study, with no systematic benchmark or comparison to other conditional-computation or event-based methods. The noisy-rounding training trick is unexplained and unstable. The claimed savings are operation counts and energy estimates rather than measured wall-clock or hardware results. The accuracy-computation tradeoff and scale optimization lack ablation and variance reporting.

Overall, this is a promising and original efficiency framework, but the empirical evidence is preliminary. I recommend acceptance with requests for systematic benchmarks, hardware measurements, and deeper analysis of training stability.

title: A STRUCTURED SELF-ATTENTIVE SENTENCE EMBEDDING
abstract: Abstract:###This paper proposes a new model for extracting an interpretable sentence embedding by introducing self-attention. Instead of using a vector, we use a 2-D matrix to represent the embedding, with each row of the matrix attending on a different part of the sentence. We also propose a self-attention mechanism and a special regularization term for the model. As a side effect, the embedding comes with an easy way of visualizing what specific parts of the sentence are encoded into the embedding. We evaluate our model on 3 different tasks: author profiling, sentiment classification and textual entailment. Results show that our model yields a significant performance gain compared to other sentence embedding methods in all of the 3 tasks.
review:
The paper introduces Sigma-Delta networks, which communicate quantized temporal differences between layers so that computation scales with input change rather than network size. Temporal-difference and integration modules preserve the network function exactly, herding discretizes changes into sparse integer spikes, and sparse dot products reduce to additions. The authors optimize layer-wise scales in pretrained networks to trade error against computation, evaluating on a toy network, Temporal-MNIST, and preliminary VGG-19 video processing.

Strengths: The core idea is novel and clearly presented. The equivalence between Sigma-Delta and rounding networks is elegant, and the sparse dot-product formulation gives a concrete route to energy savings. Scale optimization via a straight-through estimator is simple and yields sensible Pareto frontiers. Temporal-MNIST demonstrates the expected benefit of temporal redundancy, and the VGG experiment suggests roughly 4–11× computation reductions on video with modest accuracy loss. The paper is candid about preliminary results and hardware assumptions.

Weaknesses: The method is inference-only and relies on pretrained networks; training Sigma-Delta networks from scratch is not explored. Evaluation is limited to toy data and a small, qualitative video study, with no systematic benchmark or comparison to other conditional-computation or event-based methods. The noisy-rounding training trick is unexplained and unstable. Claimed savings are operation counts and energy estimates rather than measured wall-clock or hardware results. Ablations and variance reporting are absent.

Overall, this is a promising and original efficiency framework, but the empirical evidence is preliminary. I recommend acceptance with requests for systematic benchmarks, hardware measurements, and deeper analysis of training stability.

title: Regularizing CNNs with Locally Constrained Decorrelations
abstract: Abstract:###Regularization is key for deep learning since it allows training more complex models while keeping lower levels of overfitting. However, the most prevalent regularizations do not leverage all the capacity of the models since they rely on reducing the effective number of parameters. Feature decorrelation is an alternative for using the full capacity of the models but the overfitting reduction margins are too narrow given the overhead it introduces. In this paper, we show that regularizing negatively correlated features is an obstacle for effective decorrelation and present OrthoReg, a novel regularization technique that locally enforces feature orthogonality. As a result, imposing locality constraints in feature decorrelation removes interferences between negatively correlated feature weights, allowing the regularizer to reach higher decorrelation bounds, and reducing the overfitting more effectively. In particular, we show that the models regularized with OrthoReg have higher accuracy bounds even when batch normalization and dropout are present. Moreover, since our regularization is directly performed on the weights, it is especially suitable for fully convolutional neural networks, where the weight space is constant compared to the feature map space. As a result, we are able to reduce the overfitting of state-of-the-art CNNs on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and SVHN.
review:
The paper proposes OrthoReg, a regularization technique that enforces local orthogonality between feature detectors by penalizing only positively correlated weights while allowing negative correlations. The authors argue that negative correlations are beneficial (inhibitory connections, competitive learning) and that global decorrelation (penalizing all pairwise cosine similarities) hinders performance. They introduce a smooth local loss and demonstrate improvements on MNIST, CIFAR-10/100, and SVHN using ResNets, showing compatibility with dropout and LSUV initialization.

Strengths: The idea is simple, computationally efficient (regularizing weights rather than activations), and well-motivated by neuroscientific evidence on inhibitory connections. The local loss formulation is clean and the vectorized implementation is straightforward. Experiments show consistent gains over unregularized baselines and some state-of-the-art comparisons, with ablation on lambda and gamma.

Weaknesses: Theoretical justification for why negative correlations should be preserved is mostly heuristic; the local loss is an ad-hoc exponential squash. The improvements are modest in absolute terms (e.g., ResNet-110 error 6.55% to 6.29%), and the claim of state-of-the-art needs stronger statistical validation. Comparisons are limited to a few image datasets and architectures; no NLP or other domains. Hyperparameter sensitivity (lambda, gamma) is not thoroughly analyzed. The method regularizes weights, but feature detectors may not directly correspond to neurons; activation decorrelation could still be beneficial.

Overall, OrthoReg is a practical and well-presented regularizer with encouraging empirical results, but its advantages over existing decorrelation methods are incremental. I recommend acceptance, requesting more rigorous ablations, statistical significance, and broader task validation.

title: The Concrete Distribution: A Continuous Relaxation of Discrete Random Variables
abstract: Abstract:###The reparameterization trick enables optimizing large scale stochastic computation graphs via gradient descent. The essence of the trick is to refactor each stochastic node into a differentiable function of its parameters and a random variable with fixed distribution. After refactoring, the gradients of the loss propagated by the chain rule through the graph are low variance unbiased estimators of the gradients of the expected loss. While many continuous random variables have such reparameterizations, discrete random variables lack useful reparameterizations due to the discontinuous nature of discrete states. In this work we introduce Concrete random variables -- continuous relaxations of discrete random variables. The Concrete distribution is a new family of distributions with closed form densities and a simple reparameterization. Whenever a discrete stochastic node of a computation graph can be refactored into a one-hot bit representation that is treated continuously, Concrete stochastic nodes can be used with automatic differentiation to produce low-variance biased gradients of objectives (including objectives that depend on the log-probability of latent stochastic nodes) on the corresponding discrete graph. We demonstrate the effectiveness of Concrete relaxations on density estimation and structured prediction tasks using neural networks.
review:
The paper introduces Concrete random variables, continuous relaxations of discrete random variables on the simplex with closed-form densities and a simple Gumbel-softmax reparameterization. As temperature approaches zero, rounding recovers the corresponding discrete distribution, enabling biased but low-variance gradients through discrete stochastic nodes in automatic differentiation. The authors apply Concrete relaxations to density estimation and structured prediction on MNIST and Omniglot, comparing with VIMCO.

Strengths: The formulation is clean, general, and clearly explained. The Gumbel-Max motivation and softmax relaxation are intuitive, and the closed-form density and reparameterization make implementation straightforward. The zero-temperature and rounding properties provide a useful theoretical bridge. Experiments show the method is competitive with VIMCO, occasionally better or worse, while requiring no special-casing in AD libraries. The work is likely to be broadly useful for variational inference and structured latent-variable models.

Weaknesses: Gradients are biased, and the bias-variance tradeoff controlled by temperature is not analyzed in depth; practical temperature schedules appear heuristic. There is a train-test mismatch between continuous relaxation and discrete evaluation. Empirical evaluation is limited to two small image datasets and a narrow set of tasks, with no large-scale or sequence modeling experiments. Comparisons to other relaxations and REINFORCE baselines are limited, and variance/significance reporting is absent.

Overall, this is an elegant and influential relaxation with strong conceptual value and promising empirical support. I recommend acceptance, requesting deeper bias-variance analysis, temperature ablation, and broader task validation.

title: Unrolled Generative Adversarial Networks
abstract: Abstract:###We introduce a method to stabilize Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) by defining the generator objective with respect to an unrolled optimization of the discriminator. This allows training to be adjusted between using the optimal discriminator in the generator*s objective, which is ideal but infeasible in practice, and using the current value of the discriminator, which is often unstable and leads to poor solutions. We show how this technique solves the common problem of mode collapse, stabilizes training of GANs with complex recurrent generators, and increases diversity and coverage of the data distribution by the generator.
review:
The paper introduces unrolled GANs, which stabilize training by defining the generator objective with respect to K unrolled discriminator optimization steps. This interpolates between standard GAN updates (K=0) and optimizing against an approximately optimal discriminator, and the added gradient term captures how the discriminator reacts to generator changes, discouraging mode collapse. Experiments cover 2D Gaussian mixtures, RNN-based MNIST generation, augmented MNIST for discrete-mode and manifold collapse, and CIFAR-10.

Strengths: The motivation and analysis of the missing gradient term are clear and insightful. The method is simple to implement using automatic differentiation and requires no architectural changes. Toy experiments are compelling: standard GANs rotate through modes while unrolled GANs converge to the full mixture. Unrolling also stabilizes complex recurrent generators and improves discrete-mode coverage and color-manifold diversity, with gains increasing as the discriminator is weakened.

Weaknesses: Computational and memory costs scale with the number of unrolling steps, and no convergence guarantees are provided. Evaluation of diversity is difficult and somewhat indirect; CIFAR-10 visual quality is largely unchanged, and the proposed diversity metrics are suggestive but not conclusive. The choice of K and minibatch strategy during unrolling is heuristic. Comparisons are mostly internal ablations, with limited comparison to other stabilization methods outside the appendix.

Overall, unrolled GANs are a principled and effective stabilization technique with strong toy and moderate-scale evidence. I recommend acceptance, requesting cost analysis, broader baselines, and more rigorous diversity evaluation.

title: TopicRNN: A Recurrent Neural Network with Long-Range Semantic Dependency
abstract: Abstract:###In this paper, we propose TopicRNN, a recurrent neural network (RNN)-based language model designed to directly capture the global semantic meaning relating words in a document via latent topics. Because of their sequential nature, RNNs are good at capturing the local structure of a word sequence â€“ both semantic and syntactic â€“ but might face difficulty remembering long-range dependencies. Intuitively, these long-range dependencies are of semantic nature. In contrast, latent topic models are able to capture the global underlying semantic structure of a document but do not account for word ordering. The proposed TopicRNN model integrates the merits of RNNs and latent topic models: it captures local (syntactic) dependencies using an RNN and global (semantic) dependencies using latent topics. Unlike previous work on contextual RNN language modeling, our model is learned end-to-end. Empirical results on word prediction show that TopicRNN outperforms existing contextual RNN baselines. In addition, TopicRNN can be used as an unsupervised feature extractor for documents. We do this for sentiment analysis on the IMDB movie review dataset and report an error rate of 6.28%. This is comparable to the state-of-the-art 5.91% resulting from a semi-supervised approach. Finally, TopicRNN also yields sensible topics, making it a useful alternative to document models such as latent Dirichlet allocation.
review:
The paper proposes TopicRNN, a recurrent language model that combines an RNN’s local syntactic modeling with global latent topics learned end-to-end. Topics are inferred from a bag-of-words document representation excluding stop words, and their representation conditions the RNN output; a variational inference network and stop-word prediction handle document-level semantics. Experiments report PTB perplexity improvements over contextual RNN baselines and IMDB sentiment error of 6.28% using TopicRNN features.

Strengths: The motivation is clear and the architecture sensibly separates local syntax from long-range semantics. End-to-end topic learning avoids pre-trained LDA features, and the stop-word treatment is a practical contribution. PTB results are consistent across network sizes—e.g., TopicGRU with 100 neurons reaches test perplexity 112.4 versus 126.4 for an LDA-feature RNN—and the IMDB result is competitive without labels or adversarial training. Learned topics are interpretable, and the model can serve as an unsupervised document feature extractor.

Weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to PTB and IMDB, with no broader language-modeling or downstream tasks. Topic inference uses a sliding-window approximation and arbitrary 10-sentence documents, which may weaken long-document claims. Comparisons focus on older contextual RNN baselines rather than modern regularized LSTMs. The stop-word list is pre-defined, and sensitivity to topic count, document segmentation, and inference-network size is not thoroughly ablated. No variance or significance tests are reported, and generated-text quality is only qualitatively assessed.

Overall, TopicRNN is a well-motivated and effective model with promising results. I recommend acceptance, requesting broader evaluation, stronger baselines, and ablation/statistical reporting.

title: Frustratingly Short Attention Spans in Neural Language Modeling
abstract: Abstract:###Current language modeling architectures often use recurrent neural networks. Recently, various methods for incorporating differentiable memory into these architectures have been proposed. When predicting the next token, these models query information from a memory of the recent history and thus can facilitate learning mid- and long-range dependencies. However, conventional attention models produce a single output vector per time step that is used for predicting the next token as well as the key and value of a differentiable memory of the history of tokens. In this paper, we propose a key-value attention mechanism that produces separate representations for the key and value of a memory, and for a representation that encodes the next-word distribution. This usage of past memories outperforms existing memory-augmented neural language models on two corpora. Yet, we found that it mainly utilizes past memory only of the previous five representations. This led to the unexpected main finding that a much simpler model which simply uses a concatenation of output representations from the previous three-time steps is on par with more sophisticated memory-augmented neural language models.
review:
The paper proposes key-value-predict attention for neural language modeling, separating each output vector into key, value, and next-word prediction components for a differentiable memory over recent history. It compares attention, key-value, and key-value-predict models with recurrent-memory and higher-order RNN baselines on a Wikipedia corpus and the Children’s Book Test. The central empirical finding is that these memory-augmented models mostly attend to the five most recent representations, and a simple 4-gram RNN that concatenates the previous three output vectors is on par with more sophisticated attention models.

Strengths: The architectural separation is clean and well motivated, and the paper is commendably candid about the negative result on long-range attention. Experiments match parameter counts and compare against reimplemented baselines. Key-value-predict achieves the best Wikipedia perplexity (74.2 versus 82.0 for attention and 83.2 for LSTM), while the 4-gram RNN reaches 75.9, supporting the main claim. Attention visualizations and window-size ablations provide useful evidence for short effective spans.

Weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to two corpora, and CBT is a cloze-style benchmark rather than a pure language-modeling test. The paper does not establish whether longer-range attention can be encouraged by different training objectives or regularization. Gains over the simple 4-gram model are modest, and variance or significance tests are absent. Parameter matching across architectures is approximate, and the Wikipedia corpus is newly introduced and not widely benchmarked.

Overall, this is a useful and honest study with a clear architectural contribution and an important negative finding. I recommend acceptance, requesting significance reporting, broader corpora, and experiments encouraging longer attention.

title: Recurrent Hidden Semi-Markov Model
abstract: Abstract:###Segmentation and labeling of high dimensional time series data has wide applications in behavior understanding and medical diagnosis. Due to the difficulty in obtaining the label information for high dimensional data, realizing this objective in an unsupervised way is highly desirable. Hidden Semi-Markov Model (HSMM) is a classical tool for this problem. However, existing HSMM and its variants has simple conditional assumptions of observations, thus the ability to capture the nonlinear and complex dynamics within segments is limited. To tackle this limitation, we propose to incorporate the Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) to model the generative process in HSMM, resulting the Recurrent HSMM (R-HSMM). To accelerate the inference while preserving accuracy, we designed a structure encoding function to mimic the exact inference. By generalizing the penalty method to distribution space, we are able to train the model and the encoding function simultaneously. Empirical results show that the proposed R-HSMM achieves the state-of-the-art performances on both synthetic and real-world datasets.
review:
The paper proposes the Recurrent Hidden Semi-Markov Model (R-HSMM), which replaces the strong parametric emission assumptions of HSMMs with segment-specific RNN generators. It introduces a bidirectional RNN variational encoder that mimics forward-backward inference to accelerate posterior approximation, and a stochastic distributional penalty method to handle discrete latent variables during training. Experiments cover synthetic sine and Gaussian-process data and three real-world segmentation tasks: human activity, fruit fly behavior, and heart sounds.

Strengths: The model is well motivated and addresses a real limitation of HSMMs—capturing nonlinear, long-range dependencies within segments. Combining explicit duration modeling with RNN emissions is sensible, and the structured bi-RNN encoder is an effective way to approximate dynamic-programming inference. The distributional penalty method is a useful contribution for discrete-latent VAEs, and the reported 400× inference speedup with comparable accuracy is compelling. Results show clear improvements over HSMM baselines on multiple datasets.

Weaknesses: Training is complex, involving alternating updates, auxiliary distributions, and a penalty parameter, with limited theoretical convergence analysis. Sensitivity to K, D, λ, and the encoder architecture is not thoroughly ablated. Evaluation is restricted to segmentation/labeling tasks and older HSMM baselines, without comparison to modern neural segmentation methods. Exact Viterbi inference remains costly for long sequences, and the claims about exact negative Helmholtz free energy could be clarified. Reproducibility details, variance, and significance tests are limited.

Overall, R-HSMM is a novel and well-executed model with strong empirical results. I recommend acceptance, requesting more ablation, stronger baselines, and convergence analysis.

title: Deep Variational Bayes Filters: Unsupervised Learning of State Space Models from Raw Data
abstract: Abstract:###We introduce Deep Variational Bayes Filters (DVBF), a new method for unsupervised learning and identification of latent Markovian state space models. Leveraging recent advances in Stochastic Gradient Variational Bayes, DVBF can overcome intractable inference distributions via variational inference. Thus, it can handle highly nonlinear input data with temporal and spatial dependencies such as image sequences without domain knowledge. Our experiments show that enabling backpropagation through transitions enforces state space assumptions and significantly improves information content of the latent embedding. This also enables realistic long-term prediction.
review:
The paper introduces Deep Variational Bayes Filters (DVBF), an unsupervised method for learning latent Markovian state-space models from raw observations. It reparameterizes transitions as differentiable deterministic functions of latent state, control, and inferred stochastic transition parameters, so reconstruction errors backpropagate through time and shape the latent space. The authors derive a variational lower bound, use annealed training and empirical Bayes priors, and instantiate locally linear transitions. On pendulum image sequences, DVBF recovers angle and angular velocity, supports long-horizon rollouts, and outperforms the Deep Kalman Filter, which misses velocity.

Strengths: The transition-centric reparameterization is clean and well motivated, addressing a real weakness of prior time-series VAEs whose latents are optimized mainly for reconstruction. The lower-bound derivation is clear, and locally linear transitions are practical. The pendulum experiments convincingly demonstrate full-state identification and long-term prediction, with an informative DKF comparison.

Weaknesses: Evaluation is narrow, essentially one synthetic pendulum domain. Broader real-world and higher-dimensional systems are needed. Several design choices—annealing schedule, priors, number of linear models, latent dimension—lack thorough ablation. Convergence and theoretical properties are not discussed, and computational costs of long transition backpropagation are unanalyzed.

Overall, DVBF is a principled and promising method with strong proof-of-concept evidence. I recommend acceptance, requesting broader benchmarks, ablations, and computational analysis.

title: Generative Multi-Adversarial Networks
abstract: Abstract:###Generative adversarial networks (GANs) are a framework for producing a generative model by way of a two-player minimax game. In this paper, we propose the emph{Generative Multi-Adversarial Network} (GMAN), a framework that extends GANs to multiple discriminators. In previous work, the successful training of GANs requires modifying the minimax objective to accelerate training early on. In contrast, GMAN can be reliably trained with the original, untampered objective. We explore a number of design perspectives with the discriminator role ranging from formidable adversary to forgiving teacher. Image generation tasks comparing the proposed framework to standard GANs demonstrate GMAN produces higher quality samples in a fraction of the iterations when measured by a pairwise GAM-type metric.
review:
The paper proposes Generative Multi-Adversarial Networks (GMAN), extending GANs to multiple discriminators whose feedback is aggregated for the generator. It explores aggregation ranging from a formidable adversary (max) to a forgiving teacher (soft means), introduces an automatically regulated variant (GMAN*) where the generator controls temperature, and defines a pairwise GMAM metric. Experiments on MNIST, CelebA, and CIFAR-10 report faster convergence, lower variance, and better sample quality than standard GANs, with robustness to mode collapse at linear cost in batch size.

Strengths: The framework is simple and general, and it allows training with the original untampered minimax objective by making vanishing gradients unlikely when one discriminator is fooled. The ensemble interpretation and variance reduction are well motivated. GMAN* is an interesting mechanism for automatic difficulty scheduling, and the linear scaling relative to minibatch discrimination is attractive.

Weaknesses: Evaluation relies heavily on the authors’ GMAM metric, which is not widely validated; CIFAR-10 results are largely qualitative. Theoretical analysis of the multi-discriminator game, equilibria, and convergence is limited. Maintaining discriminator diversity is heuristic, boosting failed, and computational overhead of N discriminators is not quantified. Comparisons omit popular quantitative metrics and stronger baselines.

Overall, GMAN is a promising and clearly presented extension with encouraging empirical results, but evaluation and theory need strengthening. I recommend acceptance, requesting standardized metrics, cost analysis, and game-theoretic analysis.

title: Mollifying Networks
abstract: Abstract:###The optimization of deep neural networks can be more challenging than the traditional convex optimization problems due to highly non-convex nature of the loss function, e.g. it can involve pathological landscapes such as saddle-surfaces that can be difficult to escape from for algorithms based on simple gradient descent. In this paper, we attack the problem of optimization of highly non-convex neural networks objectives by starting with a smoothed -- or mollified -- objective function which becomes more complex as the training proceeds. Our proposition is inspired by the recent studies in continuation methods: similarly to curriculum methods, we begin by learning an easier (possibly convex) objective function and let it evolve during training until it eventually becomes the original, difficult to optimize objective function. The complexity of the mollified networks is controlled by a single hyperparameter that is annealed during training. We show improvements on various difficult optimization tasks and establish a relationship between recent works on continuation methods for neural networks and mollifiers.
review:
The paper proposes mollifying networks, a continuation-style training method that smooths the objective with annealed noise and identity-path stochasticity, gradually moving from a simpler (possibly convex) objective to the original nonlinear network. It connects mollifiers, weak gradients, curriculum/continuation, and stochastic depth, and applies the idea to MLPs, residual CNNs, and LSTMs. Experiments cover parity, Pentomino, CIFAR-10, character-embedding prediction, and PTB language modeling.

Strengths: The formulation is conceptually clean and unified, with a single annealing hyperparameter controlling both noise and stochastic depth. The theoretical link to weak gradients and mollifiers is useful. Results show faster convergence on deep parity and gains on Pentomino (75.15% vs 69.5%), CIFAR-10 (92.45% vs ResNet 91.78%), and PTB perplexity (123.6 vs 128.4), suggesting practical value.

Weaknesses: Empirical evidence is limited and gains are modest; stochastic depth outperforms on CIFAR-10. The claim that the smoothed objective is convex is only valid under restrictive conditions, and the annealing schedule is heuristic. No variance or significance tests are reported, and comparisons lack many strong optimization baselines. Large-scale tasks are absent, and the LSTM mollification is only lightly evaluated.

Overall, this is a novel and clearly presented continuation method with promising but preliminary results. I recommend acceptance, requesting broader benchmarks, ablation of the annealing schedule, and statistical reporting.

title: beta-VAE: Learning Basic Visual Concepts with a Constrained Variational Framework
abstract: Abstract:###Learning an interpretable factorised representation of the independent data generative factors of the world without supervision is an important precursor for the development of artificial intelligence that is able to learn and reason in the same way that humans do. We introduce beta-VAE, a new state-of-the-art framework for automated discovery of interpretable factorised latent representations from raw image data in a completely unsupervised manner. Our approach is a modification of the variational autoencoder (VAE) framework. We introduce an adjustable hyperparameter beta that balances latent channel capacity and independence constraints with reconstruction accuracy. We demonstrate that beta-VAE with appropriately tuned beta > 1 qualitatively outperforms VAE (beta = 1), as well as state of the art unsupervised (InfoGAN) and semi-supervised (DC-IGN) approaches to disentangled factor learning on a variety of datasets (celebA, faces and chairs). Furthermore, we devise a protocol to quantitatively compare the degree of disentanglement learnt by different models, and show that our approach also significantly outperforms all baselines quantitatively. Unlike InfoGAN, beta-VAE is stable to train, makes few assumptions about the data and relies on tuning a single hyperparameter, which can be directly optimised through a hyper parameter search using weakly labelled data or through heuristic visual inspection for purely unsupervised data.
review:
The paper introduces β-VAE, a modification of the VAE objective that adds a β coefficient on the KL term to constrain latent-channel capacity and encourage disentangled representations. It motivates this via a constrained optimization view, proposes a quantitative disentanglement metric based on linear classification of fixed-factor latent differences, and evaluates qualitatively on CelebA, 3D chairs, and faces, and quantitatively on a synthetic 2D-shapes dataset against VAE, InfoGAN, DC-IGN, PCA, and ICA.

Strengths: The method is simple, stable, and easy to implement, requiring only one additional hyperparameter. The qualitative results are compelling: β-VAE discovers factors such as azimuth, scale, chair width, leg style, skin color, and saturation that VAE entangles, and it often matches or exceeds InfoGAN and DC-IGN without supervision. The proposed metric is a useful step toward standardized comparison, and quantitative results show β-VAE substantially outperforming VAE and other baselines on the synthetic dataset.

Weaknesses: There is no formal guarantee that higher β yields disentanglement; the effect is empirical and dataset-dependent. The metric requires ground-truth factor labels and a linear classifier, which limits applicability to purely unsupervised settings and may bias toward linearly separable latents. Reconstruction quality degrades with high β, and the tradeoff is not systematically analyzed. Comparisons rely partly on qualitative traversals, with limited variance or significance reporting. Hyperparameter sensitivity across datasets is acknowledged but not thoroughly ablated.

Overall, β-VAE is an influential and practical framework with strong qualitative and promising quantitative evidence. I recommend acceptance, requesting more rigorous metric validation, ablation of β, and reconstruction-disentanglement analysis.

title: Offline bilingual word vectors, orthogonal transformations and the inverted softmax
abstract: Abstract:###Usually bilingual word vectors are trained *online**. Mikolov et al. showed they can also be found *offline*; whereby two pre-trained embeddings are aligned with a linear transformation, using dictionaries compiled from expert knowledge. In this work, we prove that the linear transformation between two spaces should be orthogonal. This transformation can be obtained using the singular value decomposition. We introduce a novel *inverted softmax* for identifying translation pairs, with which we improve the precision @1 of Mikolov*s original mapping from 34% to 43%, when translating a test set composed of both common and rare English words into Italian. Orthogonal transformations are more robust to noise, enabling us to learn the transformation without expert bilingual signal by constructing a *pseudo-dictionary* from the identical character strings which appear in both languages, achieving 40% precision on the same test set. Finally, we extend our method to retrieve the true translations of English sentences from a corpus of 200k Italian sentences with a precision @1 of 68%.
review:
The paper studies offline bilingual word vectors, proving that the linear map between independently trained embedding spaces should be orthogonal and can be obtained exactly via SVD. It introduces an inverted softmax to mitigate hubness in nearest-neighbor retrieval, and shows that orthogonal alignment is robust enough to use pseudo-dictionaries of identical character strings or aligned sentence pairs. Experiments on English–Italian report improved precision@1 from 34% to 43% with expert dictionaries, 40% with identical-string pseudo-dictionaries, and 68% sentence retrieval from 200k candidates.

Strengths: The theoretical argument for orthogonality is clean and insightful, and the SVD solution is exact, efficient, and comparable to CCA. The inverted softmax is a simple, well-motivated fix for hubness, and the pseudo-dictionary result is striking because it requires no expert bilingual supervision. Extending alignment to sentence vectors and sentence retrieval is a useful demonstration of generality.

Weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to English–Italian, so cross-lingual robustness is unclear. The pseudo-dictionary relies on shared character strings, which will be scarce for distant language pairs. Sentence vectors are simple normalized sums, and the 68% sentence retrieval result may not generalize to longer or noisy text. Comparisons with online bilingual embedding methods such as Bilbowa are limited, and variance/significance are not reported. The interaction between dimensionality reduction and the inverted softmax is only lightly analyzed.

Overall, this is a well-presented and theoretically grounded contribution with strong empirical gains. I recommend acceptance, requesting broader language pairs, stronger online baselines, and statistical reporting.

title: Visualizing Deep Neural Network Decisions: Prediction Difference Analysis
abstract: Abstract:###This article presents the prediction difference analysis method for visualizing the response of a deep neural network to a specific input. When classifying images, the method highlights areas in a given input image that provide evidence for or against a certain class. It overcomes several shortcoming of previous methods and provides great additional insight into the decision making process of classifiers. Making neural network decisions interpretable through visualization is important both to improve models and to accelerate the adoption of black-box classifiers in application areas such as medicine. We illustrate the method in experiments on natural images (ImageNet data), as well as medical images (MRI brain scans).
review:
The paper presents prediction difference analysis for visualizing DNN decisions, assigning signed evidence for and against a class by removing input patches and estimating prediction changes. It improves prior work with conditional sampling from surrounding patches, multivariate patch-based removal, and deep visualization of hidden layers, with experiments on ImageNet (AlexNet, GoogLeNet, VGG) and MRI data.

Strengths: The method is probabilistically grounded and produces interpretable signed evidence, distinguishing supporting from conflicting regions. Conditional sampling is a clear improvement over marginal sampling, yielding more targeted explanations. Multivariate patch removal handles pixel dependence better than single-feature deletion, and the extension to hidden layers is valuable for understanding internal representations. Qualitative results across architectures and medical images demonstrate practical usefulness, including comparisons of penultimate versus output layers and network-specific behaviors.

Weaknesses: The approach is computationally expensive, taking 20–70 minutes per ImageNet image and about 30 minutes per MRI scan, limiting practical deployment. Conditional sampling uses a simple multivariate Gaussian, which may poorly model complex image structure. Patch sizes, sampling count, and outer-window size are chosen heuristically, with limited ablation. Evaluation is largely qualitative, with no quantitative faithfulness or human-study comparison against saliency baselines. The medical demonstration is small and explicitly lacks clinical validation.

Overall, this is a well-motivated and insightful visualization method with strong qualitative examples, but efficiency and quantitative validation need strengthening. I recommend acceptance, requesting runtime analysis, better conditional models, and quantitative faithfulness evaluations.

title: Categorical Reparameterization with Gumbel-Softmax
abstract: Abstract:###Categorical variables are a natural choice for representing discrete structure in the world. However, stochastic neural networks rarely use categorical latent variables due to the inability to backpropagate through samples. In this work, we present an efficient gradient estimator that replaces the non-differentiable sample from a categorical distribution with a differentiable sample from a novel Gumbel-Softmax distribution. This distribution has the essential property that it can be smoothly annealed into a categorical distribution. We show that our Gumbel-Softmax estimator outperforms state-of-the-art gradient estimators on structured output prediction and unsupervised generative modeling tasks with categorical latent variables, and enables large speedups on semi-supervised classification.
review:
The paper introduces Gumbel-Softmax, a continuous relaxation of categorical sampling that enables reparameterized gradients through discrete latent variables. Samples are obtained by adding Gumbel noise to logits and applying a temperature-controlled softmax; as temperature anneals, samples approach one-hot categorical values. The authors also propose a straight-through variant for settings requiring discrete outputs. Experiments compare against score-function, DARN, MuProp, and straight-through estimators on structured output prediction, VAE training with Bernoulli/categorical latents, and semi-supervised classification.

Strengths: The method is simple, practical, and clearly presented. It fills an important gap by providing a low-variance path-derivative estimator for categorical variables, analogous to the reparameterization trick for continuous latents. Empirical results are consistent: Gumbel-Softmax outperforms single-sample baselines on both Bernoulli and categorical tasks, and the semi-supervised experiment shows large speedups over marginalization as the number of classes grows, with comparable accuracy. The relation to the concurrently proposed Concrete distribution is transparently noted.

Weaknesses: The estimator is biased for nonzero temperature, and the bias-variance tradeoff depends on annealing schedules that are chosen heuristically. The straight-through variant is also biased and lacks theoretical guarantees. Evaluation is limited to binarized MNIST and relatively small models, with no large-scale language, attention, or reinforcement learning experiments. Comparisons omit multi-sample estimators such as VIMCO, and variance/significance reporting is limited.

Overall, Gumbel-Softmax is an influential and widely useful contribution with strong empirical support. I recommend acceptance, requesting broader task validation, annealing ablations, and deeper bias-variance analysis.

title: Online Bayesian Transfer Learning for Sequential Data Modeling
abstract: Abstract:###We consider the problem of inferring a sequence of hidden states associated with a sequence of observations produced by an individual within a population. Instead of learning a single sequence model for the population (which does not account for variations within the population), we learn a set of basis sequence models based on different individuals. The sequence of hidden states for a new individual is inferred in an online fashion by estimating a distribution over the basis models that best explain the sequence of observations of this new individual. We explain how to do this in the context of hidden Markov models with Gaussian mixture models that are learned based on streaming data by online Bayesian moment matching. The resulting transfer learning technique is demonstrated with three real-word applications: activity recognition based on smartphone sensors, sleep classification based on electroencephalography data and the prediction of the direction of future packet flows between a pair of servers in telecommunication networks.
review:
The paper proposes an online Bayesian transfer-learning method for sequential data. It learns individual HMMs with Gaussian-mixture emissions for source individuals via Bayesian moment matching, then infers a Dirichlet posterior over basis-model weights for a new target individual as observations stream in. Predictions combine source transition and emission models according to these weights. Experiments cover smartphone activity recognition, sleep-stage classification, and packet-flow direction prediction.

Strengths: The approach directly targets subject variability and is genuinely online, avoiding mini-batches and learning-rate tuning. BMM provides a tractable alternative to exact Bayesian learning, and the basis-weight formulation is simple and interpretable. Computational complexity is discussed, and the method is demonstrated on three real-world domains.

Weaknesses: Evaluation appears limited to HMM/GMM baselines and does not compare against modern deep sequence models or stronger transfer-learning methods. The Markov and Gaussian-mixture assumptions may be restrictive for complex sensor and telecommunication data. Basis models remain fixed, and only mixture weights adapt, limiting target-specific adaptation. Scalability to many source individuals (quadratic in K) and high-dimensional features is not fully analyzed. Ablations on the numbers of sources, hidden states, and mixture components are limited, and variance or significance tests are absent. The experimental section in the provided text is truncated, making reproducibility harder to assess.

Overall, this is a practical and clearly motivated transfer-learning method with useful real-world applications, but the empirical comparison and scalability analysis need strengthening. I recommend acceptance, requesting broader baselines, ablations, and statistical reporting.

title: Latent Sequence Decompositions
abstract: Abstract:###Sequence-to-sequence models rely on a fixed decomposition of the target sequences into a sequence of tokens that may be words, word-pieces or characters. The choice of these tokens and the decomposition of the target sequences into a sequence of tokens is often static, and independent of the input, output data domains. This can potentially lead to a sub-optimal choice of token dictionaries, as the decomposition is not informed by the particular problem being solved. In this paper we present Latent Sequence Decompositions (LSD), a framework in which the decomposition of sequences into constituent tokens is learnt during the training of the model. The decomposition depends both on the input sequence and on the output sequence. In LSD, during training, the model samples decompositions incrementally, from left to right by locally sampling between valid extensions. We experiment with the Wall Street Journal speech recognition task. Our LSD model achieves 12.9% WER compared to a character baseline of 14.8% WER. When combined with a convolutional network on the encoder, we achieve a WER of 9.6%.
review:
The paper introduces Latent Sequence Decompositions (LSD), a sequence-to-sequence framework that learns latent tokenizations of output sequences, allowing variable-length word pieces chosen as a function of both input and output. Training marginalizes over decompositions via a left-to-right sampling estimator with ε-greedy exploration, and decoding uses beam search over word-piece sequences. On WSJ ASR, LSD improves WER from 14.8% (character baseline) to 12.9%, and to 9.6% when combined with a CNN encoder.

Strengths: The idea is simple and well motivated: fixed character/word decompositions are often suboptimal, especially in speech where segmentation should depend on acoustics. The probabilistic formulation and gradient derivation are clear, and the empirical gains are substantial without an external language model. The comparison to a MaxExt deterministic decomposition is useful, and analyses of learned piece-length distributions support the claim that LSD learns nontrivial tokenizations.

Weaknesses: The training estimator is explicitly biased because it samples valid extensions left-to-right rather than from the true posterior, and ε-greedy exploration is heuristic. Decoding approximates the marginal by maximizing over a single decomposition, which may miss probability mass from alternative segmentations. Evaluation is limited to WSJ ASR; other seq2seq tasks and larger datasets are absent. Vocabulary construction is frequency-based, and sensitivity to token-set size, n, and exploration schedule is only lightly ablated. Variance and significance are not reported.

Overall, LSD is a novel and effective framework with strong ASR results, but its approximate inference and narrow evaluation need strengthening. I recommend acceptance, requesting broader tasks, ablation, and analysis of the biased estimator.

title: Paleo: A Performance Model for Deep Neural Networks
abstract: Abstract:###Although various scalable deep learning software packages have been proposed, it remains unclear how to best leverage parallel and distributed computing infrastructure to accelerate their training and deployment. Moreover, the effectiveness of existing parallel and distributed systems varies widely based on the neural network architecture and dataset under consideration. In order to efficiently explore the space of scalable deep learning systems and quickly diagnose their effectiveness for a given problem instance, we introduce an analytical performance model called Paleo. Our key observation is that a neural network architecture carries with it a declarative specification of the computational requirements associated with its training and evaluation. By extracting these requirements from a given architecture and mapping them to a specific point within the design space of software, hardware and communication strategies, Paleo can efficiently and accurately model the expected scalability and performance of a putative deep learning system. We show that Paleo is robust to the choice of network architecture, hardware, software, communication schemes, and parallelization strategies. We further demonstrate its ability to accurately model various recently published scalability results for CNNs such as NiN, Inception and AlexNet.
review:
The paper introduces PALEO, an analytical performance model for deep neural network training and deployment. It decomposes execution time into computation and communication, deriving per-layer FLOPs, memory IO, hardware speed, communication scheme, and parallelization strategy from the architecture and system configuration. A platform percent-of-peak calibration captures software inefficiency. PALEO is validated layer-wise on AlexNet and VGG-16 with TensorFlow, then used to reproduce published scalability results for NiN/FireCaffe, Inception/TensorFlow, and AlexNet hybrid parallelism, plus hypothetical cloud and GAN studies.

Strengths: The approach is practical, architecture-aware, and combines computation, communication, and parallelization in one model. The FLOP formulations, convolution algorithm selection, communication schemes, and PPP calibration are clearly described. Case studies show useful accuracy: AlexNet forward/backward estimates are close, and projected speedups broadly track FireCaffe and Krizhevsky’s hybrid results. The model can guide system design and diagnose bottlenecks without full implementation.

Weaknesses: Accuracy depends heavily on calibrated PPP and hardware/software parameters, and errors remain (e.g., AlexNet backward 118 ms vs. 155 ms; fc6 underestimation). The model covers mainly CNNs/GANs, synchronous deterministic communication, and ignores scheduling, memory limits, and training dynamics. Large-scale projections are sometimes optimistic (51.6× vs. 39× for NiN). No variance or confidence estimates are reported.

Overall, PALEO is a useful and well-executed performance-modeling contribution. I recommend acceptance, requesting error analysis, broader architectures, and uncertainty reporting.

title: Combining policy gradient and Q-learning
abstract: Abstract:###Policy gradient is an efficient technique for improving a policy in a reinforcement learning setting. However, vanilla online variants are on-policy only and not able to take advantage of off-policy data. In this paper we describe a new technique that combines policy gradient with off-policy Q-learning, drawing experience from a replay buffer. This is motivated by making a connection between the fixed points of the regularized policy gradient algorithm and the Q-values. This connection allows us to estimate the Q-values from the action preferences of the policy, to which we apply Q-learning updates. We refer to the new technique as â€˜PGQLâ€™, for policy gradient and Q-learning. We also establish an equivalency between action-value fitting techniques and actor-critic algorithms, showing that regularized policy gradient techniques can be interpreted as advantage function learning algorithms. We conclude with some numerical examples that demonstrate improved data efficiency and stability of PGQL. In particular, we tested PGQL on the full suite of Atari games and achieved performance exceeding that of both asynchronous advantage actor-critic (A3C) and Q-learning.
review:
The paper proposes PGQL, which combines entropy-regularized policy gradient with off-policy Q-learning. The key theoretical insight is that at a fixed point of regularized policy gradient, the policy can be interpreted as a softmax over the induced advantage function, yielding a Q-value estimate from the policy’s action preferences. PGQL then refines this estimate with Q-learning updates from a replay buffer. The authors also establish an equivalence between actor-critic and action-value fitting methods and bound the Bellman residual of the induced policy, showing it vanishes as regularization decreases. Experiments on Atari are reported to outperform A3C and Q-learning.

Strengths: The theoretical connection is clean and well motivated, and the equivalence result helps unify two major RL families. The Bellman residual analysis provides useful justification for small entropy regularization. Combining on-policy policy improvement with off-policy replay targets data efficiency and stability, which is a practically important direction.

Weaknesses: The empirical section is only briefly summarized in the provided text; detailed learning curves, hyperparameter sensitivity, variance across seeds, and ablation of the Q-learning component are not shown. The method introduces additional hyperparameters and relies on the accuracy of the policy-derived Q estimate, especially with function approximation. The theoretical equivalence assumes tabular or well-specified settings, and the Bellman bound depends on action-set size and temperature. Comparisons with more recent off-policy actor-critic methods are limited.

Overall, PGQL is a theoretically appealing and promising combination of policy gradient and Q-learning, with encouraging Atari results. I recommend acceptance, requesting fuller empirical reporting, ablations, and analysis under function approximation.

title: Density estimation using Real NVP
abstract: Abstract:###Unsupervised learning of probabilistic models is a central yet challenging problem in machine learning. Specifically, designing models with tractable learning, sampling, inference and evaluation is crucial in solving this task.
