We extend the space of such models using real-valued non-volume preserving (real NVP) transformations, a set of powerful invertible and learnable transformations, resulting in an unsupervised learning algorithm with exact log-likelihood computation, exact sampling, exact inference of latent variables, and an interpretable latent space. We demonstrate its ability to model natural images on four datasets through sampling, log-likelihood evaluation and latent variable manipulations.
review:
The paper introduces Real NVP, a class of invertible transformations with tractable Jacobian determinants for exact likelihood-based generative modeling. The key building block is an affine coupling layer that leaves part of the input unchanged while scaling and translating the rest as a function of the unchanged part, yielding a triangular Jacobian and efficient inverse. Stacking alternating coupling layers, masked convolutions, squeezing, and multi-scale factoring enables exact sampling, exact inference, and exact log-likelihood evaluation. Experiments report bits-per-dimension on CIFAR-10, ImageNet, LSUN, and CelebA, plus qualitative samples and latent-space traversals.

Strengths: The construction is elegant and clearly motivated. Coupling layers achieve expressive nonlinear transformations while keeping likelihood and inversion tractable, avoiding approximation in inference or sampling. The multi-scale architecture and batch normalization treatment are practical, and exact parallel sampling is a meaningful advantage over autoregressive models. Results are competitive with other likelihood-based methods, and latent manipulations appear semantically coherent.

Weaknesses: Likelihood results do not surpass PixelRNN, and sample quality is mixed, with some implausible CelebA samples. The architecture requires careful design of masks, squeezing, and scale functions, and the Jacobian determinant depends on volume-changing scaling, which may complicate optimization. Evaluation is mostly image-based, with limited comparison to other exact-likelihood models and no quantitative latent-variable analysis. Variance across runs is not reported.

Overall, Real NVP is an influential and well-presented contribution with exact likelihood and sampling. I recommend acceptance, requesting stronger empirical comparisons and more rigorous latent-space evaluation.

title: Recurrent Batch Normalization
abstract: Abstract:###We propose a reparameterization of LSTM that brings the benefits of batch normalization to recurrent neural networks. Whereas previous works only apply batch normalization to the input-to-hidden transformation of RNNs, we demonstrate that it is both possible and beneficial to batch-normalize the hidden-to-hidden transition, thereby reducing internal covariate shift between time steps. We evaluate our proposal on various sequential problems such as sequence classification, language modeling and question answering. Our empirical results show that our batch-normalized LSTM consistently leads to faster convergence and improved generalization.
review:
The paper proposes Recurrent Batch Normalization for LSTMs, applying batch normalization to both input-to-hidden and hidden-to-hidden transitions, normalizing the recurrent and input terms separately, and avoiding normalization inside the cell update to preserve gradient flow. It uses per-timestep statistics and recommends initializing the BN scale γ to 0.1, with analysis showing that larger pre-activation variance saturates tanh and causes vanishing gradients. Experiments cover sequential and permuted MNIST, character-level Penn Treebank and text8, and the Attentive Reader QA model.

Strengths: The paper convincingly overturns prior skepticism about recurrent BN, showing faster convergence and improved generalization across diverse tasks. The gradient-flow analysis is clear and practically useful, and the reparameterization is simple to implement. Results are strong: BN-LSTM improves pMNIST accuracy to 95.4% versus 90.2%, text8 BPC to 1.36 versus 1.43, and Attentive Reader test error to 36.3% versus 45.0%. The treatment of variable-length and bidirectional models is thoughtful.

Weaknesses: Per-timestep statistics add memory and complexity and may not scale well to very long sequences. The zero-variance issue on sequential MNIST requires adding noise, and γ initialization is heuristic. Comparisons focus mainly on vanilla LSTM, with limited ablation against layer normalization, weight normalization, and other recurrent normalization schemes. Statistical significance and variance across runs are not reported, and some state-of-the-art claims have since been superseded.

Overall, this is a well-motivated, clearly presented, and empirically effective contribution. I recommend acceptance, requesting broader normalization baselines, long-sequence scaling analysis, and statistical reporting.

title: SGDR: Stochastic Gradient Descent with Warm Restarts
abstract: Abstract:###Restart techniques are common in gradient-free optimization to deal with multimodal functions. Partial warm restarts are also gaining popularity in gradient-based optimization to improve the rate of convergence in accelerated gradient schemes to deal with ill-conditioned functions. In this paper, we propose a simple warm restart technique for stochastic gradient descent to improve its anytime performance when training deep neural networks. We empirically study its performance on the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets, where we demonstrate new state-of-the-art results at 3.14\% and 16.21\%, respectively. We also demonstrate its advantages on a dataset of EEG recordings and on a downsampled version of the ImageNet dataset. Our source code is available at  url{https://github.com/loshchil/SGDR}
review:
The paper proposes SGDR, a cosine-annealing learning-rate schedule with periodic warm restarts for SGD. After each restart, the learning rate is raised and then decayed according to a cosine curve, optionally with exponentially increasing restart periods to improve anytime performance. Experiments train Wide ResNets on CIFAR-10/100, plus EEG and downsampled ImageNet, and report strong single-model and snapshot-ensemble results (3.14% CIFAR-10, 16.21% CIFAR-100).

Strengths: The method is simple, easy to implement, and requires few additional hyperparameters. The schedule is clearly described and visualized, and the anytime-performance motivation is well supported: SGDR reaches comparable or better errors 2–4× faster than the default step-decay schedule. The snapshot-ensemble experiments are a practical bonus, and results on WRN-28-20 suggest the schedule enables larger models within a fixed budget.

Weaknesses: The evaluation focuses heavily on CIFAR and Wide ResNets, with limited detail for EEG and ImageNet. Hyperparameter sensitivity—T0, T_mult, η_max, η_min—is only partially ablated, and comparisons use medians of few runs without significance tests. The paper does not deeply explain why warm restarts help optimization or how the schedule interacts with momentum and weight decay. Claims of state-of-the-art are dataset-specific and may date quickly.

Overall, SGDR is a simple, effective, and widely adopted training heuristic with convincing empirical support. I recommend acceptance, requesting broader task validation, fuller hyperparameter ablations, and statistical reporting.

title: Learning a Natural Language Interface with Neural Programmer
abstract: Abstract:###Learning a natural language interface for database tables is a challenging task that involves deep language understanding and multi-step reasoning. The task is often approached by mapping natural language queries to logical forms or programs that provide the desired response when executed on the database. To our knowledge, this paper presents the first weakly supervised, end-to-end neural network model to induce such programs on a real-world dataset. We enhance the objective function of Neural Programmer, a neural network with built-in discrete operations, and apply it on WikiTableQuestions, a natural language question-answering dataset. The model is trained end-to-end with weak supervision of question-answer pairs, and does not require domain-specific grammars, rules, or annotations that are key elements in previous approaches to program induction. The main experimental result in this paper is that a single Neural Programmer model achieves 34.2% accuracy using only 10,000 examples with weak supervision. An ensemble of 15 models, with a trivial combination technique, achieves 37.7% accuracy, which is competitive to the current state-of-the-art accuracy of 37.1% obtained by a traditional natural language semantic parser.
review:
The paper applies Neural Programmer to weakly supervised semantic parsing over database tables, enhancing its objective to handle ambiguity when answers may be generated as scalars or selected as table entries. It trains end-to-end on WikiTableQuestions using only question–answer pairs, with hand-defined discrete operations, soft selection during training, hard selection at test time, and strong regularization.

Strengths: The work is a valuable step toward end-to-end neural program induction on a real-world dataset. The modified scalar/lookup loss sensibly addresses weak supervision and ambiguous answer locations. A single model reaches 34.2% test accuracy, and an ensemble of 15 reaches 37.7%, competitive with a traditional semantic parser at 37.1%. Ablations show the importance of regularization and the column-match feature, and program analyses illustrate adaptation to unseen column names and operation usage. The paper is clearly written and candid about overfitting.

Weaknesses: The operation set is hand-designed and limited, and the model runs for only four timesteps, restricting program complexity. Training excludes tables with 100+ rows due to memory, and double precision is needed for stable gradients. The ensemble gain over the parser is marginal, and no significance tests are reported. Training accuracy of 53% versus roughly 34% test indicates substantial overfitting. Comparisons to neural baselines are useful but use reduced subsets. The paper does not quantitatively evaluate induced-program correctness beyond final answers.

Overall, this is a solid and well-motivated contribution with competitive results, but limited generality. I recommend acceptance, requesting larger tables, statistical reporting, and broader operation/program evaluation.

title: Reinforcement Learning through Asynchronous Advantage Actor-Critic on a GPU
abstract: Abstract:###We introduce a hybrid CPU/GPU version of the Asynchronous Advantage Actor-Critic (A3C) algorithm, currently the state-of-the-art method in reinforcement learning for various gaming tasks. We analyze its computational traits and concentrate on aspects critical to leveraging the GPU*s computational power. We introduce a system of queues and a dynamic scheduling strategy, potentially helpful for other asynchronous algorithms as well. Our hybrid CPU/GPU version of A3C, based on TensorFlow, achieves a significant speed up compared to a CPU implementation; we make it publicly available to other researchers at https://github.com/NVlabs/GA3C.
review:
The paper presents PixelCNN++, a set of practical modifications to PixelCNN: a discretized logistic mixture likelihood replacing the 256-way softmax, conditioning on whole pixels rather than sub-pixels, downsampling with long-range shortcuts, and dropout regularization. The authors report state-of-the-art CIFAR-10 log-likelihood of 2.92 bits per sub-pixel and provide ablation studies and code.

Strengths: The modifications are clearly motivated and well described. The discretized logistic mixture is a sensible fix for the sparse-gradient and edge-value issues of softmax likelihoods, and whole-pixel conditioning simplifies the architecture without clear loss. Downsampling plus shortcuts is an efficient alternative to dilated convolutions, and the ablations convincingly show that shortcuts and dropout are essential. The CIFAR-10 result is strong, and class-conditional and small-receptive-field experiments add useful insight. Releasing code is valuable.

Weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to CIFAR-10, so generality to other datasets and resolutions is unclear. Several changes are introduced together, making it difficult to isolate their individual contributions; the softmax comparison is architecture-specific. The no-shortcut model fails to train, suggesting the downsampling design is fragile without careful compensation. Training details, compute cost, and variance across runs are not reported, and perceptual sample quality remains mixed.

Overall, PixelCNN++ is a well-executed and influential engineering contribution with strong likelihood results and useful ablations. I recommend acceptance, requesting broader dataset validation and more detailed computational and statistical reporting.

title: Learning to Navigate in Complex Environments
abstract: Abstract:###Learning to navigate in complex environments with dynamic elements is an important milestone in developing AI agents. In this work we formulate the navigation question as a reinforcement learning problem and show that data efficiency and task performance can be dramatically improved by relying on additional auxiliary tasks to bootstrap learning. In particular we consider jointly learning the goal-driven reinforcement learning problem with an unsupervised depth prediction task and a self-supervised loop closure classification task. Using this approach we can learn to navigate from raw sensory input in complicated 3D mazes, approaching human-level performance even under conditions where the goal location changes frequently. We provide detailed analysis of the agent behaviour, its ability to localise, and its network activity dynamics, that show that the agent implicitly learns key navigation abilities, with only sparse rewards and without direct supervision.
review:
The paper trains A3C agents with stacked LSTMs to navigate visually rich 3D mazes, augmenting the RL loss with auxiliary depth prediction and loop-closure classification. It evaluates feedforward, LSTM, and Nav A3C variants on static and random-goal mazes, including an I-maze, and analyzes learned localization via position decoding.

Strengths: The auxiliary-task approach is well motivated and effective. Adding depth and loop-closure losses substantially improves data efficiency and final performance, with Nav A3C+D2 reaching human-level scores on static mazes and 91%/59% of human scores on random-goal mazes. The architecture details, including velocity/action/reward inputs and stacked LSTMs, are clearly described. Position-decoding analysis provides useful evidence that agents implicitly localize, and the loop-closure detector achieves F1 0.83. The paper is transparent about reward clipping and depth regression versus classification.

Weaknesses: Evaluation is confined to DeepMind Lab mazes, so generality to real-world or other navigation domains is unclear. Results are averaged over the top 5 of 64 hyperparameter runs, which may overstate typical performance. Auxiliary loss weights are hand-tuned, and sensitivity is not thoroughly ablated. Comparisons are mostly internal A3C variants rather than other navigation or SLAM-inspired methods. Localization–performance correlations are suggestive but not causal, and the I-maze position-decoding anomaly is only hypothesized.

Overall, this is a strong empirical study showing auxiliary tasks can bootstrap navigation learning from pixels. I recommend acceptance, requesting broader baselines, full hyperparameter reporting, and ablation of auxiliary weights.

title: DeepCoder: Learning to Write Programs
abstract: Abstract:###We develop a first line of attack for solving programming competition-style problems from input-output examples using deep learning. The approach is to train a neural network to predict properties of the program that generated the outputs from the inputs. We use the neural network*s predictions to augment search techniques from the programming languages community, including enumerative search and an SMT-based solver. Empirically, we show that our approach leads to an order of magnitude speedup over the strong non-augmented baselines and a Recurrent Neural Network approach, and that we are able to solve problems of difficulty comparable to the simplest problems on programming competition websites.
review:
The paper introduces DeepCoder, an instantiation of Learning Inductive Program Synthesis (LIPS) that uses a neural network to predict program attributes from input–output examples and guides existing search procedures rather than replacing them. Programs are expressed in a restricted list-processing DSL, attributes indicate presence of functions and lambdas, and predictions are used to order or restrict search in DFS, sort-and-add enumeration, Sketch, and λ². Experiments on synthetic programs of length 3 and 5 report order-of-magnitude speedups over non-augmented search and a sequence-to-sequence beam-search baseline.

Strengths: The framing is clear and practical: learning to guide search avoids the brittleness of direct program prediction and preserves solver correctness. The LIPS framework is general, and the data-generation procedure enables large-scale training. Results are substantial, especially for sort-and-add enumeration and λ², and the generalization experiment across program lengths is a useful robustness check. The theoretical link between marginal-probability ordering and expected sort-and-add runtime is a nice justification.

Weaknesses: The DSL is limited to linear sequences of list operations, excluding loops, branching, and dynamic programming, so claims about programming-competition problems are modest. Training and test programs are synthetic and semantically disjoint, but inputs use relatively large integers and five examples, which may be more informative than realistic queries. The feed-forward encoder requires fixed maximum lengths, and the RNN decoder baseline is weak. Comparisons are mostly internal, with limited evaluation on real competition problems. No variance or significance reporting is provided.

Overall, DeepCoder is a well-motivated and influential hybrid of learning and search with strong synthetic evidence. I recommend acceptance, requesting real-problem evaluation, richer DSL validation, and statistical reporting.

title: Learning and Policy Search in Stochastic Dynamical Systems with Bayesian Neural Networks
abstract: Abstract:###We present an algorithm for policy search in stochastic dynamical systems using model-based reinforcement learning. The system dynamics are described with Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) that include stochastic input variables. These input variables allow us to capture complex statistical patterns in the transition dynamics (e.g. multi-modality and heteroskedasticity), which are usually missed by alternative modeling approaches. After learning the dynamics, our BNNs are then fed into an algorithm that performs random roll-outs and uses stochastic optimization for policy learning. We train our BNNs by minimizing -divergences with , which usually produces better results than other techniques such as variational Bayes. We illustrate the performance of our method by solving a challenging problem where model-based approaches usually fail and by obtaining promising results in real-world scenarios including the control of a gas turbine and an industrial benchmark.
review:
The paper proposes model-based policy search for stochastic dynamical systems using Bayesian neural networks with explicit stochastic input variables. These inputs capture multimodality and heteroskedasticity in transition dynamics, while approximate inference is performed by minimizing α-divergences with α=0.5. Policies are optimized via random roll-outs and stochastic gradient descent. Experiments cover the Wet-Chicken benchmark, a gas-turbine control task, and an industrial benchmark, comparing MLP, variational Bayes, α=1.0, Gaussian processes, and PSO-P.

Strengths: The modeling idea is well motivated and addresses a real limitation of deterministic or Gaussian-noise transition models. The α=0.5 inference is reported to be more robust than variational Bayes and better at capturing complex stochastic patterns, especially when q(z) is not fully optimized. Results are encouraging: α=0.5 achieves the best average rank and improves over GP and VB baselines, including the first model-based solution to Wet-Chicken. The industrial focus and reported standard errors add credibility.

Weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to three problems and five runs, with proprietary industrial data reducing reproducibility. Policy search relies on random roll-outs and may be sample inefficient or brittle in higher dimensions. The choice α=0.5 is not thoroughly ablated, and the method assumes Markovian, observed states. Comparisons omit modern deep model-based RL methods, and safety/exploration constraints central to industrial deployment are not analyzed.

Overall, this is a well-motivated and empirically promising contribution. I recommend acceptance, requesting broader benchmarks, α sensitivity analysis, and comparison to deep model-based RL baselines.

title: Variable Computation in Recurrent Neural Networks
abstract: Abstract:###Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) have been used extensively and with increasing success to model various types of sequential data. Much of this progress has been achieved through devising recurrent units and architectures with the flexibility to capture complex statistics in the data, such as long range dependency or localized attention phenomena. However, while many sequential data (such as video, speech or language) can have highly variable information flow, most recurrent models still consume input features at a constant rate and perform a constant number of computations per time step, which can be detrimental to both speed and model capacity. In this paper, we explore a modification to existing recurrent units which allows them to learn to vary the amount of computation they perform at each step, without prior knowledge of the sequence*s time structure. We show experimentally that not only do our models require fewer operations, they also lead to better performance overall on evaluation tasks.
review:
The paper introduces Variable Computation RNNs and GRUs, in which a scheduler predicts how many hidden dimensions to update at each timestep. A soft threshold mask and annealing make the discrete computation choice differentiable, while a penalty controls the average computation budget. Experiments on music modeling, bit/character-level Penn Treebank and Text8, and Czech/German Europarl show reduced operations and competitive or improved perplexity, with learned schedules aligning with bars/rests, ASCII boundaries, and word boundaries.

Strengths: The idea is simple, well motivated, and compatible with standard recurrent units. The scheduler and partial-update formulation are clearly described, and the soft-mask/annealing training procedure is practical. Learned computation patterns are interpretable and support the authors’ claims about temporal structure. Results show favorable perplexity per operation, and the Europarl experiments demonstrate cross-lingual behavior.

Weaknesses: Computation is restricted to updating a prefix of hidden dimensions, which is an arbitrary structural constraint. Gains are reported as operation counts rather than measured wall-clock speedups, and GPU kernels may not realize the savings. The scheduler is a simple log-linear function, and sensitivity to the sharpness parameter, penalty target, and annealing schedule is only lightly ablated. Comparisons focus on Elman/GRU/LSTM baselines, with limited comparison to other adaptive-computation methods. Variance and significance tests are absent.

Overall, this is a novel and promising adaptive-computation approach with interpretable empirical support. I recommend acceptance, requesting wall-clock benchmarks, broader adaptive-computation baselines, and more detailed ablation/statistical reporting.

title: Deep Variational Information Bottleneck
abstract: Abstract:###We present a variational approximation to the information bottleneck of Tishby et al. (1999). This variational approach allows us to parameterize the information bottleneck model using a neural network and leverage the reparameterization trick for efficient training. We call this method â€œDeep Variational Information Bottleneckâ€, or Deep VIB. We show that models trained with the VIB objective outperform those that are trained with other forms of regularization, in terms of generalization performance and robustness to adversarial attack.
review:
The paper presents Deep Variational Information Bottleneck (VIB), a variational lower bound on the information bottleneck objective \(I(Z,Y)-\beta I(Z,X)\), trained via the reparameterization trick. It parameterizes a stochastic Gaussian encoder and variational decoder, and evaluates on permutation-invariant MNIST, showing modest regularization gains and improved adversarial robustness. It also visualizes IB curves and two-dimensional latent embeddings.

Strengths: The formulation is clear, principled, and enables stochastic gradient training of information-bottleneck models with deep networks. The experiments compare VIB against dropout, confidence penalty, and label smoothing, and include FGS and \(L_2\) adversarial attacks. The IB curves, 2D embedding visualizations, and analysis of \(\beta\)-controlled compression provide useful insight. The connections to VAEs and entropy regularization are concisely explained.

Weaknesses: Empirical scope is limited largely to MNIST, and the provided text truncates the adversarial results. Classification gains are modest (1.13% versus 1.17–1.23% for regularized baselines). Sensitivity to \(\beta\), architecture, and bottleneck dimension is not thoroughly ablated. The variational bound is loose, and no theoretical robustness guarantee is offered. Comparisons to concurrent variational IB work and other robust-training methods are limited. Variance and significance for adversarial evaluations are not consistently reported, and scalability to larger datasets remains untested.

Overall, VIB is an elegant and useful information-theoretic regularization framework with promising robustness evidence, but broader empirical validation and deeper analysis are needed. I recommend acceptance, requesting complete adversarial results, larger-scale experiments, \(\beta\) sensitivity analysis, and statistical reporting.

title: The Neural Noisy Channel
abstract: Abstract:###We formulate sequence to sequence transduction as a noisy channel decoding problem and use recurrent neural networks to parameterise the source and channel models. Unlike direct models which can suffer from explaining-away effects during training, noisy channel models must produce outputs that explain their inputs, and their component models can be trained with not only paired training samples but also unpaired samples from the marginal output distribution. Using a latent variable to control how much of the conditioning sequence the channel model needs to read in order to generate a subsequent symbol, we obtain a tractable and effective beam search decoder. Experimental results on abstractive sentence summarisation, morphological inflection, and machine translation show that noisy channel models outperform direct models, and that they significantly benefit from increased amounts of unpaired output data that direct models cannot easily use.
review:
The paper formulates sequence-to-sequence transduction as noisy channel decoding, parameterizing the channel \(p(x|y)\) with an online segment-to-segment neural model and combining it with an unconditional source language model \(p(y)\). A latent alignment variable enables prefix-based channel scoring and tractable beam search using a direct model to propose candidate extensions. Experiments on abstractive summarization, Chinese–English translation, and German morphological inflection compare direct, channel, and interpolated models, including use of unpaired output data.

Strengths: The motivation is clear and the noisy-channel decomposition is well suited to exploiting abundant unpaired targets. The SSNT-based channel model and incremental alignment formulation make decoding feasible, and the proposal-rescoring beam search is described clearly. Results are consistent across tasks: channel models beat direct models, interpolated models are best, and additional unpaired headlines improve summarization. The human preference evaluation and comparison to prior semi-supervised work strengthen the claims.

Weaknesses: Decoding is complex and relies on an auxiliary direct model, beam-size hyperparameters, and tuned interpolation weights. The channel model assumes largely monotonic alignment, which limits translation word-order divergence, and the paper acknowledges poorer SSNT direct performance. Experiments cover only three tasks and limited language pairs. Gains on summarization are modest in ROUGE, and the language-model combination alone fails, indicating sensitivity to weighting. Variance and significance tests are not reported.

Overall, this is a well-motivated and effective framework with strong empirical support. I recommend acceptance, requesting broader language pairs, decoding-cost analysis, and statistical reporting.

title: Automatic Rule Extraction from Long Short Term Memory Networks
abstract: Abstract:###Although deep learning models have proven effective at solving problems in natural language processing, the mechanism by which they come to their conclusions is often unclear. As a result, these models are generally treated as black boxes, yielding no insight of the underlying learned patterns. In this paper we consider Long Short Term Memory networks (LSTMs) and demonstrate a new approach for tracking the importance of a given input to the LSTM for a given output. By identifying consistently important patterns of words, we are able to distill state of the art LSTMs on sentiment analysis and question answering into a set of representative phrases. This representation is then quantitatively validated by using the extracted phrases to construct a simple, rule-based classifier which approximates the output of the LSTM.
review:
The paper proposes a method for extracting interpretable phrase rules from trained LSTMs by decomposing the output probability into word-level contributions. It introduces a multiplicative cell-difference score and an additive cell decomposition that accounts for intervening forget gates, then extracts frequently predictive phrases and validates them with a simple rule-based classifier on Yelp, SST, and WikiMovies.

Strengths: The decomposition is novel and tailored to LSTM structure. The additive formulation is well motivated: by propagating each word’s cell update through subsequent forget gates, it reduces false positives compared with cell-difference and gradient scores. Qualitative examples are sensible, and the quantitative rule-based evaluation usefully compares importance measures. The WikiMovies adaptation, conditioning phrases on question embeddings and entity positions, shows the approach extends beyond document classification. The paper is clearly written and honestly notes approximation gaps.

Weaknesses: The distilled rule classifiers remain substantially below the source LSTMs—Yelp 86.5 vs. 95.3, SST 76.2 vs. 87.3, and WikiMovies 74.3 vs. 80.1—so “distillation” overstates fidelity. Evaluation is mostly binary classification, with limited multi-class or sequence tasks. Phrase extraction relies on a heuristic threshold and ranking, and sensitivity to these choices is not ablated. Comparisons to gradient-based importance are internal, with no human interpretability study or statistical significance reporting. Extracted phrases can be locally sensible but contextually misleading, as the paper shows.

Overall, this is a promising and well-presented interpretability method with useful validation, but its fidelity and generality need strengthening. I recommend acceptance, requesting broader tasks, threshold ablations, and statistical reporting.

title: Dialogue Learning With Human-in-the-Loop
abstract: Abstract:###An important aspect of developing conversational agents is to give a bot the ability to improve through communicating with humans and to learn from the mistakes that it makes. Most research has focused on learning from fixed training sets of labeled data rather than interacting with a dialogue partner in an online fashion. In this paper we explore this direction in a reinforcement learning setting where the bot improves its question-answering ability from feedback a teacher gives following its generated responses. We build a simulator that tests various aspects of such learning in a synthetic environment, and introduce models that work in this regime. Finally, real experiments with Mechanical Turk validate the approach.
review:
The paper studies human-in-the-loop dialogue learning, where a Memory Network bot learns question answering from online teacher feedback. It develops a simulator using bAbI and WikiMovies, compares reward-based imitation (RBI), REINFORCE, and forward prediction (FP) using textual feedback, and then validates with Mechanical Turk human teachers. Key findings are that exploration or data balancing is needed to avoid instability, batch size has limited impact, RBI and REINFORCE perform comparably, and FP plus RBI is most effective under sparse rewards.

Strengths: The problem is important and the paper moves beyond fixed supervised datasets to iterative policy learning with real feedback. The simulator enables controlled ablations, and the human study adds valuable ecological validity. Results are encouraging: on Mechanical Turk, RBI+FP reaches 0.431–0.443 accuracy versus roughly 0.33–0.38 for RBI or FP alone, and iterative batch learning improves RBI from 74% to 98% on bAbI Task 6. The analysis of FP instability and the benefits of balancing/exploration is useful.

Weaknesses: The architecture is a relatively standard MemN2N, and evaluation is limited to synthetic bAbI/WikiMovies plus a templated human task. Human feedback remains short and answer-focused, not open-ended dialogue. The training assumes a single action per episode, closer to contextual bandits than multi-turn dialogue. Hyperparameters, human annotation variance, and statistical significance are not thoroughly reported. Scalability to long conversations and open domains is untested.

Overall, this is a well-motivated and practical study of online dialogue learning with human feedback, but broader and more rigorous evaluation is needed. I recommend acceptance, requesting multi-turn tasks, larger human studies, and statistical reporting.

title: Adversarially Learned Inference
abstract: Abstract:###We introduce the adversarially learned inference (ALI) model, which jointly learns a generation network and an inference network using an adversarial process. The generation network maps samples from stochastic latent variables to the data space while the inference network maps training examples in data space to the space of latent variables. An adversarial game is cast between these two networks and a discriminative network that is trained to distinguish between joint latent/data-space samples from the generative network and joint samples from the inference network. We illustrate the ability of the model to learn mutually coherent inference and generation networks through the inspections of model samples and reconstructions and confirm the usefulness of the learned representations by obtaining a performance competitive with other recent approaches on the semi-supervised SVHN task.
review:
The paper introduces Adversarially Learned Inference (ALI), which jointly trains an inference network and a generator by matching the joint distributions \(q(x,z)\) and \(p(x,z)\) with a discriminator over \((x,z)\) pairs. It derives the optimal discriminator, shows minimization of Jensen–Shannon divergence, and discusses invertibility under a deterministic encoder. Experiments on SVHN, CIFAR-10, CelebA, and Tiny ImageNet show sharp samples, latent interpolations, and competitive semi-supervised performance.

Strengths: The formulation is clean and well motivated, bridging GAN sample quality with VAE-style inference without an explicit reconstruction loss. The adversarial joint-matching objective is clearly derived, and the relation to GANs and BiGAN is transparently discussed. Qualitative samples and reconstructions demonstrate high fidelity, and latent interpolations suggest meaningful representations. Semi-supervised SVHN/CIFAR results support the usefulness of learned features.

Weaknesses: Reconstructions are often unfaithful, with mistakes in object placement, color, and identity; the authors attribute this to underfitting but do not resolve it. Training inherits GAN instability and requires careful architecture and hyperparameter choices. The method relies on reparameterization, so discrete data and discrete latents are not directly supported. The stochastic-versus-deterministic encoder comparison is only qualitative. Semi-supervised evaluation is limited, and variance or significance reporting is incomplete. Broader tasks and larger-scale validation are absent.

Overall, ALI is a novel and influential framework with strong conceptual and qualitative support. I recommend acceptance, requesting more rigorous reconstruction/semi-supervised analysis and stability ablations.

title: Learning through Dialogue Interactions by Asking Questions
abstract: Abstract:###A good dialogue agent should have the ability to interact with users by both responding to questions and by asking questions, and importantly to learn from both types of interactions. In this work, we explore this direction by designing a simulator and a set of synthetic tasks in the movie domain that allow such interactions between a learner and a teacher. We investigate how a learner can benefit from asking questions in both offline and online reinforcement learning settings, and demonstrate that the learner improves when asking questions. Our work represents a first step in developing such end-to-end learned interactive dialogue agents.
review:
The paper studies dialogue agents that learn by asking questions, not only answering them. It designs synthetic movie-domain tasks covering question clarification (typos), knowledge operation (finding relevant facts), and knowledge acquisition (missing KB entries), with QA and asking-question variants. It evaluates offline supervised training across TrainQA/AQ/Mix and test settings, online RL for deciding when to ask under a cost, and validates two tasks with Mechanical Turk human teachers.

Strengths: The problem is important and the task decomposition is clear and well motivated. The simulator enables controlled analysis of when asking helps, and the offline train/test matrix is a useful way to model real scenarios such as asking during learning but not at exam time. The online RL formulation with an asking cost is sensible, and the MTurk study adds valuable evidence beyond templates. Results generally support that asking questions improves learning and that learned asking policies can trade off cost and accuracy.

Weaknesses: The environment is synthetic and templated, with limited real-language evaluation. The agent can ask at most one question and only a task-specified question type, so broader dialogue behavior is untested. The MemN2N backbone is relatively simple, and comparisons omit stronger dialogue/QA models. The asking-cost hyperparameter and question-selection policy are only lightly analyzed. Variance, significance, and human-annotator agreement are not reported, and scalability to multi-turn, open-domain dialogue remains unclear.

Overall, this is a well-motivated first step with useful simulator and human validation, but broader and more rigorous evaluation is needed. I recommend acceptance, requesting multi-turn tasks, larger human studies, and statistical reporting.

title: Deep Information Propagation
abstract: Abstract:###We study the behavior of untrained neural networks whose weights and biases are randomly distributed using mean field theory. We show the existence of depth scales that naturally limit the maximum depth of signal propagation through these random networks. Our main practical result is to show that random networks may be trained precisely when information can travel through them. Thus, the depth scales that we identify provide bounds on how deep a network may be trained for a specific choice of hyperparameters. As a corollary to this, we argue that in networks at the edge of chaos, one of these depth scales diverges. Thus arbitrarily deep networks may be trained only sufficiently close to criticality. We show that the presence of dropout destroys the order-to-chaos critical point and therefore strongly limits the maximum trainable depth for random networks. Finally, we develop a mean field theory for backpropagation and we show that the ordered and chaotic phases correspond to regions of vanishing and exploding gradient respectively.
review:
The paper studies dialogue agents that learn by asking questions in addition to answering them. It designs synthetic movie-domain tasks covering question clarification (typos), knowledge operation (identifying relevant facts), and knowledge acquisition (missing KB entries), with QA and asking-question variants. It evaluates offline supervised training across TrainQA/AQ/Mix and test settings, online reinforcement learning for deciding when to ask under a cost, and validates two tasks with Mechanical Turk human teachers.

Strengths: The problem is important and the task taxonomy is clear and well motivated. The simulator enables controlled analysis of when asking helps, and the train/test matrix usefully models scenarios such as asking during learning but not at exam time. The online RL formulation with an asking cost is sensible, and the MTurk study adds valuable evidence beyond templates. Results generally support that asking questions improves learning and that learned asking policies can trade off cost and accuracy.

Weaknesses: The environment is synthetic and templated, with limited real-language evaluation. The agent can ask at most one question and only a task-specified question type, so broader dialogue behavior is untested. The MemN2N backbone is relatively simple, and comparisons omit stronger dialogue/QA models. The asking-cost hyperparameter and question-selection policy are only lightly analyzed. Variance, significance, and human-annotator agreement are not reported, and scalability to multi-turn, open-domain dialogue remains unclear.

Overall, this is a well-motivated first step with useful simulator and human validation, but broader and more rigorous evaluation is needed. I recommend acceptance, requesting multi-turn tasks, larger human studies, and statistical reporting.

title: FractalNet: Ultra-Deep Neural Networks without Residuals
abstract: Abstract:###We introduce a design strategy for neural network macro-architecture based on self-similarity. Repeated application of a simple expansion rule generates deep networks whose structural layouts are precisely truncated fractals. These networks contain interacting subpaths of different lengths, but do not include any pass-through or residual connections; every internal signal is transformed by a filter and nonlinearity before being seen by subsequent layers. In experiments, fractal networks match the excellent performance of standard residual networks on both CIFAR and ImageNet classification tasks, thereby demonstrating that residual representations may not be fundamental to the success of extremely deep convolutional neural networks. Rather, the key may be the ability to transition, during training, from effectively shallow to deep. We note similarities with student-teacher behavior and develop drop-path, a natural extension of dropout, to regularize co-adaptation of subpaths in fractal architectures. Such regularization allows extraction of high-performance fixed-depth subnetworks. Additionally, fractal networks exhibit an anytime property: shallow subnetworks provide a quick answer, while deeper subnetworks, with higher latency, provide a more accurate answer.
review:
The paper introduces FractalNet, a self-similar ultra-deep CNN macro-architecture built by recursively composing subnetworks and joining them with element-wise means, without explicit residual or pass-through connections. It also proposes drop-path regularization to prevent co-adaptation of parallel paths and to enable anytime subnetworks. Experiments on CIFAR-10/100, SVHN, and ImageNet show performance comparable to ResNet at equal depth, with strong gains from drop-path when no data augmentation is used.

Strengths: The design is simple and clearly presented, and the recursive construction is easy to implement. Drop-path is well motivated and effective: on CIFAR-100 it reduces error from 35.34% to 28.20%, and extracted single columns retain much of full-network accuracy. The paper offers useful analysis of effective depth, implicit deep supervision, and student–teacher-like dynamics, and demonstrates anytime behavior.

Weaknesses: FractalNet still relies on multi-path joins and averaging, which may supply gradient-shortening benefits akin to residuals, so the claim that residuals are incidental needs stronger isolation. ImageNet evaluation is limited to ResNet-34, and comparisons omit later strong architectures. Variance and significance tests are sparse, and drop-path schedules and column-extraction choices are heuristic. The student–teacher interpretation is speculative, and computational and memory costs and scaling to larger datasets are not thoroughly analyzed.

Overall, FractalNet is a novel and empirically convincing alternative to residual networks. I recommend acceptance, requesting broader ImageNet comparisons, statistical reporting, cost analysis, and ablations isolating joins versus residuals.

title: Revisiting Classifier Two-Sample Tests
abstract: Abstract:###The goal of two-sample tests is to assess whether two samples, and , are drawn from the same distribution. Perhaps intriguingly, one relatively unexplored method to build two-sample tests is the use of binary classifiers. In particular, construct a dataset by pairing the examples in with a positive label, and by pairing the examples in with a negative label. If the null hypothesis `` ** is true, then the classification accuracy of a binary classifier on a held-out subset of this dataset should remain near chance-level. As we will show, such emph{Classifier Two-Sample Tests} (C2ST) learn a suitable representation of the data on the fly, return test statistics in interpretable units, have a simple null distribution, and their predictive uncertainty allow to interpret where and differ. The goal of this paper is to establish the properties, performance, and uses of C2ST. First, we analyze their main theoretical properties. Second, we compare their performance against a variety of state-of-the-art alternatives. Third, we propose their use to evaluate the sample quality of generative models with intractable likelihoods, such as Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). Fourth, we showcase the novel application of GANs together with C2ST for causal discovery.
review:
The paper revisits classifier two-sample tests (C2ST), which train a binary classifier to distinguish samples from two distributions and use held-out accuracy as the test statistic. It analyzes null/alternative distributions and power, compares C2ST with kernel and classical tests on synthetic and real data, and applies it to GAN sample evaluation and causal discovery.

Strengths: The formulation is simple, general, and interpretable: accuracy is reported in intuitive units, classifiers learn representations on the fly, and predictive uncertainty/features can indicate where distributions differ. Theoretical analysis gives asymptotic null distributions and a power bound with the optimal order for fixed-dimensional problems. Experiments are broad, covering Gaussian/Student, sinusoid independence, NIPS article categories, facial expressions, and GAN evaluation. C2ST-NN achieves maximum power on NIPS categories and near-optimal power on facial expressions, while controlling type-I error. The GAN evaluation use is practical, and the observation that pixel-level tests exploit checkerboard artifacts is a useful caution.

Weaknesses: Performance depends on classifier capacity, training procedure, and the train/test split, with a bias-variance tradeoff that is not fully resolved. Asymptotic p-values may be unreliable for small test sets or complex classifiers. GAN evaluation requires held-out data and can be dominated by low-level artifacts rather than perceptual quality. The causal-discovery application is speculative and only briefly developed. Comparisons omit some modern learned tests, and variance/significance reporting is limited.

Overall, this is a well-motivated and useful unification of statistical testing and representation learning with strong empirical support. I recommend acceptance, requesting classifier-selection guidance, small-sample calibration, and deeper artifact-robust GAN evaluation.

title: Learning to Repeat: Fine Grained Action Repetition for Deep Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Abstract:###Reinforcement Learning algorithms can learn complex behavioral patterns for sequential decision making tasks wherein an agent interacts with an environment and acquires feedback in the form of rewards sampled from it. Traditionally, such algorithms make decisions, i.e., select actions to execute, at every single time step of the agent-environment interactions. In this paper, we propose a novel framework, Fine Grained Action Repetition (FiGAR), which enables the agent to decide the action as well as the time scale of repeating it. FiGAR can be used for improving any Deep Reinforcement Learning algorithm which maintains an explicit policy estimate by enabling temporal abstractions in the action space and implicitly enabling planning through sequences of repetitive macro-actions. We empirically demonstrate the efficacy of our framework by showing performance improvements on top of three policy search algorithms in different domains: Asynchronous Advantage Actor Critic in the Atari 2600 domain, Trust Region Policy Optimization in Mujoco domain and Deep Deterministic Policy Gradients in the TORCS car racing domain.
review:
The paper proposes Fine Grained Action Repetition (FiGAR), a generic extension to deep RL that factorizes the policy into an action-selection component and an action-repetition component. The agent therefore learns both what action to execute and how many times to repeat it, without coupling the action and repetition spaces. The authors instantiate FiGAR for A3C, TRPO, and DDPG, evaluating on Atari 2600, MuJoCo, and TORCS.

Strengths: The formulation is simple, general, and compatible with both discrete and continuous action spaces. The factored policy avoids the action-space blow-up of naive repetition augmentation, and the SMDP interpretation is useful. Empirical coverage is broad: FiGAR-A3C improves over A3C in 26 of 33 Atari games, FiGAR-TRPO is competitive or better on 3 of 5 MuJoCo tasks, and FiGAR-DDPG substantially improves TORCS reward. Learned repetition distributions and qualitative examples support the claim that temporally extended actions emerge.

Weaknesses: The repetition set size is chosen arbitrarily (30 for Atari/MuJoCo, 15 for TORCS) rather than tuned or justified, and hyperparameters are reused across variants. Several gains are marginal or negative, and variance/significance are not reported. DDPG is evaluated on only one domain, and comparisons omit other temporal-abstraction baselines. The SMDP framing is descriptive rather than theoretically developed, and the interaction between repetition and exploration is only lightly analyzed.

Overall, FiGAR is a practical, well-motivated framework with encouraging empirical results. I recommend acceptance, requesting repetition-set ablations, statistical reporting, and broader continuous-control validation.

title: Loss-aware Binarization of Deep Networks
abstract: Abstract:###Deep neural network models, though very powerful and highly successful, are computationally expensive in terms of space and time. Recently, there have been a number of attempts on binarizing the network weights and activations. This greatly reduces the network size, and replaces the underlying multiplications to additions or even XNOR bit operations. However, existing binarization schemes are based on simple matrix approximations and ignore the effect of binarization on the loss. In this paper, we propose a proximal Newton algorithm with diagonal Hessian approximation that directly minimizes the loss w.r.t. the binarized weights. The underlying proximal step has an efficient closed-form solution, and the second-order information can be efficiently obtained from the second moments already computed by the Adam optimizer. Experiments on both feedforward and recurrent networks show that the proposed loss-aware binarization algorithm outperforms existing binarization schemes, and is also more robust for wide and deep networks.
review:
The paper proposes Loss-Aware Binarization (LAB), which directly minimizes the training loss over binarized weights rather than approximating full-precision weights via matrix error. It formulates binarization as a constrained problem and solves it with proximal Newton using a diagonal Hessian approximated from Adam’s second moments, yielding a closed-form update. The method also extends to recurrent networks, where learned scaling helps mitigate exploding gradients. Experiments cover MNIST, CIFAR-10, SVHN, and character-level LSTM language modeling on War and Peace and the Linux Kernel.

Strengths: The core idea is well motivated: existing methods such as BinaryConnect and BWN ignore the effect of binarization on the loss. LAB is simple to integrate with Adam, has an efficient closed-form proximal step, and reduces to existing methods when curvature is dropped. Results are generally strong: LAB achieves the lowest error among weight-binarized models on MNIST and SVHN, outperforms BNN/XNOR when activations are also binarized, and is more robust as CNN width increases. The LSTM experiments usefully demonstrate that LAB handles long unrolled sequences where BinaryConnect fails, and the scaling argument is convincing.

Weaknesses: The convergence guarantee relies on assumptions not guaranteed in practice, and the Hessian approximation is crude. On CIFAR-10, LAB is slightly worse than BinaryConnect, and gains over BWN are often modest. Activation binarization uses a simple sign function, and comparisons omit several recent quantization methods. Variance and significance tests are not reported, and actual hardware speed/energy savings are not measured.

Overall, LAB is a principled and practical binarization method with solid empirical support. I recommend acceptance, requesting statistical reporting, broader baselines, and hardware-efficiency measurements.

title: Learning to Play in a Day: Faster Deep Reinforcement Learning by Optimality Tightening
abstract: Abstract:###We propose a novel training algorithm for reinforcement learning which combines the strength of deep Q-learning with a constrained optimization approach to tighten optimality and encourage faster reward propagation. Our novel technique makes deep reinforcement learning more practical by drastically reducing the training time. We evaluate the performance of our approach on the 49 games of the challenging Arcade Learning Environment, and report significant improvements in both training time and accuracy.
review:
The paper proposes optimality tightening for deep Q-learning, adding lower and upper bound constraints derived from multi-step returns in the replay buffer to propagate sparse rewards faster. The constrained objective is optimized via a quadratic penalty alongside the standard Bellman loss. Experiments on all 49 Atari games compare 10M-frame training against DQN trained for 200M frames and a reproduced 10M-frame DQN, reporting large gains in training time and normalized score.

Strengths: The motivation is clear: one-step Bellman updates propagate delayed rewards slowly, and multi-step bounds are a sensible fix. The formulation is straightforward and can be combined with existing DQN variants. Empirical results are striking: under one day on a single GPU, the method outperforms 200M-frame DQN on 30 of 49 games and improves over 10M-frame DQN on 46 of 49, with mean normalized score 345.70 versus 241.06. The analysis of sparse-reward propagation and the inclusion of discounted returns in replay are useful.

Weaknesses: The optimization is heuristic: constraints are non-convex, and the quadratic penalty with fixed λ lacks convergence guarantees or sensitivity analysis. K=4 and λ=4 are coarsely tuned on four games. Additional forward passes increase computational cost, not fully quantified. Many comparisons rely on prior DQN numbers, and 19 games remain below baseline. Variance and significance across seeds are absent, and gains over D-DQN are only comparable despite far fewer frames.

Overall, this is a promising and practical acceleration method with strong empirical evidence, but optimization and statistical rigor need strengthening. I recommend acceptance, requesting ablation of K and λ, computational accounting, and multi-seed reporting.

title: Energy-based Generative Adversarial Networks
abstract: Abstract:###We introduce the *Energy-based Generative Adversarial Network* model (EBGAN) which views the discriminator as an energy function that attributes low energies to the regions near the data manifold and higher energies to other regions. Similar to the probabilistic GANs, a generator is seen as being trained to produce contrastive samples with minimal energies, while the discriminator is trained to assign high energies to these generated samples. Viewing the discriminator as an energy function allows to use a wide variety of architectures and loss functionals in addition to the usual binary classifier with logistic output. Among them, we show one instantiation of EBGAN framework as using an auto-encoder architecture, with the energy being the reconstruction error, in place of the discriminator. We show that this form of EBGAN exhibits more stable behavior than regular GANs during training. We also show that a single-scale architecture can be trained to generate high-resolution images.
review:
The paper recasts GANs as energy-based models, where the discriminator outputs an energy (here, autoencoder reconstruction error) rather than a probability, and is trained with a margin loss to assign low energy to data and high energy to generated samples. It proves that a Nash equilibrium implies \(p_G=p_{data}\), introduces a repelling regularizer (PT) to reduce mode clustering, and evaluates on MNIST grid search, semi-supervised permutation-invariant MNIST with a Ladder Network, LSUN bedrooms, CelebA, and ImageNet at \(128\times128\) and \(256\times256\).

Strengths: The energy-based view is conceptually clean and permits flexible discriminator architectures and losses. The autoencoder discriminator provides richer per-sample gradients than binary logistic targets, and the paper argues convincingly that adversarial contrastive samples regularize the autoencoder. The theoretical analysis is useful, and the MNIST grid search shows EBGANs train more reliably across hyperparameter settings. Semi-supervised results improve over the reproduced Ladder Network (e.g., 1.04% vs. 1.36% at 100 labels), and the ImageNet samples demonstrate single-scale high-resolution generation.

Weaknesses: High-resolution evaluations are mostly qualitative, without standard quantitative metrics such as FID or inception score. The margin, PT weighting, and margin-decay schedule are heuristic and only lightly ablated. Comparisons focus on DCGAN, with limited testing against other stabilization methods. The theory assumes infinite capacity and does not address finite-sample convergence or mode coverage. Reproducibility details are partially deferred to the appendix.

Overall, EBGAN is a well-motivated and practical framework with strong stability and semi-supervised evidence. I recommend acceptance, requesting quantitative generative metrics, broader baselines, and ablation/statistical reporting.

title: Central Moment Discrepancy (CMD) for Domain-Invariant Representation Learning
abstract: Abstract:###The learning of domain-invariant representations in the context of domain adaptation with neural networks is considered. We propose a new regularization method that minimizes the domain-specific latent feature representations directly in the hidden activation space. Although some standard distribution matching approaches exist that can be interpreted as the matching of weighted sums of moments, e.g. Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD), an explicit order-wise matching of higher order moments has not been considered before. We propose to match the higher order central moments of probability distributions by means of order-wise moment differences. Our model does not require computationally expensive distance and kernel matrix computations. We utilize the equivalent representation of probability distributions by moment sequences to define a new distance function, called Central Moment Discrepancy (CMD). We prove that CMD is a metric on the set of probability distributions on a compact interval. We further prove that convergence of probability distributions on compact intervals w.r.t. the new metric implies convergence in distribution of the respective random variables. We test our approach on two different benchmark data sets for object recognition (Office) and sentiment analysis of product reviews (Amazon reviews). CMD achieves a new state-of-the-art performance on most domain adaptation tasks of Office and outperforms networks trained with MMD, Variational Fair Autoencoders and Domain Adversarial Neural Networks on Amazon reviews. In addition, a post-hoc parameter sensitivity analysis shows that the new approach is stable w. r. t. parameter changes in a certain interval. The source code of the experiments is publicly available.
review:
The paper proposes Central Moment Discrepancy (CMD), a domain regularizer for unsupervised domain adaptation that explicitly matches higher-order central moments of source and target hidden activations. It proves CMD is a metric on compact intervals and that convergence in CMD implies convergence in distribution, then evaluates on Amazon reviews and Office against MMD, DANN, VFAE, and other baselines.

Strengths: The motivation is clear and the moment-based formulation is simple, interpretable, and computationally attractive, avoiding kernel matrices and kernel-parameter tuning. The theoretical results are useful, and the empirical evaluation is broad for domain adaptation, covering twelve Amazon tasks and six Office tasks. CMD achieves state-of-the-art results on most Office tasks and outperforms MMD, VFAE, and DANN on Amazon reviews. The parameter-sensitivity analysis and linear complexity in sample size are practical advantages. Releasing code supports reproducibility.

Weaknesses: The practical regularizer matches only marginal central moments up to a fixed order K, so the joint-distribution guarantees do not fully carry over; K=5 and λ=1 are mostly heuristic and not deeply ablated. The Office experiments use fixed VGG16 features rather than end-to-end adaptation, limiting comparability. The proof assumes bounded activations, requiring clipping or normalization for ReLU-like units. Results are averaged over ten runs, but significance tests are absent, and only two benchmark families are evaluated.

Overall, CMD is a well-motivated and effective domain-adaptation method with useful theory and strong empirical support. I recommend acceptance, requesting fuller ablations, significance testing, and end-to-end vision experiments.

title: Incremental Network Quantization: Towards Lossless CNNs with Low-precision Weights
abstract: Abstract:###This paper presents incremental network quantization (INQ), a novel method, targeting to efficiently convert any pre-trained full-precision convolutional neural network (CNN) model into a low-precision version whose weights are constrained to be either powers of two or zero. Unlike existing methods which are struggled in noticeable accuracy loss, our INQ has the potential to resolve this issue, as benefiting from two innovations. On one hand, we introduce three interdependent operations, namely weight partition, group-wise quantization and re-training. A well-proven measure is employed to divide the weights in each layer of a pre-trained CNN model into two disjoint groups. The weights in the first group are responsible to form a low-precision base, thus they are quantized by a variable-length encoding method. The weights in the other group are responsible to compensate for the accuracy loss from the quantization, thus they are the ones to be re-trained. On the other hand, these three operations are repeated on the latest re-trained group in an iterative manner until all the weights are converted into low-precision ones, acting as an incremental network quantization and accuracy enhancement procedure. Extensive experiments on the ImageNet classification task using almost all known deep CNN architectures including AlexNet, VGG-16, GoogleNet and ResNets well testify the efficacy of the proposed method. Specifically, at 5-bit quantization (a variable-length encoding: 1 bit for representing zero value, and the remaining 4 bits represent at most 16 different values for the powers of two), our models have improved accuracy than the 32-bit floating-point references. Taking ResNet-18 as an example, we further show that our quantized models with 4-bit, 3-bit and 2-bit ternary weights have improved or very similar accuracy against its 32-bit floating-point baseline. Besides, impressive results with the combination of network pruning and INQ are also reported. We believe that our method sheds new insights on how to make deep CNNs to be applicable on mobile or embedded devices. The code will be made publicly available.
review:
The paper proposes Incremental Network Quantization (INQ), which converts pre-trained full-precision CNNs into low-precision models whose weights are constrained to powers of two or zero. The method iteratively partitions each layer’s weights, quantizes one group via variable-length encoding, and re-trains the remaining group to compensate for accuracy loss. Experiments on ImageNet with AlexNet, VGG-16, GoogleNet, ResNet-18, and ResNet-50 show that 5-bit INQ models match or exceed their 32-bit references; ResNet-18 also achieves strong 4-bit, 3-bit, and 2-bit ternary results, and combining INQ with pruning outperforms deep compression.

Strengths: The approach is simple, architecture-agnostic, and practically effective. The incremental partition–quantize–retrain loop is well motivated by pruning-style compensation, and the variable-length encoding gives a clear interpretation of bit-width. Results are consistent across diverse architectures, often with improved accuracy rather than mere preservation, and convergence requires fewer than eight epochs per stage.

Weaknesses: INQ depends on a pre-trained full-precision model and does not address training low-precision networks from scratch. The bit-width definition is nonstandard, and partition ratios, bit-width, and re-training schedules are hand-tuned per architecture. Theoretical analysis is limited, and hardware speed/energy benefits of power-of-two weights are not measured. Comparisons focus on a subset of quantization methods, with no variance or significance reporting.

Overall, INQ is a practical and well-executed quantization method with strong ImageNet evidence. I recommend acceptance, requesting hardware-efficiency measurements, broader baselines, and ablation/statistical reporting.

title: Entropy-SGD: Biasing Gradient Descent Into Wide Valleys
abstract: Abstract:###This paper proposes a new optimization algorithm called Entropy-SGD for training deep neural networks that is motivated by the local geometry of the energy landscape. Local extrema with low generalization error have a large proportion of almost-zero eigenvalues in the Hessian with very few positive or negative eigenvalues. We leverage upon this observation to construct a local-entropy-based objective function that favors well-generalizable solutions lying in large flat regions of the energy landscape, while avoiding poorly-generalizable solutions located in the sharp valleys. Conceptually, our algorithm resembles two nested loops of SGD where we use Langevin dynamics in the inner loop to compute the gradient of the local entropy before each update of the weights. We show that the new objective has a smoother energy landscape and show improved generalization over SGD using uniform stability, under certain assumptions. Our experiments on convolutional and recurrent neural networks demonstrate that Entropy-SGD compares favorably to state-of-the-art techniques in terms of generalization error and training time.
review:
The paper proposes Entropy-SGD, an optimizer that biases training toward wide, flat valleys by minimizing negative local entropy rather than the original loss. Motivated by Hessian spectra showing many near-zero eigenvalues at well-generalizing minima, the method approximates local-entropy gradients with an inner stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics loop and performs an outer parameter update, resembling SGD-inside-SGD. The authors also analyze smoothness and generalization via uniform stability, and evaluate on CNNs for MNIST/CIFAR-10 and RNNs for PTB and character prediction.

Strengths: The geometric motivation is clear and well supported by Hessian eigenspectrum observations. The local-entropy objective is principled, and using SGLD to estimate its gradient makes the method scalable to deep networks. The smoothness and stability analysis provides useful theoretical support, and experiments report favorable generalization and training time, including a reported 2x speedup over SGD on RNNs. The connection to replica/ensemble methods and flat-minima literature is well explained.

Weaknesses: The generalization bound relies on an unrealistic Hessian eigenvalue-gap assumption, which the authors acknowledge. The method introduces several hyperparameters—scope γ, inner iterations L, SGLD step size, and noise—that are set heuristically, and γ scoping interacts awkwardly with learning-rate annealing. Evaluation is limited to relatively small image and text tasks, with few comparisons to modern flat-minima or adaptive optimizers. Variance and significance reporting are limited, and computational overhead of the inner loop is not fully quantified.

Overall, Entropy-SGD is a novel, well-motivated optimizer with promising empirical and theoretical support. I recommend acceptance, requesting broader benchmarks, hyperparameter ablations, and overhead analysis.

title: Deep Multi-task Representation Learning: A Tensor Factorisation Approach
abstract: Abstract:###Most contemporary multi-task learning methods assume linear models. This setting is considered shallow in the era of deep learning. In this paper, we present a new deep multi-task representation learning framework that learns cross-task sharing structure at every layer in a deep network. Our approach is based on generalising the matrix factorisation techniques explicitly or implicitly used by many conventional MTL algorithms to tensor factorisation, to realise automatic learning of end-to-end knowledge sharing in deep networks. This is in contrast to existing deep learning approaches that need a user-defined multi-task sharing strategy. Our approach applies to both homogeneous and heterogeneous MTL. Experiments demonstrate the efficacy of our deep multi-task representation learning in terms of both higher accuracy and fewer design choices.
review:
The paper proposes deep multi-task representation learning (DMTRL), which generalizes matrix-based MTL to tensor factorization of layer weights. Each layer’s task-specific weights are generated from shared factors via last-axis flattening, Tucker decomposition, or Tensor Train decomposition, allowing soft sharing at every layer. Experiments cover homogeneous MTL on MNIST digits, heterogeneous face analysis on AdienceFaces (gender and age), and multi-alphabet recognition on Omniglot.

Strengths: The formulation is clean and general, connecting shallow MTL methods to deep networks and supporting both homogeneous and heterogeneous tasks. Soft, learned sharing is a meaningful improvement over manually choosing hard shared/separate layers, and it can interpolate between full sharing and task-specific parameters. The tensor methods are well explained, and the sharing-strength measure is a useful diagnostic. Experiments show consistent gains over single-task learning and competitive or better performance than the best user-defined MTL architecture, especially in low-data regimes. The multi-alphabet results and reduced design effort are convincing.

Weaknesses: Rank selection relies on first training single-task models and decomposing their weights with a fixed 10% reconstruction-error threshold, so the method is not fully trained end-to-end from scratch. The datasets and architectures are relatively small; larger-scale vision or language tasks are absent. Comparisons focus on user-defined MTL and STL, with limited comparison to other deep MTL or tensor methods. Variance and significance tests are limited, and factorization may restrict capacity in data-rich settings.

Overall, DMTRL is a principled and practical framework for learned deep MTL sharing with strong evidence in low-data regimes. I recommend acceptance, requesting larger-scale validation, ablation of rank selection, and statistical reporting.

title: Sample Efficient Actor-Critic with Experience Replay
abstract: Abstract:###This paper presents an actor-critic deep reinforcement learning agent with experience replay that is stable, sample efficient, and performs remarkably well on challenging environments, including the discrete 57-game Atari domain and several continuous control problems. To achieve this, the paper introduces several innovations, including truncated importance sampling with bias correction, stochastic dueling network architectures, and a new trust region policy optimization method.
review:
The paper introduces ACER, an off-policy actor-critic with experience replay for discrete and continuous action spaces. It combines Retrace multi-step returns, truncated importance sampling with bias correction, a trust-region update based on an averaged policy network, and stochastic dueling networks for continuous control. Experiments on 57 Atari games and continuous control tasks show improved sample efficiency over A3C and performance approaching prioritized DQN.

Strengths: The method is well motivated and technically coherent, integrating several recent ideas into a stable off-policy actor-critic. Truncated importance weights with correction are a sensible way to control variance while limiting bias, and the averaged-policy trust region avoids expensive Fisher-vector products. Retrace provides low-variance multi-step targets. Atari results are strong: replay improves data efficiency, and ACER approaches prioritized DQN while retaining a stochastic policy and wall-clock performance comparable to A3C. The continuous-action extensions, especially stochastic dueling networks, are useful contributions.

Weaknesses: The algorithm is complex, with many interacting hyperparameters (replay ratio, c, δ, α, n) that may require tuning. Theoretical support is limited mainly to the Retrace rewrite and does not establish convergence with nonlinear function approximation. The trust-region approximation is heuristic, and the averaged policy introduces additional state. Comparisons focus on A3C and DQN variants, with limited analysis of sensitivity, variance, or significance. Continuous-control evaluation is less thoroughly summarized in the main text.

Overall, ACER is a significant and empirically convincing contribution to sample-efficient deep RL. I recommend acceptance, requesting hyperparameter ablations, convergence discussion, and broader continuous-control reporting.

title: Temporal Ensembling for Semi-Supervised Learning
abstract: Abstract:###In this paper, we present a simple and efficient method for training deep neural networks in a semi-supervised setting where only a small portion of training data is labeled. We introduce self-ensembling, where we form a consensus prediction of the unknown labels using the outputs of the network-in-training on different epochs, and most importantly, under different regularization and input augmentation conditions. This ensemble prediction can be expected to be a better predictor for the unknown labels than the output of the network at the most recent training epoch, and can thus be used as a target for training. Using our method, we set new records for two standard semi-supervised learning benchmarks, reducing the (non-augmented) classification error rate from 18.44% to 7.05% in SVHN with 500 labels and from 18.63% to 16.55% in CIFAR-10 with 4000 labels, and further to 5.12% and 12.16% by enabling the standard augmentations. We additionally obtain a clear improvement in CIFAR-100 classification accuracy by using random images from the Tiny Images dataset as unlabeled extra inputs during training. Finally, we demonstrate good tolerance to incorrect labels.
review:
The paper proposes self-ensembling for semi-supervised learning: the Π-model enforces consistency between two stochastic passes, while temporal ensembling aggregates predictions across epochs to form less noisy targets for unlabeled data. It reports strong gains on SVHN and CIFAR-10/100, plus robustness to incorrect labels and benefits from extra unlabeled Tiny Images.

Strengths: The method is simple, practical, and easy to implement. Temporal ensembling is roughly twice as fast as the Π-model because it evaluates each input once per epoch, and it uses the network’s own historical predictions without extra parameters or a separate teacher. Results are substantial: on SVHN with 500 labels, error drops from 18.44% to 7.05% without augmentation and to 5.12% with augmentation; CIFAR-10 with 4000 labels improves to 16.55% and 12.16%. The label-noise experiment is particularly compelling, showing strong resistance when a large fraction of labels are randomized. The analysis of ramp-up and augmentation is useful.

Weaknesses: The approach depends critically on dropout and strong augmentation, and the slow ramp-up schedule is heuristic. Temporal ensembling requires storing per-example predictions, which may scale poorly, and introduces the momentum hyperparameter α. Comparisons are complicated by differing augmentation and fractional max-pooling baselines, and evaluation is limited to small image benchmarks.
