There is little theoretical analysis of why historical ensembles are reliable early in training.

Overall, this is an effective and influential semi-supervised method with strong empirical support. I recommend acceptance, requesting scalability analysis, broader datasets, and more controlled comparisons.

title: On Detecting Adversarial Perturbations
abstract: Abstract:###Machine learning and deep learning in particular has advanced tremendously on perceptual tasks in recent years. However, it remains vulnerable against adversarial perturbations of the input that have been crafted specifically to fool the system while being quasi-imperceptible to a human. In this work, we propose to augment deep neural networks with a small ``detector** subnetwork which is trained on the binary classification task of distinguishing genuine data from data containing adversarial perturbations. Our method is orthogonal to prior work on addressing adversarial perturbations, which has mostly focused on making the classification network itself more robust. We show empirically that adversarial perturbations can be detected surprisingly well even though they are quasi-imperceptible to humans. Moreover, while the detectors have been trained to detect only a specific adversary, they generalize to similar and weaker adversaries. In addition, we propose an adversarial attack that fools both the classifier and the detector and a novel training procedure for the detector that counteracts this attack.
review:
The paper proposes augmenting a classifier with a small detector subnetwork trained to distinguish genuine inputs from adversarial examples using intermediate features. Detectors are trained post-hoc on balanced real/adversarial data and evaluated on CIFAR-10 and a 10-class ImageNet subset under fast, iterative, and DeepFool attacks. The authors also introduce a dynamic adversary that jointly targets classifier and detector, plus dynamic adversary training to harden the detector.

Strengths: The approach is simple, orthogonal to classifier robustness, and empirically surprisingly effective: detection exceeds 80–90% for attacks that severely reduce accuracy, and detectors generalize across similar attacks and from stronger to weaker adversaries. The dynamic-adversary analysis is valuable, and dynamic training improves robustness to adaptive attacks. The boundary-tilting discussion gives useful intuition.

Weaknesses: Detectors are trained for specific adversaries; transfer is asymmetric and poor for some attacks. Attachment depth and detector architecture are dataset/architecture-specific and only lightly ablated. Evaluation is limited to CIFAR-10 and 10-class ImageNet, with no comparison to other detection methods or false-positive analysis on natural atypical inputs. The dynamic adversary still degrades static detectors, and stronger adaptive attacks are not explored. No statistical significance or calibration analysis is reported.

Overall, this is a practical and well-motivated adversarial detection method with promising empirical results, but broader evaluation and adaptive-attack robustness need strengthening. I recommend acceptance, requesting more baselines, false-positive analysis, and stronger adaptive attacks.

title: Training deep neural-networks using a noise adaptation layer
abstract: Abstract:###The availability of large datsets has enabled neural networks to achieve impressive recognition results. However, the presence of inaccurate class labels is known to deteriorate the performance of even the best classifiers in a broad range of classification problems. Noisy labels also tend to be more harmful than noisy attributes. When the observed label is noisy, we can view the correct label as a latent random variable and model the noise processes by a communication channel with unknown parameters. Thus we can apply the EM algorithm to find the parameters of both the network and the noise and to estimate the correct label. In this study we present a neural-network approach that optimizes the same likelihood function as optimized by the EM algorithm. The noise is explicitly modeled by an additional softmax layer that connects the correct labels to the noisy ones. This scheme is then extended to the case where the noisy labels are dependent on the features in addition to the correct labels. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach outperforms previous methods.
review:
The paper proposes a noise adaptation layer for training deep networks with noisy labels. A second softmax maps true-label predictions to observed noisy labels, optionally conditioned on input features (s- and c-models), allowing joint optimization of network and noise parameters. The authors connect this to EM for a latent true label and use initialization from a baseline network’s confusion matrix. Experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-100 with injected label noise compare against standard training and Reed et al. bootstrapping variants.

Strengths: The formulation is clean, easy to implement by adding one softmax layer, and optimizes the same likelihood as EM without alternating full retraining. The s-model exactly recovers the label-dependent noise channel, while the c-model handles feature-dependent noise. Results consistently improve over baselines across noise levels and training-set fractions, and the sparse second softmax reduces quadratic class complexity with little performance loss. Confidence intervals via bootstrapping are reported.

Weaknesses: Noise is synthetic and generated by a fixed permutation, which may not reflect real annotation errors. Evaluation is limited to MNIST and CIFAR-100 with small/medium class sets; large-scale and real noisy-label datasets are absent. Initialization and sparsification are heuristic, and the c-model’s added complexity is only modestly analyzed. Comparisons focus on Reed et al. and baseline training, omitting other robust-loss or co-teaching methods. Variance across architectures and sensitivity to noise-model misspecification are not fully explored.

Overall, this is a simple, well-motivated, and effective approach with promising results, but broader and more realistic validation is needed. I recommend acceptance, requesting real noisy datasets, larger class sets, and more baselines.

title: Learning to Compose Words into Sentences with Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Abstract:###We use reinforcement learning to learn tree-structured neural networks for computing representations of natural language sentences. In contrast with prior work on tree-structured models, in which the trees are either provided as input or predicted using supervision from explicit treebank annotations, the tree structures in this work are optimized to improve performance on a downstream task. Experiments demonstrate the benefit of learning task-specific composition orders, outperforming both sequential encoders and recursive encoders based on treebank annotations. We analyze the induced trees and show that while they discover some linguistically intuitive structures (e.g., noun phrases, simple verb phrases), they are different than conventional English syntactic structures.
review:
The paper uses reinforcement learning to learn task-specific tree structures for sentence representation with a Tree LSTM/SPINN composer. Instead of relying on treebank parses, a policy network samples SHIFT/REDUCE actions, and downstream task performance provides the reward. The authors compare right-to-left, left-to-right, bidirectional, supervised-syntax, semi-supervised, and fully latent-syntax models on sentiment classification, semantic relatedness, natural language inference, and sentence generation.

Strengths: The motivation is clear and the approach is simple: tree structures are optimized for the downstream objective rather than linguistic annotation. The policy-gradient formulation and action constraints are straightforward, and the semi-supervised variant sensibly initializes with parse supervision before relaxing it. Experiments are broad across four tasks, and latent syntax consistently outperforms fixed composition orders, including supervised syntax, on SST, SICK, and SNLI. The analysis of induced trees, including bracketing agreement and observed left-branching tendencies, adds useful insight.

Weaknesses: The gains are often modest—for example, SST 86.5 vs. 85.3 supervised syntax—and variance across runs is not fully reported. Reinforcement learning adds training cost and instability, and the policy is learned per task, limiting reuse. Evaluation uses relatively small models and does not compare against stronger contemporary architectures. The induced structures are only loosely linguistic, so claims about discovering syntax should be tempered. Hyperparameter sensitivity and reward-design choices are not thoroughly ablated.

Overall, this is a well-motivated and empirically promising framework for task-driven composition. I recommend acceptance, requesting stronger baselines, statistical reporting, and more detailed analysis of training stability.

title: Delving into Transferable Adversarial Examples and Black-box Attacks
abstract: Abstract:###An intriguing property of deep neural networks is the existence of adversarial examples, which can transfer among different architectures. These transferable adversarial examples may severely hinder deep neural network-based applications. Previous works mostly study the transferability using small scale datasets. In this work, we are the first to conduct an extensive study of the transferability over large models and a large scale dataset, and we are also the first to study the transferability of targeted adversarial examples with their target labels. We study both non-targeted and targeted adversarial examples, and show that while transferable non-targeted adversarial examples are easy to find, targeted adversarial examples generated using existing approaches almost never transfer with their target labels. Therefore, we propose novel ensemble-based approaches to generating transferable adversarial examples. Using such approaches, we observe a large proportion of targeted adversarial examples that are able to transfer with their target labels for the first time. We also present some geometric studies to help understanding the transferable adversarial examples. Finally, we show that the adversarial examples generated using ensemble-based approaches can successfully attack Clarifai.com, which is a black-box image classification system.
review:
The paper studies transferability of adversarial examples at ImageNet scale, covering non-targeted and targeted attacks across ResNet-50/101/152, VGG-16, and GoogLeNet. It shows non-targeted examples transfer readily, while existing single-model methods rarely transfer targeted labels. It then proposes ensemble-based generation, which substantially improves targeted transfer, and analyzes geometric properties such as near-orthogonal gradient directions and aligned decision boundaries. Finally, it demonstrates black-box attacks against Clarifai.com.

Strengths: The large-scale transferability study is valuable and goes beyond MNIST/CIFAR. The targeted-transfer finding is important, and the ensemble approach yields a clear improvement—targeted matching rates rise to roughly 60–99% on held-out models, while non-targeted ensemble attacks achieve near-perfect transfer with lower RMSD. The geometric analysis provides useful intuition, and the Clarifai attack demonstrates real-world black-box relevance despite unknown models, training data, and label sets.

Weaknesses: The evaluation uses only 100 images and older ImageNet models, limiting statistical strength and contemporary relevance. Ensemble attacks use four white-box models and evaluate the fifth, so the black-box setting is somewhat favorable. Targeted attacks require larger RMSD, and no formal guarantees or defense evaluation are provided. Black-box results are qualitative and lack query budgets or success-rate confidence intervals. Comparisons omit several stronger transfer methods and adaptive defenses.

Overall, this is a well-motivated and empirically useful study with an important targeted-transfer contribution. I recommend acceptance, requesting larger-scale evaluation, modern baselines, defense testing, and statistical reporting.

title: Identity Matters in Deep Learning
abstract: Abstract:###An emerging design principle in deep learning is that each layer of a deep artificial neural network should be able to easily express the identity transformation. This idea not only motivated various normalization techniques, such as batch normalization, but was also key to the immense success of residual networks. In this work, we put the principle of identity parameterization on a more solid theoretical footing alongside further empirical progress. We first give a strikingly simple proof that arbitrarily deep linear residual networks have no spurious local optima. The same result for feed-forward networks in their standard parameterization is substantially more delicate. Second, we show that residual networks with ReLu activations have universal finite-sample expressivity in the sense that the network can represent any function of its sample provided that the model has more parameters than the sample size. Directly inspired by our theory, we experiment with a radically simple residual architecture consisting of only residual convolutional layers and ReLu activations, but no batch normalization, dropout, or max pool. Our model improves significantly on previous all-convolutional networks on the CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and ImageNet classification benchmarks.
review:
The paper puts the identity-parameterization principle on firmer theoretical and empirical footing. It proves that arbitrarily deep linear residual networks have no spurious critical points under a small-norm condition, whereas standard linear feed-forward networks are harder to analyze. It further shows that residual networks with ReLU activations have universal finite-sample expressivity with \(O(n\log n+r^2)\) parameters. Motivated by these results, the authors train a simple all-convolutional residual architecture without batch normalization, dropout, or max pooling, using near-zero initialization and a fixed random final projection, and report strong CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet results.

Strengths: The theoretical results are clean, intuitive, and elegantly highlight why residual parameterization helps optimization. The small-norm optimum theorem gives useful insight into depth and regularization. The expressivity construction is simple and supports the minimalist architecture. Empirically, the all-convolutional model is competitive with standard ResNets and improves over prior all-convolutional networks, despite removing common normalization and regularization components.

Weaknesses: The optimization analysis is limited to linear networks, so implications for nonlinear ReLU residual networks remain heuristic. The expressivity result does not address optimization or generalization. The empirical evaluation is restricted to older CIFAR/ImageNet settings, with limited ablations, variance reporting, or significance tests. The fixed random final layer and near-zero initialization are interesting but underexplored. Comparisons to modern residual variants are limited.

Overall, this is a thoughtful and well-presented contribution connecting theory and practice. I recommend acceptance, requesting broader empirical validation, ablations, and deeper nonlinear analysis.

title: Adversarial Feature Learning
abstract: Abstract:###The ability of the Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) framework to learn generative models mapping from simple latent distributions to arbitrarily complex data distributions has been demonstrated empirically, with compelling results showing generators learn to *linearize semantics* in the latent space of such models. Intuitively, such latent spaces may serve as useful feature representations for auxiliary problems where semantics are relevant. However, in their existing form, GANs have no means of learning the inverse mapping -- projecting data back into the latent space. We propose Bidirectional Generative Adversarial Networks (BiGANs) as a means of learning this inverse mapping, and demonstrate that the resulting learned feature representation is useful for auxiliary supervised discrimination tasks, competitive with contemporary approaches to unsupervised and self-supervised feature learning.
review:
The paper proposes Bidirectional Generative Adversarial Networks (BiGANs), which augment a GAN generator with an encoder that maps data back to latent space. A joint discriminator distinguishes between encoder pairs \((x,E(x))\) and generator pairs \((G(z),z)\). The authors prove that at the global optimum the encoder and generator invert each other, and relate the objective to an \(\ell_0\) autoencoder. They evaluate learned encoder features on permutation-invariant MNIST and ImageNet classification, comparing against GAN discriminator features and latent-regressor baselines.

Strengths: The formulation is simple, generic, and theoretically grounded. The joint adversarial game is clearly motivated, and the inversion theorem provides a strong conceptual justification for using the encoder as an unsupervised feature extractor. The \(\ell_0\) autoencoder interpretation is insightful. Experiments on ImageNet are ambitious, and the learned features are competitive with contemporary self-supervised and weakly supervised approaches. The generalized BiGAN formulation also usefully allows higher-resolution encoder inputs than generator outputs.

Weaknesses: The theoretical guarantees assume optimal discriminators and deterministic modules, while practical training is non-convex and unstable. The encoder-generator inversion is only approximate in practice. Evaluation focuses on classification transfer, with limited analysis of feature quality, reconstruction, or latent semantics. Comparisons are restricted to a few baselines, and variance or significance tests are sparse. The method inherits GAN training difficulties and hyperparameter sensitivity.

Overall, BiGAN is a well-motivated and influential framework with useful theory and competitive empirical results. I recommend acceptance, requesting more stable training analysis, broader feature-learning benchmarks, and statistical reporting.

title: Towards the Limit of Network Quantization
abstract: Abstract:###Network quantization is one of network compression techniques to reduce the redundancy of deep neural networks. It reduces the number of distinct network parameter values by quantization in order to save the storage for them. In this paper, we design network quantization schemes that minimize the performance loss due to quantization given a compression ratio constraint. We analyze the quantitative relation of quantization errors to the neural network loss function and identify that the Hessian-weighted distortion measure is locally the right objective function for the optimization of network quantization. As a result, Hessian-weighted k-means clustering is proposed for clustering network parameters to quantize. When optimal variable-length binary codes, e.g., Huffman codes, are employed for further compression, we derive that the network quantization problem can be related to the entropy-constrained scalar quantization (ECSQ) problem in information theory and consequently propose two solutions of ECSQ for network quantization, i.e., uniform quantization and an iterative solution similar to Lloyd*s algorithm. Finally, using the simple uniform quantization followed by Huffman coding, we show from our experiments that the compression ratios of 51.25, 22.17 and 40.65 are achievable for LeNet, 32-layer ResNet and AlexNet, respectively.
review:
The paper proposes loss-aware network quantization schemes. It shows that quantization-induced loss can be approximated by a Hessian-weighted distortion measure, proposes Hessian-weighted k-means clustering, and connects compression-constrained quantization with Huffman coding to entropy-constrained scalar quantization (ECSQ). It introduces uniform quantization and an iterative ECSQ solution, uses Adam second-moment estimates as a Hessian surrogate, and quantizes all layers jointly. Experiments on LeNet/MNIST, 32-layer ResNet/CIFAR-10, and AlexNet/ImageNet report compression ratios of 51.25, 22.17, and 40.65 with little or no accuracy loss.

Strengths: The formulation is principled and clearly explains why conventional k-means is suboptimal. Hessian weighting captures parameter importance within and across layers, enabling joint quantization and avoiding combinatorial per-layer compression allocation. Replacing Hessian with Adam second moments is practical and empirically effective. The ECSQ connection is insightful and supports uniform quantization plus Huffman coding. Results are strong, with ablations covering pruning, fine-tuning, and small-sample Hessian estimation.

Weaknesses: The analysis relies on a diagonal Hessian and local quadratic approximation at a trained minimum, which may be inaccurate for highly nonconvex networks. Evaluation is limited to three model/dataset pairs, without variance estimates or modern architectures. Coding/table overhead, actual memory savings, and hardware speedups are not measured. Sensitivity to clustering, ECSQ, and fine-tuning hyperparameters is only partially explored, and comparisons to recent quantization methods are limited.

Overall, this is a well-motivated and empirically strong quantization framework. I recommend acceptance, requesting broader validation, overhead analysis, and statistical reporting.

title: Faster CNNs with Direct Sparse Convolutions and Guided Pruning
abstract: Abstract:###Phenomenally successful in practical inference problems, convolutional neural networks (CNN) are widely deployed in mobile devices, data centers, and even supercomputers. The number of parameters needed in CNNs, however, are often large and undesirable. Consequently, various methods have been developed to prune a CNN once it is trained. Nevertheless, the resulting CNNs offer limited benefits. While pruning the fully connected layers reduces a CNN*s size considerably, it does not improve inference speed noticeably as the compute heavy parts lie in convolutions. Pruning CNNs in a way that increase inference speed often imposes specific sparsity structures, thus limiting the achievable sparsity levels. We present a method to realize simultaneously size economy and speed improvement while pruning CNNs. Paramount to our success is an efficient general sparse-with-dense matrix multiplication implementation that is applicable to convolution of feature maps with kernels of arbitrary sparsity patterns. Complementing this, we developed a performance model that predicts sweet spots of sparsity levels for different layers and on different computer architectures. Together, these two allow us to demonstrate 3.1-7.3x convolution speedups over dense convolution in AlexNet, on Intel Atom, Xeon, and Xeon Phi processors, spanning the spectrum from mobile devices to supercomputers.
review:
The paper proposes direct sparse convolution for CNNs with arbitrary element-wise sparsity, a roofline-based performance model, and Guided Sparsity Learning (GSL) to prune layers where sparse convolution can yield speedups. The main strengths are the practical sparse SpMDM formulation that avoids lowering, the analytical model identifying useful sparsity ranges, and the co-design of pruning with hardware performance. Results on AlexNet and GoogLeNet show meaningful layer-wise convolution speedups (3.1–7.3× on Atom, Xeon, Xeon Phi) with limited accuracy loss, and the open-source implementation aids reproducibility.

Weaknesses: evaluation is largely layer-wise rather than end-to-end, so overall inference gains are unclear. The study uses older architectures and Caffe-era models; modern networks, GPUs, and tensor cores are not evaluated. The performance model relies on measured overheads (α, β) that may vary substantially across implementations and platforms. Accuracy results include up to 3% top-1 drop, and comparisons with pruning baselines are limited. GSL’s benefits depend on model predictions and hyperparameter choices; sensitivity is not fully explored. The paper also does not deeply analyze sparse pattern irregularity, load balance, or training overhead. Overall, a solid systems/ML co-design contribution with convincing layer-level evidence, but stronger end-to-end and broader platform/architecture evaluation would strengthen the claims. The paper is well organized and technically sound, and the open-source release is valuable.

title: Stick-Breaking Variational Autoencoders
abstract: Abstract:###We extend Stochastic Gradient Variational Bayes to perform posterior inference for the weights of Stick-Breaking processes. This development allows us to define a Stick-Breaking Variational Autoencoder (SB-VAE), a Bayesian nonparametric version of the variational autoencoder that has a latent representation with stochastic dimensionality. We experimentally demonstrate that the SB-VAE, and a semi-supervised variant, learn highly discriminative latent representations that often outperform the Gaussian VAEâ€™s.
review:
This paper introduces a Stick-Breaking Variational Autoencoder (SB-VAE), extending SGVB to GEM random variables by using differentiable reparameterizations (Kumaraswamy, Gamma, Gauss-logit) for Beta-like stick fractions. The authors also propose a semi-supervised variant and evaluate unsupervised/semi-supervised image tasks. The main contribution is a clean, practical bridge between Bayesian nonparametric priors and amortized variational inference, with closed-form or approximate KL terms and a linear-time stick-composition layer. The Kumaraswamy parameterization is well motivated and empirically best among the three.

Strengths include the novel formulation, clear derivation, and experiments showing that SB-VAE latents preserve class structure better than Gaussian VAE latents in kNN classification, despite slightly worse marginal likelihood. The adaptive-capacity analysis on MNIST+rot is interesting.

Weaknesses are mainly empirical scope and evidence strength. The SB-VAE underperforms the Gaussian VAE in marginal likelihood, and the adaptive-width effect is modest. Experiments use small image datasets and simple architectures, with limited comparison to strong nonparametric or mixture VAEs; the semi-supervised results are not fully developed in the excerpt. The Gaussian baseline's prior variance is not cross-validated, which may bias comparisons. The paper leaves inference for the full random measure open and relies on truncated posteriors. Overall, a solid methodological contribution with promising but not yet conclusive empirical support.

title: Batch Policy Gradient Methods for Improving Neural Conversation Models
abstract: Abstract:###We study reinforcement learning of chat-bots with recurrent neural network architectures when the rewards are noisy and expensive to obtain. For instance, a chat-bot used in automated customer service support can be scored by quality assurance agents, but this process can be expensive, time consuming and noisy. Previous reinforcement learning work for natural language uses on-policy updates and/or is designed for on-line learning settings. We demonstrate empirically that such strategies are not appropriate for this setting and develop an off-policy batch policy gradient method (_x0008_pg). We demonstrate the efficacy of our method via a series of synthetic experiments and an Amazon Mechanical Turk experiment on a restaurant recommendations dataset.
review:
This paper addresses RL for Seq2Seq chatbots when rewards are noisy, expensive, and available only in batch. The proposed Batch Policy Gradient (BPG) uses off-policy importance sampling, λ-returns computed from logged future actions/rewards, and simple value-function estimators. The motivation is well argued: on-policy/online RL is poorly matched to QA-labeled customer-service data. The derivation is clear, and the synthetic Europarl experiment usefully ablates ML initialization, importance sampling, and online vs batch updates.

Weaknesses: the method is largely an adaptation of off-policy actor-critic ideas to logged Seq2Seq data, with limited theoretical novelty; the approximate gradient drops the ∇Q term and relies on prior justification. Off-policy correction depends on q(a|s), which in practice is learned from unlabelled data; misspecification and product importance weights can destabilize training, and clipping is heuristic. The GTD(λ) value estimator shows little long-run benefit over a constant baseline. Only the top decoder LSTM and softmax are updated, treating lower layers as environment, which restricts the approach and weakens claims about full RNN policy learning. Evidence in the excerpt is mainly a synthetic task with 500 labeled examples; the promised Mechanical Turk restaurant experiment is needed to substantiate practical impact. Comparisons to recent NLP policy-gradient methods are limited. Overall, a well-motivated and practical batch-RL contribution, but stronger empirical validation and analysis of behavior-policy estimation are needed.

title: Support Regularized Sparse Coding and Its Fast Encoder
abstract: Abstract:###Sparse coding represents a signal by a linear combination of only a few atoms of a learned over-complete dictionary. While sparse coding exhibits compelling performance for various machine learning tasks, the process of obtaining sparse code with fixed dictionary is independent for each data point without considering the geometric information and manifold structure of the entire data. We propose Support Regularized Sparse Coding (SRSC) which produces sparse codes that account for the manifold structure of the data by encouraging nearby data in the manifold to choose similar dictionary atoms. In this way, the obtained support regularized sparse codes capture the locally linear structure of the data manifold and enjoy robustness to data noise. We present the optimization algorithm of SRSC with theoretical guarantee for the optimization over the sparse codes. We also propose a feed-forward neural network termed Deep Support Regularized Sparse Coding (Deep-SRSC) as a fast encoder to approximate the sparse codes generated by SRSC. Extensive experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of SRSC and Deep-SRSC.
review:
This paper proposes Support Regularized Sparse Coding (SRSC), which encourages neighboring data to share dictionary atoms rather than merely similar ℓ2 codes, thereby capturing locally linear manifold structure and improving noise robustness. The authors develop an alternating dictionary/code optimization with a PGD-style coordinate-descent update, provide convergence analysis and a bound relative to the global solution, and introduce Deep-SRSC as a feed-forward encoder for fast approximation. The support-regularization motivation is clear and distinguishes SRSC from Laplacian/ℓ2-RSC. The theoretical analysis is a useful contribution, and the proposed encoder addresses an important computational limitation of sparse coding.

Weaknesses include the nonconvex, non-lower-semicontinuous support term: the PGD-style update is only approximate, and the convergence guarantee depends on the condition G^A_ki ≥ 0, which is observed empirically but not guaranteed. When this fails, the ε-fallback weakens the optimization and theory. The coordinate-descent procedure is expensive, and the claimed ISTA-like efficiency omits neighbor/support bookkeeping and dictionary-learning costs. Deep-SRSC is promising but its approximation error and speed-accuracy tradeoff need more systematic evaluation. The experimental section in the excerpt focuses on clustering; broader comparisons with manifold-regularized sparse coding, sensitivity to KNN graph and γ, and runtime/scalability are needed. Overall, a solid and well-motivated method with interesting theory, but stronger empirical scope and clearer handling of the nonconvex support regularization would strengthen the claims.

title: Tying Word Vectors and Word Classifiers: A Loss Framework for Language Modeling
abstract: Abstract:###Recurrent neural networks have been very successful at predicting sequences of words in tasks such as language modeling. However, all such models are based on the conventional classification framework, where the model is trained against one-hot targets, and each word is represented both as an input and as an output in isolation. This causes inefficiencies in learning both in terms of utilizing all of the information and in terms of the number of parameters needed to train. We introduce a novel theoretical framework that facilitates better learning in language modeling, and show that our framework leads to tying together the input embedding and the output projection matrices, greatly reducing the number of trainable variables. Our framework leads to state of the art performance on the Penn Treebank with a variety of network models.
review:
This paper proposes a loss framework for RNN language modeling that augments cross-entropy with a KL term toward an embedding-derived soft target, and theoretically motivates tying input embeddings and output projection. Experiments on PTB and Wikitext-2 show consistent perplexity improvements for augmented loss (AL), reused embeddings (RE), and both (REAL), with REAL achieving strong PTB results.

Strengths: the idea is simple and well motivated; the connection between soft targets and embedding tying is insightful; the paper validates the subspace-proximity prediction empirically; and RE substantially reduces parameters while improving perplexity. The empirical study across network sizes and datasets is useful.

Weaknesses: the theoretical analysis relies on strong assumptions—equal embedding/hidden dimensions, zero bias, zero training loss, large temperature, full rank, and centered inner products—so it only partially explains practical behavior. The embedding-derived target \(\tilde y\) is iterative and may reinforce existing embedding geometry or early-training errors; stability and sensitivity to \(\alpha\), \(\tau\), and embedding initialization are not sufficiently analyzed. The method adds soft-target computation and requires tied dimensions. Comparisons to concurrent tying work are brief, and state-of-the-art claims should be qualified because some baselines are ensembles or different architectures. Ablations are mostly final perplexities; training cost, variance across seeds, and qualitative error analysis are limited. Overall, a clear and useful contribution with convincing empirical gains, but the theory-to-practice gap and hyperparameter robustness deserve more discussion.

title: Towards Deep Interpretability (MUS-ROVER II): Learning Hierarchical Representations of Tonal Music
abstract: Abstract:###Music theory studies the regularity of patterns in music to capture concepts underlying music styles and composers* decisions. This paper continues the study of building emph{automatic theorists} (rovers) to learn and represent music concepts that lead to human interpretable knowledge and further lead to materials for educating people. Our previous work took a first step in algorithmic concept learning of tonal music, studying high-level representations (concepts) of symbolic music (scores) and extracting interpretable rules for composition. This paper further studies the representation emph{hierarchy} through the learning process, and supports emph{adaptive} 2D memory selection in the resulting language model. This leads to a deeper-level interpretability that expands from individual rules to a dynamic system of rules, making the entire rule learning process more cognitive. The outcome is a new rover, MUS-ROVER RN{2}, trained on Bach*s chorales, which outputs customizable syllabi for learning compositional rules. We demonstrate comparable results to our music pedagogy, while also presenting the differences and variations. In addition, we point out the rover*s potential usages in style recognition and synthesis, as well as applications beyond music.
review:
This paper extends MUS-ROVER, an automatic music theorist, with hierarchical rule learning and adaptive memory selection for Bach chorales. It introduces a conceptual hierarchy over feature-induced partitions, an informational hierarchy from rule traces, hierarchical filters for pruning, and a two-dimensional n-gram/feature memory with Bayesian-surprise-based selection. The system outputs customizable syllabi and compares learned rules to music pedagogy. Strengths include the interpretable, compositional feature language; the clear teacher-student self-learning loop; and the useful distinction between precomputed conceptual and trace-specific informational hierarchy. The 2D memory and pace-control syllabus customization are well motivated for pedagogy. The paper is conceptually rich and addresses an important goal: interpretable hierarchical representation learning outside standard black-box models.

Weaknesses: empirical validation is limited. Evaluation centers on qualitative examples, rule lists, and comparison to pedagogy, without quantitative benchmarks, ablations isolating hierarchy/filter/memory components, or measures of syllabus quality. The feature universe and descriptors are hand-designed, which constrains generality and may bake in domain assumptions despite raw-input claims. Hyperparameters (δ, γ, c, n-gram range) and their sensitivity are not thoroughly analyzed. Computational scaling of partition DAG construction and adaptive selection is unclear. The musical claims would benefit from expert evaluation beyond illustrative tables. Overall, an ambitious and interesting interpretability contribution, but stronger quantitative evaluation and component ablations are needed.

title: Discrete Variational Autoencoders
abstract: Abstract:###Probabilistic models with discrete latent variables naturally capture datasets composed of discrete classes. However, they are difficult to train efficiently, since backpropagation through discrete variables is generally not possible. We present a novel method to train a class of probabilistic models with discrete latent variables using the variational autoencoder framework, including backpropagation through the discrete latent variables. The associated class of probabilistic models comprises an undirected discrete component and a directed hierarchical continuous component. The discrete component captures the distribution over the disconnected smooth manifolds induced by the continuous component. As a result, this class of models efficiently learns both the class of objects in an image, and their specific realization in pixels, from unsupervised data; and outperforms state-of-the-art methods on the permutation-invariant MNIST, Omniglot, and Caltech-101 Silhouettes datasets.
review:
This paper introduces Discrete VAEs, combining an undirected discrete RBM prior with directed continuous latent layers. The key idea is to smooth binary latents with continuous variables ζ via a spike-and-exponential transformation, yielding an invertible conditional-marginal CDF and enabling reparameterized, low-variance gradients through discrete variables. A hierarchical autoregressive posterior addresses explaining-away, and the construction connects nicely to dropout/batch-normalization-like stochastic nonlinearities. The motivation—modeling disconnected manifolds with discrete class variables and continuous deformations—is clear and well argued.

Strengths include the novel smoothing formulation, explicit differentiable autoencoding path, and a principled hierarchical posterior that avoids naive REINFORCE variance. The method is clearly presented and potentially broadly applicable.

Weaknesses: the smoothing transformation is itself a strong modeling choice that alters the latent space; its effect on ELBO tightness and discrete-variable interpretability is not fully analyzed. Sensitivity to β, smoothing family, and posterior hierarchy depth is unclear. The RBM prior and KL estimation add computational complexity, and risks of posterior collapse or continuous ζ dominating z deserve discussion. The excerpt does not provide sufficient experimental detail to substantiate the claimed state-of-the-art results; ablations isolating smoothing, hierarchy, and RBM prior would be valuable. Overall, a promising and technically interesting contribution, but stronger empirical and theoretical validation is needed.

title: Do Deep Convolutional Nets Really Need to be Deep and Convolutional?
abstract: Abstract:###Yes, they do. This paper provides the first empirical demonstration that deep convolutional models really need to be both deep and convolutional, even when trained with methods such as distillation that allow small or shallow models of high accuracy to be trained. Although previous research showed that shallow feed-forward nets sometimes can learn the complex functions previously learned by deep nets while using the same number of parameters as the deep models they mimic, in this paper we demonstrate that the same methods cannot be used to train accurate models on CIFAR-10 unless the student models contain multiple layers of convolution. Although the student models do not have to be as deep as the teacher model they mimic, the students need multiple convolutional layers to learn functions of comparable accuracy as the deep convolutional teacher.
review:
This paper empirically revisits whether shallow students can match deep convolutional teachers on CIFAR-10 under equal parameter budgets. Using a strong 16-CNN ensemble teacher, logit distillation, and Bayesian hyperparameter optimization, the authors show that non-convolutional MLPs remain far below convolutional students, and that multiple convolutional layers (3–4) are needed for high accuracy. The controlled methodology, thorough tuning, and clear comparison to Ba and Caruana are strengths. The parameter-budget focus is appropriate for separating representational effects from capacity. The negative result is convincing for CIFAR-10 and usefully distinguishes convolution from mere depth. The results support practical guidance that convolution is crucial for image tasks even under distillation.

However, the evidence is limited to one dataset; ImageNet experiments are incomplete. The claim that shallow models “cannot” work is really a failure under a specific search budget and distillation setup, not a proof. “Shallow” is used for both few-layer MLPs and few-conv-layer CNNs, which muddies the conclusion. The teacher is a large ensemble and students use precomputed logits, so results may depend on distillation details. Hyperparameter optimization reduces but does not eliminate search bias. Ablations on augmentation and teacher size would help. The observation that dropout hurts mimic students is interesting but underexplored. Overall, a solid empirical contribution with a clear message, but broader datasets, stronger architectural search, and clearer definitions would strengthen the generality of the claims.

title: Geometry of Polysemy
abstract: Abstract:###Vector representations of words have heralded a transformational approach to classical problems in NLP; the most popular example is word2vec. However, a single vector does not suffice to model the polysemous nature of many (frequent) words, i.e., words with multiple meanings. In this paper, we propose a three-fold approach for unsupervised polysemy modeling: (a) context representations, (b) sense induction and disambiguation and (c) lexeme (as a word and sense pair) representations. A key feature of our work is the finding that a sentence containing a target word is well represented by a low-rank subspace, instead of a point in a vector space. We then show that the subspaces associated with a particular sense of the target word tend to intersect over a line (one-dimensional subspace), which we use to disambiguate senses using a clustering algorithm that harnesses the Grassmannian geometry of the representations. The disambiguation algorithm, which we call -Grassmeans, leads to a procedure to label the different senses of the target word in the corpus -- yielding lexeme vector representations, all in an unsupervised manner starting from a large (Wikipedia) corpus in English. Apart from several prototypical target (word,sense) examples and a host of empirical studies to intuit and justify the various geometric representations, we validate our algorithms on standard sense induction and disambiguation datasets and present new state-of-the-art results.
review:
This paper proposes a Grassmannian geometric approach to unsupervised polysemy modeling. Contexts containing a target word are represented as low-dimensional subspaces spanned by word embeddings; senses are hypothesized to correspond to common intersection directions of these subspaces. The authors introduce K-Grassmeans clustering for sense induction, hard and soft disambiguation, and then learn lexeme embeddings from labeled contexts. They validate the intersection hypothesis on monosemous and polysemous examples and report strong results on word sense induction and lexeme-similarity benchmarks, including a new WSI dataset.

Strengths include a clear, novel geometric intuition; concrete empirical support for the low-rank context and intersection hypotheses; and a simple, scalable word-specific clustering algorithm. The method is fully unsupervised and the qualitative examples are persuasive.

Weaknesses include reliance on a fixed context window, bag-of-words PCA subspaces, and a known number of senses K; robustness to these choices is not fully analyzed. The intersection hypothesis is empirically motivated but lacks theoretical guarantees, and K-Grassmeans remains a heuristic with random initialization. Lexeme representation is indirect because intersection vectors are poorly isotropic; the paper acknowledges this but does not fully resolve it. Comparisons and ablations should better isolate the contributions of subspace geometry, clustering, and labeling choices. Overall, an interesting and promising contribution, but stronger robustness analysis, theoretical grounding, and ablation studies would improve confidence.

title: Learning Invariant Representations Of Planar Curves
abstract: Abstract:###We propose a metric learning framework for the construction of invariant geometric functions of planar curves for the Euclidean and Similarity group of transformations. We leverage on the representational power of convolutional neural networks to compute these geometric quantities. In comparison with axiomatic constructions, we show that the invariants approximated by the learning architectures have better numerical qualities such as robustness to noise, resiliency to sampling, as well as the ability to adapt to occlusion and partiality. Finally, we develop a novel multi-scale representation in a similarity metric learning paradigm.
review:
This paper casts invariant planar-curve representation as metric learning. A Siamese CNN with contrastive loss is trained on positive Euclidean/similarity-transformed curve pairs and negative pairs, producing pointwise signatures. The authors compare learned signatures with differential curvature and integral invariants, and build multi-scale variants via evolved/smoothed negatives. Experiments on MPEG-7 contours suggest improved noise robustness and sampling resilience, plus qualitative scale-space behavior.

Strengths: the problem is well motivated, the geometry-learning connection is interesting, and the Siamese setup is simple and clearly described. The comparison to axiomatic differential and integral invariants is useful, and the multi-scale construction via negative-example design is a creative data-driven analog of scale space. Robustness experiments are relevant and visually persuasive.

Weaknesses: invariance is encouraged only through training pairs, not architecturally guaranteed; approximation error and failure modes are not quantified. Similarity-group invariance and reflection handling are claimed but only partially evaluated. The contrastive loss and negative sampling choices are critical yet under-ablated; margin, smoothing levels, and dataset construction sensitivity are unclear. The learned signature is not proven to be a complete differential invariant, so the geometric interpretation is weaker than stated. Evaluation is limited to MPEG-7-derived curves, with small retrieval experiments and no downstream correspondence/classification benchmarks. Multi-scale behavior is qualitative. Overall, an original and promising bridge between metric learning and numerical geometry, but stronger theoretical characterization, ablations, and broader quantitative evaluation are needed.

title: Reasoning with Memory Augmented Neural Networks for Language Comprehension
abstract: Abstract:###Hypothesis testing is an important cognitive process that supports human reasoning. In this paper, we introduce a computational hypothesis testing approach based on memory augmented neural networks. Our approach involves a hypothesis testing loop that reconsiders and progressively refines a previously formed hypothesis in order to generate new hypotheses to test. We apply the proposed approach to language comprehension task by using Neural Semantic Encoders (NSE). Our NSE models achieve the state-of-the-art results showing an absolute improvement of 1.2% to 2.6% accuracy over previous results obtained by single and ensemble systems on standard machine comprehension benchmarks such as the Children*s Book Test (CBT) and Who-Did-What (WDW) news article datasets.
review:
This paper proposes a hypothesis-testing loop for cloze-style QA using Neural Semantic Encoders. The query memory is iteratively updated by retrieving document words, and a write module either gates query updates or predicts termination, enabling dynamic multi-step reasoning. Experiments on CBT and WDW show modest improvements over prior single and ensemble systems.

Strengths: the iterative query-regression mechanism is intuitive, and the two halting strategies—query gating with fixed maximum steps and adaptive termination—are cleanly integrated into end-to-end backpropagation. The comparison table is comprehensive, and the adaptive model achieves the best CBT-NE and WDW results.

Weaknesses: gains are modest, and the query-gating model’s performance varies with T and appears to overfit on CBT. The adaptive halting probabilities are not analyzed—e.g., distribution of halting steps, calibration, or compute savings—so the claimed dynamic reasoning is only indirectly supported. The architecture has many interacting components (read/compose/write, gating, termination), but ablations isolating their contributions are limited. The “hypothesis testing” framing is conceptually appealing but not formally connected to the optimization or evaluation. Evaluation is restricted to two datasets, and robustness to embedding choice, anonymization, and hyperparameters is unclear. Overall, a solid and well-motivated model with competitive results, but stronger analysis of halting behavior, ablations, and broader validation are needed to substantiate the benefits of dynamic reasoning.

title: Learning Recurrent Representations for Hierarchical Behavior Modeling
abstract: Abstract:###We propose a framework for detecting action patterns from motion sequences and modeling the sensory-motor relationship of animals, using a generative recurrent neural network. The network has a discriminative part (classifying actions) and a generative part (predicting motion), whose recurrent cells are laterally connected, allowing higher levels of the network to represent high level behavioral phenomena. We test our framework on two types of tracking data, fruit fly behavior and online handwriting. Our results show that 1) taking advantage of unlabeled sequences, by predicting future motion, significantly improves action detection performance when training labels are scarce, 2) the network learns to represent high level phenomena such as writer identity and fly gender, without supervision, and 3) simulated motion trajectories, generated by treating motion prediction as input to the network, look realistic and may be used to qualitatively evaluate whether the model has learnt generative control rules.
review:
This paper proposes BESNet/BENet, a recurrent framework that jointly classifies actions and predicts future motion using laterally connected discriminative and generative paths. The model is evaluated on fruit-fly behavior and online handwriting, showing that motion prediction as an auxiliary task improves action detection when labels are scarce, that hidden states capture high-level factors such as gender and writer identity, and that simulated trajectories appear realistic.

Strengths include a clear and biologically motivated architecture, a useful semi-supervised formulation that exploits unlabeled sequences, and evaluation across two complementary domains. The label-fraction experiment is the most convincing result, and the embedding of action labels in recurrent state units is a sensible design.

Weaknesses: several claims rest on qualitative evidence. Simulation realism and learned control rules are not quantitatively evaluated, and discovery of gender/identity is demonstrated without systematic clustering or linear-probe metrics. Gains over prior handcrafted methods on Fly-vs-Fly are comparable rather than decisive, and filtering is needed for bout-level performance. The handwriting annotations are hand-made on a subset, limiting generality. Ablations do not fully isolate lateral connections, generative path, and label embedding. Hyperparameter sweeps are described as rough, and variance across runs is not reported. Overall, an interesting and promising model with a strong semi-supervised motivation, but stronger quantitative evaluation of simulation, discovery, and component ablations would improve confidence.

title: Adversarial Machine Learning at Scale
abstract: Abstract:###Adversarial examples are malicious inputs designed to fool machine learning models. They often transfer from one model to another, allowing attackers to mount black box attacks without knowledge of the target model*s parameters. Adversarial training is the process of explicitly training a model on adversarial examples, in order to make it more robust to attack or to reduce its test error on clean inputs. So far, adversarial training has primarily been applied to small problems. In this research, we apply adversarial training to ImageNet. Our contributions include: (1) recommendations for how to succesfully scale adversarial training to large models and datasets, (2) the observation that adversarial training confers robustness to single-step attack methods, (3) the finding that multi-step attack methods are somewhat less transferable than single-step attack methods, so single-step attacks are the best for mounting black-box attacks, and (4) resolution of a ``label leaking** effect that causes adversarially trained models to perform better on adversarial examples than on clean examples, because the adversarial example construction process uses the true label and the model can learn to exploit regularities in the construction process.
review:
This paper scales adversarial training to ImageNet with Inception v3 and studies one-step versus iterative attacks, transferability, model capacity, and the newly identified “label leaking” effect. The main strengths are practical: concrete recommendations for batch-normalized large-scale adversarial training, mixing clean and adversarial examples in each batch, and randomizing perturbation magnitude. The empirical demonstration that one-step adversarial training substantially improves robustness to one-step attacks—while clean accuracy drops only slightly—is convincing and useful. The label-leaking analysis is particularly valuable: it explains why FGSM-trained and FGSM-evaluated models can appear more accurate on adversarial than clean inputs, and it motivates label-free attack construction for evaluation.

Weaknesses include limited defense against iterative attacks; training on one-step examples does not confer robustness to stronger iterative methods. The paper is largely empirical and does not provide a theoretical account of capacity, transferability, or label leaking. Some recommendations (batch composition, λ, perturbation distribution) are justified by internal experiments but lack sensitivity analysis or variance across runs. Transferability results are only partially presented in the excerpt. The claim that larger models monotonically improve robustness under adversarial training is interesting but based on a limited capacity range. Overall, a strong and influential systems-oriented contribution with practical guidance and a useful caution about evaluation methodology, though robustness remains far from comprehensive and further theoretical and ablation work would strengthen the claims.

title: Predicting Medications from Diagnostic Codes with Recurrent Neural Networks
abstract: Abstract:###It is a surprising fact that electronic medical records are failing at one of their primary purposes, that of tracking the set of medications that the patient is actively taking. Studies estimate that up to 50% of such lists omit active drugs, and that up to 25% of all active medications do not appear on the appropriate patient list. Manual efforts to maintain these lists involve a great deal of tedious human labor, which could be reduced by computational tools to suggest likely missing or incorrect medications on a patientâ€™s list. We report here an application of recurrent neural networks to predict the likely therapeutic classes of medications that a patient is taking, given a sequence of the last 100 billing codes in their record. Our best model was a GRU that achieved high prediction accuracy (micro-averaged AUC 0.93, Label Ranking Loss 0.076), limited by hardware constraints on model size. Additionally, examining individual cases revealed that many of the predictions marked incorrect were likely to be examples of either omitted medications or omitted billing codes, supporting our assertion of a substantial number of errors and omissions in the data, and the likelihood of models such as these to help correct them.
review:
This paper applies recurrent neural networks to predict active medication classes from sequences of recent ICD-9 billing codes. Using a large Vanderbilt EMR dataset (3.3M instances), the authors compare GRU, LSTM, a similarly configured feed-forward network, random forests, and a constant-prevalence baseline. The GRU achieves the best results (micro-AUC 0.927, label ranking loss 0.076), with LSTM close behind. The paper is well motivated, clinically relevant, and unusually large-scale for this task. The controlled comparison against a matched feed-forward network is useful, and case analyses convincingly illustrate likely missing medications and billing codes. The embedding analysis adds interpretability.

Weaknesses: the performance gain from recurrence over the feed-forward baseline is small (~0.01 AUC), suggesting limited use of temporal order. The model predicts medication classes rather than specific medications, and evaluation may be optimistic because training and test labels share the same noisy EMR documentation process. The authors interpret errors as label noise, but this is not independently validated; an audit of a sample against external ground truth would strengthen the claim. The paper lacks calibration, decision-threshold analysis, and per-class error breakdowns. Hardware constraints limited model size, so scaling trends remain unclear. Comparison to prior medication-prediction work is mostly qualitative. The clinical utility claims are plausible but not prospectively evaluated. Overall, a solid applied contribution with strong scale and clear clinical motivation, but stronger validation, richer input features, and more rigorous noise analysis are needed.

title: Recurrent Mixture Density Network for Spatiotemporal Visual Attention
abstract: Abstract:###In many computer vision tasks, the relevant information to solve the problem at hand is mixed to irrelevant, distracting information. This has motivated researchers to design attentional models that can dynamically focus on parts of images or videos that are salient, e.g., by down-weighting irrelevant pixels. In this work, we propose a spatiotemporal attentional model that learns where to look in a video directly from human fixation data. We model visual attention with a mixture of Gaussians at each frame. This distribution is used to express the probability of saliency for each pixel. Time consistency in videos is modeled hierarchically by: 1) deep 3D convolutional features to represent spatial and short-term time relations and 2) a long short-term memory network on top that aggregates the clip-level representation of sequential clips and therefore expands the temporal domain from few frames to seconds. The parameters of the proposed model are optimized via maximum likelihood estimation using human fixations as training data, without knowledge of the action in each video. Our experiments on Hollywood2 show state-of-the-art performance on saliency prediction for video. We also show that our attentional model trained on Hollywood2 generalizes well to UCF101 and it can be leveraged to improve action classification accuracy on both datasets.
review:
This paper proposes a Recurrent Mixture Density Network (RMDN) for spatiotemporal video saliency, combining frozen C3D clip features, an LSTM for temporal aggregation, and a Gaussian-mixture MDN trained on human fixations. The model is evaluated on Hollywood2 and transferred to UCF101, showing strong saliency-prediction results and modest gains in action classification when saliency is used as soft attention.

Strengths: the architecture is clean and well motivated; the MDN formulation naturally represents multi-modal fixation distributions; and using C3D plus LSTM extends temporal context beyond short optical-flow windows. The comparison against a central-bias baseline and prior saliency methods is useful, and the ablation of recurrence and LSTM vs RNN supports the design. Runtime is also attractive.

Weaknesses: the C3D network is frozen and pre-trained for action recognition, so the claimed end-to-end learning is limited, and saliency performance may depend heavily on that representation. Evaluation is primarily on one eye-tracking dataset (Hollywood2), with transfer to UCF101 for classification but not for saliency. The number of GMM components, fixation subsampling, and hyperparameter sensitivity are only partially analyzed. Action-recognition gains appear modest and are not accompanied by detailed statistical tests or per-class analysis. The “first deep spatiotemporal saliency” claim is somewhat strong given related video-saliency work. Overall, a solid and effective model with good empirical results, but stronger ablations, broader saliency evaluation, and clearer separation of representation versus recurrence contributions would improve confidence.

title: Inductive Bias of Deep Convolutional Networks through Pooling Geometry
abstract: Abstract:###Our formal understanding of the inductive bias that drives the success of convolutional networks on computer vision tasks is limited. In particular, it is unclear what makes hypotheses spaces born from convolution and pooling operations so suitable for natural images. In this paper we study the ability of convolutional networks to model correlations among regions of their input. We theoretically analyze convolutional arithmetic circuits, and empirically validate our findings on other types of convolutional networks as well. Correlations are formalized through the notion of separation rank, which for a given partition of the input, measures how far a function is from being separable. We show that a polynomially sized deep network supports exponentially high separation ranks for certain input partitions, while being limited to polynomial separation ranks for others. The network*s pooling geometry effectively determines which input partitions are favored, thus serves as a means for controlling the inductive bias. Contiguous pooling windows as commonly employed in practice favor interleaved partitions over coarse ones, orienting the inductive bias towards the statistics of natural images. Other pooling schemes lead to different preferences, and this allows tailoring the network to data that departs from the usual domain of natural imagery. In addition to analyzing deep networks, we show that shallow ones support only linear separation ranks, and by this gain insight into the benefit of functions brought forth by depth - they are able to efficiently model strong correlation under favored partitions of the input.
review:
The paper analyzes convolutional arithmetic circuits to explain how pooling geometry shapes inductive bias via separation rank, the minimal number of separable terms for a partition of input patches. It proves separation rank equals a matricization rank of the coefficient tensor, shows deep networks support exponentially high ranks for favored partitions while shallow networks support only linear ranks, and argues contiguous pooling favors interleaved partitions aligned with natural-image statistics. Empirical validation extends to rectifier networks with max/average pooling.

Strengths: The theoretical contribution is elegant and nontrivial. Linking pooling geometry to correlation modeling through separation rank gives a precise, interpretable account of architectural prior. The depth-efficiency connection is well motivated, and the paper is generally clear.

Weaknesses: The analysis relies on strong assumptions—linear pointwise activations, product pooling, non-overlapping uniform windows, and linearly independent representation functions. Practical relevance to ReLU/max/average networks is only empirical, not formal. The claim that contiguous pooling matches natural-image statistics is plausible but under-supported in the excerpt; stronger quantitative experiments would help. Also, separation rank is a surrogate for L2 distance from separability, and general lower bounds are not provided. The paper could better discuss limitations and how pooling geometry should be selected for non-natural data. Overall, a solid theoretical contribution with clear limitations.

title: Efficient Representation of Low-Dimensional Manifolds using Deep Networks
abstract: Abstract:###We consider the ability of deep neural networks to represent data that lies near a low-dimensional manifold in a high-dimensional space. We show that deep networks can efficiently extract the intrinsic, low-dimensional coordinates of such data. Specifically we show that the first two layers of a deep network can exactly embed points lying on a monotonic chain, a special type of piecewise linear manifold, mapping them to a low-dimensional Euclidean space. Remarkably, the network can do this using an almost optimal number of parameters. We also show that this network projects nearby points onto the manifold and then embeds them with little error. Experiments demonstrate that training with stochastic gradient descent can indeed find efficient representations similar to the one presented in this paper.
review:
The paper studies whether deep ReLU networks can efficiently represent data near a low-dimensional manifold. It gives a constructive proof that two hidden layers can exactly embed points on a monotonic chain of affine subspaces into the manifold’s intrinsic coordinates, using one additional hidden unit per segment and nearly optimal parameter count. It further analyzes projection error for noisy points and sketches extensions to more general manifolds.

Strengths: The geometric construction is clear and elegant, and the near-optimal parameter efficiency is a meaningful theoretical result. The error analysis is valuable, especially the bounded-curvature case, and the paper connects its construction to manifold learning and depth-efficiency literature. The writing is generally accessible.

Weaknesses: The main results are representational existence proofs, not learnability results; no training dynamics or empirical validation are provided. The analysis is restricted to monotonic chains with strong assumptions—intersecting affine segments, flattenability, and controlled curvature. The worst-case error can be unbounded for poorly chosen separating hyperplanes, and practical implications for noisy real data remain unclear. The extension to general nonlinear manifolds is high-level. Comparisons to chart-based approaches such as Shaham et al. could be sharper.

Overall, this is a solid theoretical contribution with clear limitations. I recommend acceptance with revisions clarifying assumptions, practical relevance, and scope.

title: Semi-Supervised Classification with Graph Convolutional Networks
abstract: Abstract:###We present a scalable approach for semi-supervised learning on graph-structured data that is based on an efficient variant of convolutional neural networks which operate directly on graphs. We motivate the choice of our convolutional architecture via a localized first-order approximation of spectral graph convolutions. Our model scales linearly in the number of graph edges and learns hidden layer representations that encode both local graph structure and features of nodes. In a number of experiments on citation networks and on a knowledge graph dataset we demonstrate that our approach outperforms related methods by a significant margin.
review:
The paper introduces Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) for semi-supervised node classification. It derives a simple layer-wise propagation rule as a first-order Chebyshev approximation of spectral graph convolutions, adds a renormalization trick for stability, and evaluates on citation networks and NELL.

Strengths: The derivation is clear and well motivated; the renormalization trick is practical and addresses exploding/vanishing gradients. The model is simple, scales linearly in the number of edges, and achieves strong accuracy with very few labels and fast training. The ablation comparing propagation variants supports the design choices. The paper is well written and likely influential.

Weaknesses: The spectral motivation relies on several approximations (K=1, λmax≈2, parameter sharing) whose theoretical justification is largely heuristic; the gap between the derived model and true spectral convolution is not fully characterized. Full-batch training limits scalability, and mini-batch extensions are left open. Experiments are limited to transductive citation and knowledge graphs of moderate size; no inductive or large-scale evaluation is provided. Hyperparameters are tuned on Cora and reused, and main results are averaged over random initializations but not multiple splits. The model may oversmooth with depth, with deeper models relegated to the appendix. Comparisons to recent graph neural methods are limited.

Overall, the contribution is significant and the method is simple and effective. I recommend acceptance, with clarifications on the approximations, scalability, and broader empirical validation.

title: Sparsely-Connected Neural Networks: Towards Efficient VLSI Implementation of Deep Neural Networks
abstract: Abstract:###Recently deep neural networks have received considerable attention due to their ability to extract and represent high-level abstractions in data sets. Deep neural networks such as fully-connected and convolutional neural networks have shown excellent performance on a wide range of recognition and classification tasks. However, their hardware implementations currently suffer from large silicon area and high power consumption due to the their high degree of complexity. The power/energy consumption of neural networks is dominated by memory accesses, the majority of which occur in fully-connected networks. In fact, they contain most of the deep neural network parameters. In this paper, we propose sparsely-connected networks, by showing that the number of connections in fully-connected networks can be reduced by up to 90% while improving the accuracy performance on three popular datasets (MNIST, CIFAR10 and SVHN). We then propose an efficient hardware architecture based on linear-feedback shift registers to reduce the memory requirements of the proposed sparsely-connected networks. The proposed architecture can save up to 90% of memory compared to the conventional implementations of fully-connected neural networks. Moreover, implementation results show up to 84% reduction in the energy consumption of a single neuron of the proposed sparsely-connected networks compared to a single neuron of fully-connected neural networks.
review:
The paper proposes sparsely-connected neural networks that randomly remove connections in fully-connected layers using LFSR-generated binary masks, and outlines a VLSI architecture exploiting the same generators to reduce memory and energy. Experiments on MNIST, CIFAR10, and SVHN report that up to 90% of connections can be removed without accuracy loss, sometimes with improvement, and that the approach combines well with binarization/ternarization.

Strengths: The idea is simple and hardware-oriented; using LFSRs to avoid storing explicit connection indices is a practical motivation. The empirical results across three datasets are reasonably broad, and the combination with BinaryConnect/TernaryConnect is relevant for efficient inference.

Weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited—random fixed pruning is related to known pruning and stochastic connectivity work, and the paper lacks comparisons to magnitude-based or structured pruning under equal parameter budgets. Accuracy gains over dense baselines are not analyzed; they may reflect regularization from random sparsity, and no variance or significance is reported. The LFSR scheme still requires storing seeds and generator configuration, and the hardware evaluation appears to compare a single neuron rather than full-system area, memory, and energy. The paper does not clarify whether masks are fixed before training or resampled, nor how sparsity interacts with batch normalization and optimizer dynamics. CIFAR10/SVHN baselines are limited, and state-of-the-art comparisons are selective.

Overall, the work is practical but incremental, with insufficient hardware validation and ablation. I recommend borderline rejection unless stronger analysis and full-system results are added.

title: Adversarial Training Methods for Semi-Supervised Text Classification
abstract: Abstract:###Adversarial training provides a means of regularizing supervised learning algorithms while virtual adversarial training is able to extend supervised learning algorithms to the semi-supervised setting. However, both methods require making small perturbations to numerous entries of the input vector, which is inappropriate for sparse high-dimensional inputs such as one-hot word representations. We extend adversarial and virtual adversarial training to the text domain by applying perturbations to the word embeddings in a recurrent neural network rather than to the original input itself. The proposed method achieves state of the art results on multiple benchmark semi-supervised and purely supervised tasks. We provide visualizations and analysis showing that the learned word embeddings have improved in quality and that while training, the model is less prone to overfitting.
review:
The paper extends adversarial and virtual adversarial training to text classification by perturbing word embeddings in an LSTM rather than discrete one-hot inputs. It combines this with recurrent language-model pretraining and evaluates on IMDB, Elec, RCV1, Rotten Tomatoes, and DBpedia, reporting state-of-the-art or competitive error rates and qualitative embedding improvements.

Strengths: The adaptation is sensible and clearly motivated: continuous embeddings admit bounded perturbations, and normalized embeddings prevent a trivial large-norm solution. Virtual adversarial training enables use of unlabeled text, fitting semi-supervised classification. Experiments span multiple datasets and include random-perturbation controls, learning curves, and nearest-neighbor analyses. Results are strong on IMDB, Elec, and RCV1, and the method is simple, adding mainly epsilon.

Weaknesses: The core technique is an application of existing VAT rather than a new algorithm. Gains are entangled with language-model pretraining and embedding dropout; ablations isolate epsilon but not pretraining. On Rotten Tomatoes, VAT alone underperforms the baseline, and the authors' explanation is post hoc. Only one perturbation norm constraint is emphasized, with limited sensitivity analysis. No significance tests or multiple-split variance are reported for most datasets. The embedding-normalization scheme uses corpus frequencies and may complicate deployment. Computational overhead of perturbation and backpropagation is not quantified.

Overall, this is a useful and well-executed empirical contribution. I recommend acceptance, with clarifications on pretraining confounds, hyperparameter sensitivity, and computational cost.

title: Fine-grained Analysis of Sentence Embeddings Using Auxiliary Prediction Tasks
abstract: Abstract:###There is a lot of research interest in encoding variable length sentences into fixed length vectors, in a way that preserves the sentence meanings. Two common methods include representations based on averaging word vectors, and representations based on the hidden states of recurrent neural networks such as LSTMs. The sentence vectors are used as features for subsequent machine learning tasks or for pre-training in the context of deep learning. However, not much is known about the properties that are encoded in these sentence representations and about the language information they capture. We propose a framework that facilitates better understanding of the encoded representations. We define prediction tasks around isolated aspects of sentence structure (namely sentence length, word content, and word order), and score representations by the ability to train a classifier to solve each prediction task when using the representation as input. We demonstrate the potential contribution of the approach by analyzing different sentence representation mechanisms. The analysis sheds light on the relative strengths of different sentence embedding methods with respect to these low level prediction tasks, and on the effect of the encoded vectorâ€™s dimensionality on the resulting representations.
review:
The paper proposes a fine-grained framework for analyzing sentence embeddings via auxiliary prediction tasks: sentence length, word content, and word order. It compares CBOW, LSTM autoencoders across dimensions, and skip-thought vectors, with controlled permuted-sentence experiments.

Strengths: The methodology is simple, general, and task-independent, applicable to arbitrary sentence representations. The three tasks are well chosen as basic structural properties, and the controlled experiments—random-word and permuted-sentence variants—are informative.
