The findings are actionable: CBOW encodes length through embedding norms and order through language statistics; LSTM autoencoders capture content and order but are less reliant on natural word order; dimensionality affects tasks differently; BLEU is a poor proxy for encoder quality. The paper is clearly written and appropriately acknowledges limitations.

Weaknesses: The tasks measure surface properties only, not syntax or semantics, so conclusions about representation quality are narrow. The study is empirical on Wikipedia and may not generalize across domains. Comparisons are partly unfair: skip-thought uses a different corpus and 4800 dimensions. Classifier capacity and training details could confound task accuracy. The word-content and order tasks use randomly sampled words, which may not reflect systematic linguistic structure. The analysis of why CBOW works is post hoc but supported. No downstream task validation is provided.

Overall, this is a useful diagnostic contribution rather than a new embedding method. I recommend acceptance, with clearer caveats on task scope and fairness of comparisons.

title: Pointer Sentinel Mixture Models
abstract: Abstract:###Recent neural network sequence models with softmax classifiers have achieved their best language modeling performance only with very large hidden states and large vocabularies. Even then they struggle to predict rare or unseen words even if the context makes the prediction unambiguous. We introduce the pointer sentinel mixture architecture for neural sequence models which has the ability to either reproduce a word from the recent context or produce a word from a standard softmax classifier. Our pointer sentinel-LSTM model achieves state of the art language modeling performance on the Penn Treebank (70.9 perplexity) while using far fewer parameters than a standard softmax LSTM. In order to evaluate how well language models can exploit longer contexts and deal with more realistic vocabularies and corpora we also introduce the freely available WikiText corpus.
review:
The paper introduces pointer sentinel mixture models for language modeling, combining a standard softmax-RNN with a pointer over recent context, and a sentinel-based gate that decides how much probability mass to assign to each. It reports state-of-the-art PTB perplexity (70.9) with fewer parameters and releases WikiText.

Strengths: The architecture is simple and well motivated. Integrating the gate into pointer attention via a sentinel is elegant, allowing the model to back off to the vocabulary when copying is inappropriate. The mixture formulation handles repeated words and OOV tokens from context, and parameter overhead is modest. Experiments are solid on PTB, and WikiText addresses real limitations of PTB.

Weaknesses: The pointer window is fixed and finite, so long-range copying beyond L steps is impossible; the paper offers little analysis of window-size sensitivity or sentinel behavior. Regenerating stale RNN outputs after each update increases training cost, and truncated BPTT choices are heuristic. Evaluation is largely PTB; WikiText results are not fully developed in the excerpt, and comparisons use different dropout/zoneout configurations. The model is only tested with LSTM, despite claims of generality. Ablations separating sentinel gating from pointer-sum attention would strengthen the contribution. OOV and rare-word benefits are asserted but not systematically quantified.

Overall, this is a well-executed and useful contribution. I recommend acceptance, with additional ablations and analysis of gate behavior and window size.

title: An Actor-Critic Algorithm for Sequence Prediction
abstract: Abstract:###We present an approach to training neural networks to generate sequences using actor-critic methods from reinforcement learning (RL). Current log-likelihood training methods are limited by the discrepancy between their training and testing modes, as models must generate tokens conditioned on their previous guesses rather than the ground-truth tokens. We address this problem by introducing a textit{critic} network that is trained to predict the value of an output token, given the policy of an textit{actor} network. This results in a training procedure that is much closer to the test phase, and allows us to directly optimize for a task-specific score such as BLEU. Crucially, since we leverage these techniques in the supervised learning setting rather than the traditional RL setting, we condition the critic network on the ground-truth output. We show that our method leads to improved performance on both a synthetic task, and for German-English machine translation. Our analysis paves the way for such methods to be applied in natural language generation tasks, such as machine translation, caption generation, and dialogue modelling.
review:
The paper applies actor-critic reinforcement learning to supervised sequence prediction, targeting the train–test discrepancy of teacher forcing. A critic conditioned on the ground-truth output estimates token values; the actor is trained by a policy-gradient-like objective, with target critic, delayed actor, variance penalty for large action spaces, reward shaping, and log-likelihood pretraining. Experiments on synthetic spelling correction and German–English translation show improvements over maximum likelihood and REINFORCE.

Strengths: The motivation is clear, and the policy-gradient derivation is clean. Conditioning the critic on ground truth is a sensible way to reduce variance in the supervised setting, and the stabilizers are practically motivated. The synthetic task provides a controlled setting, and comparisons to REINFORCE-critic are informative.

Weaknesses: The method is complex, with many interacting components—pretraining, target networks, delayed actor, variance regularization, reward shaping—without sufficient ablation or sensitivity analysis. Convergence is not guaranteed, and the variance penalty for large vocabularies is heuristic. The critic’s access to ground truth at training time may limit applicability. Translation results are only partially shown in the excerpt, and no variance or significance is reported. Comparisons to scheduled sampling and minimum-risk training are missing. Training cost relative to MLE is not quantified. The claim of unbiasedness holds only with an exact critic.

Overall, this is a solid methodological contribution with promising results. I recommend acceptance with revisions adding ablations, variance estimates, and clearer translation analysis.

title: Understanding Trainable Sparse Coding with Matrix Factorization
abstract: Abstract:###Sparse coding is a core building block in many data analysis and machine learning pipelines. Typically it is solved by relying on generic optimization techniques, such as the Iterative Soft Thresholding Algorithm and its accelerated version (ISTA, FISTA). These methods are optimal in the class of first-order methods for non-smooth, convex functions. However, they do not exploit the particular structure of the problem at hand nor the input data distribution. An acceleration using neural networks, coined LISTA, was proposed in cite{Gregor10}, which showed empirically that one could achieve high quality estimates with few iterations by modifying the parameters of the proximal splitting appropriately. In this paper we study the reasons for such acceleration. Our mathematical analysis reveals that it is related to a specific matrix factorization of the Gram kernel of the dictionary, which attempts to nearly diagonalise the kernel with a basis that produces a small perturbation of the ball. When this factorization succeeds, we prove that the resulting splitting algorithm enjoys an improved convergence bound with respect to the non-adaptive version. Moreover, our analysis also shows that conditions for acceleration occur mostly at the beginning of the iterative process, consistent with numerical experiments. We further validate our analysis by showing that on dictionaries where this factorization does not exist, adaptive acceleration fails.
review:
The paper studies why LISTA accelerates sparse coding relative to ISTA. It derives a non-asymptotic convergence bound based on factorizing the dictionary Gram matrix as B ≈ A^T S A, with A unitary, S diagonal, and PSD residual, plus an ℓ1 commutation error. When this factorization is good, the adaptive proximal step has improved constants; the analysis also predicts that gains concentrate in early iterations and vanish near the optimum. The authors introduce FacNet, a constrained LISTA variant, and use synthetic dictionaries to test when acceleration occurs or fails.

Strengths: The matrix-factorization perspective is original and gives a clear certificate for acceleration. The bound is interpretable, and the phase-transition/diminishing-returns insight is valuable. The counterexample construction and FacNet experiments support the sufficiency claim.

Weaknesses: The theory relies on strong conditions—unitary A, PSD residual, small ℓ1 commutation—that may not hold for learned LISTA layers. Improving an upper bound is not a guarantee of actual speedup, and the necessity claim is only empirical/“somewhat necessary.” The experiments are mostly synthetic and excerpted; real dictionary-learning and image sparse-coding benchmarks are needed. Comparisons with LFISTA, different sparsity levels, and sensitivity to μ and layer count are limited. The conclusion that shared-layer weights are less effective deserves more direct ablation.

Overall, this is a solid theoretical contribution. I recommend acceptance with revisions strengthening empirical validation and clarifying necessity versus sufficiency.

title: Tighter bounds lead to improved classifiers
abstract: Abstract:###The standard approach to supervised classification involves the minimization of a log-loss as an upper bound to the classification error. While this is a tight bound early on in the optimization, it overemphasizes the influence of incorrectly classified examples far from the decision boundary. Updating the upper bound during the optimization leads to improved classification rates while transforming the learning into a sequence of minimization problems. In addition, in the context where the classifier is part of a larger system, this modification makes it possible to link the performance of the classifier to that of the whole system, allowing the seamless introduction of external constraints.
review:
The paper proposes replacing log-loss with a sequence of tighter upper bounds on expected classification error. Lemma 1 gives a linearized probability bound, leading to Algorithm 1, which repeatedly reweights each example by its current predicted probability and minimizes a weighted log-loss. Experiments with generalized linear models on Covertype, Alpha, MNIST, and IJCNN show that T>1 improves test error in underfitting regimes but gives no gain when overfitting dominates. The paper also links the objective to one-step policy optimization, ROC-constrained learning, and an “Undecided” action.

Strengths: The motivation is clear and the bound is simple, with matching value and gradient at ν=θ. The reweighting scheme is easy to implement and directly targets classification error rather than likelihood. Gains on Covertype and IJCNN are significant, and the policy-optimization interpretation is interesting.

Weaknesses: Empirical validation is limited to convex GLMs; the claimed extension to deep networks is not tested. Computational cost of repeated inner optimizations and sensitivity to T are not fully analyzed. Baselines such as calibrated losses, focal loss, or cost-sensitive training are missing. Alpha shows no improvement, and the constrained-ROC result is inconsistent with the asymmetric-cost experiment, which the authors leave unexplained. Convergence of the alternating scheme is not established. The “Undecided” discussion suggests the model may remain unchanged with sufficient capacity, limiting its practical value.

Overall, this is a promising but preliminary contribution. I recommend borderline acceptance with stronger baselines, deep-network experiments, and convergence analysis.

title: HolStep: A Machine Learning Dataset for Higher-order Logic Theorem Proving
abstract: Abstract:###Large computer-understandable proofs consist of millions of intermediate logical steps. The vast majority of such steps originate from manually selected and manually guided heuristics applied to intermediate goals. So far, machine learning has generally not been used to filter or generate these steps. In this paper, we introduce a new dataset based on Higher-Order Logic (HOL) proofs, for the purpose of developing new machine learning-based theorem-proving strategies. We make this dataset publicly available under the BSD license. We propose various machine learning tasks that can be performed on this dataset, and discuss their significance for theorem proving. We also benchmark a set of simple baseline machine learning models suited for the tasks (including logistic regression convolutional neural networks and recurrent neural networks). The results of our baseline models show the promise of applying machine learning to HOL theorem proving.
review:
The paper proposes compressive autoencoders for lossy image compression. It handles non-differentiable rounding via a straight-through gradient—identity in the backward pass while keeping rounding in the forward pass—and approximates the discrete entropy rate with a differentiable upper bound using Jensen’s inequality and Gaussian scale mixtures. A sub-pixel convolutional architecture enables efficient high-resolution encoding/decoding, and scale parameters allow variable bit rates. On Kodak, the method is competitive with JPEG 2000 and outperforms an RNN-based approach on perceptual metrics.

Strengths: The approach is simple and practical. Keeping quantization in the forward pass while passing gradients through is a sensible way to avoid the decoder inverting a smooth approximation. The entropy upper bound is clean, and the sub-pixel design is computationally attractive. Experiments use multiple metrics and compare against strong codecs.

Weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to 24 Kodak images, with training on Flickr crops, so generalization is uncertain. Header bits are excluded for JPEG/JPEG 2000 but only a one-byte ensemble index is added for the proposed method, which may bias rate comparisons. The ensemble-per-image encoder selection increases encoding cost and is not ablated against a single model. The identity gradient is empirically justified but lacks theoretical analysis, and the rate model uses histograms rather than jointly learned entropy coding, creating a potential train–test mismatch. Ablations for rounding alternatives, GSM scales, and incremental training are limited.

Overall, this is a solid applied contribution. I recommend acceptance with fairer rate accounting and broader evaluation.

title: Why Deep Neural Networks for Function Approximation?
abstract: Abstract:###Recently there has been much interest in understanding why deep neural networks are preferred to shallow networks. We show that, for a large class of piecewise smooth functions, the number of neurons needed by a shallow network to approximate a function is exponentially larger than the corresponding number of neurons needed by a deep network for a given degree of function approximation. First, we consider univariate functions on a bounded interval and require a neural network to achieve an approximation error of uniformly over the interval. We show that shallow networks (i.e., networks whose depth does not depend on ) require neurons while deep networks (i.e., networks whose depth grows with ) require neurons. We then extend these results to certain classes of important multivariate functions. Our results are derived for neural networks which use a combination of rectifier linear units (ReLUs) and binary step units, two of the most popular type of activation functions. Our analysis builds on a simple observation: the multiplication of two bits can be represented by a ReLU.
review:
The paper proves depth-separation results for function approximation with ReLU and binary step units. For sufficiently smooth univariate and certain multivariate functions, deep networks with Θ(log(1/ε)) layers achieve ε-approximation with polylog(1/ε) neurons, whereas shallow networks with o(log(1/ε)) layers require Ω(poly(1/ε)) neurons. The construction exploits binary expansions and the fact that ReLU can implement multiplication of bits; the lower bound is argued via strong convexity/smoothness.

Strengths: The results are clearly stated and the upper-bound constructions are explicit, covering polynomials, smooth functions, products, compositions, and multivariate polynomials. The comparison with shallow-network bounds is informative, and the paper connects to prior depth-separation work. The observation that BSUs plus ReLUs enable efficient binary expansion is neat.

Weaknesses: The architecture relies heavily on binary step units, which are non-standard in practice; the significance for ReLU-only networks is unclear. Smoothness assumptions and coefficient constraints are strong, and the polylog bounds hide constants that may be large. The lower bound appears to require particular smoothness/strong-convexity conditions, limiting generality. Multivariate bounds grow polynomially in dimension and degree, so the practical advantage is narrower than the headline suggests. The paper would benefit from discussing tightness, constants, and robustness to approximate BSUs.

Overall, this is a valuable theoretical contribution with clear limitations. I recommend acceptance, with clarifications on activation assumptions and practical implications.

title: Hierarchical Multiscale Recurrent Neural Networks
abstract: Abstract:###Learning both hierarchical and temporal representation has been among the long- standing challenges of recurrent neural networks. Multiscale recurrent neural networks have been considered as a promising approach to resolve this issue, yet there has been a lack of empirical evidence showing that this type of models can actually capture the temporal dependencies by discovering the latent hierarchical structure of the sequence. In this paper, we propose a novel multiscale approach, called the hierarchical multiscale recurrent neural network, that can capture the latent hierarchical structure in the sequence by encoding the temporal dependencies with different timescales using a novel update mechanism. We show some evidence that the proposed model can discover underlying hierarchical structure in the sequences without using explicit boundary information. We evaluate our proposed model on character-level language modelling and handwriting sequence generation.
review:
The paper proposes Hierarchical Multiscale Recurrent Neural Networks (HM-RNNs), which learn latent hierarchical temporal structure without explicit boundaries. Each layer has a binary boundary detector and selects among UPDATE, COPY, and FLUSH, allowing higher layers to update less frequently and preserving state losslessly between segments. The model is trained with a straight-through estimator and a slope-annealing trick. Experiments on character-level language modeling (Penn Treebank, Text8, Hutter Prize Wikipedia) and handwriting generation show strong BPC results, and visualizations suggest learned boundaries align with words.

Strengths: The architecture is well motivated and the UPDATE/COPY/FLUSH mechanism is a clean way to combine hard segment boundaries with LSTM states. Learning timescales rather than fixing them is valuable, and the empirical results are competitive or state-of-the-art on several benchmarks. The boundary visualizations provide useful qualitative evidence.

Weaknesses: The model is complex, with many interacting components—boundary detectors, top-down gating, hard resets, straight-through gradients, and slope annealing—whose individual contributions are not fully isolated. Slope-annealing schedules appear ad hoc and were not used consistently across datasets. Computational savings from sparse updates are asserted but not quantified. Evaluation is limited to character-level modeling and handwriting; broader sequence tasks and comparisons to clockwork/scheduled-sampling baselines would strengthen claims. Training stability and sensitivity to layer count and boundary thresholds are underexplored. The interpretation of learned boundaries as hierarchy is suggestive but not rigorously validated.

Overall, this is an original and empirically promising contribution. I recommend acceptance with additional ablations, runtime analysis, and broader evaluation.

title: Neural Photo Editing with Introspective Adversarial Networks
abstract: Abstract:###The increasingly photorealistic sample quality of generative image models suggests their feasibility in applications beyond image generation. We present the Neural Photo Editor, an interface that leverages the power of generative neural networks to make large, semantically coherent changes to existing images. To tackle the challenge of achieving accurate reconstructions without loss of feature quality, we introduce the Introspective Adversarial Network, a novel hybridization of the VAE and GAN. Our model efficiently captures long-range dependencies through use of a computational block based on weight-shared dilated convolutions, and improves generalization performance with Orthogonal Regularization, a novel weight regularization method. We validate our contributions on CelebA, SVHN, and CIFAR-100, and produce samples and reconstructions with high visual fidelity.
review:
The paper presents the Neural Photo Editor, which edits images by backpropagating local paintbrush errors into a generative model’s latent space, plus the Introspective Adversarial Network (IAN), a VAE/GAN hybrid sharing discriminator features for inference. It also introduces Multiscale Dilated Convolution (MDC) blocks and Orthogonal Regularization. Experiments cover CelebA, SVHN, CIFAR-10/100, and ImageNet, with qualitative samples and an ablation on reconstruction metrics.

Strengths: The editing interface is practical and well motivated, and the masking scheme for transferring edits onto real photos is simple and sensible. Sharing the discriminator as an encoder is parameter-efficient, and the ternary adversarial loss is an interesting way to enrich discriminator supervision. The ablation on CelebA is informative, and the CIFAR-100 DenseNet experiments provide quantitative support for MDC and Orthogonal Regularization.

Weaknesses: The editor evaluation is largely qualitative; no user study, editing-success rate, or comparison to iGAN is provided. The mask and gradient-step heuristics have several hyperparameters whose sensitivity is unexplored. The ternary loss and Orthogonal Regularization are motivated heuristically, with limited theoretical or ablation depth. The IAN is complex, and contributions of individual losses are only partially isolated. The semi-supervised SVHN result is mentioned but not shown in the excerpt. MDC gains are modest relative to added complexity, and comparisons to recent generative models are limited.

Overall, this is a solid applied contribution with a compelling interface. I recommend acceptance with stronger quantitative evaluation of editing and clearer ablations.

title: Dropout with Expectation-linear Regularization
abstract: Abstract:###Dropout, a simple and effective way to train deep neural networks, has led to a number of impressive empirical successes and spawned many recent theoretical investigations. However, the gap between dropoutâ€™s training and inference phases, introduced due to tractability considerations, has largely remained under-appreciated. In this work, we first formulate dropout as a tractable approximation of some latent variable model, leading to a clean view of parameter sharing and enabling further theoretical analysis. Then, we introduce (approximate) expectation-linear dropout neural networks, whose inference gap we are able to formally characterize. Algorithmically, we show that our proposed measure of the inference gap can be used to regularize the standard dropout training objective, resulting in an explicit control of the gap. Our method is as simple and efficient as standard dropout. We further prove the upper bounds on the loss in accuracy due to expectation-linearization, describe classes of input distributions that expectation-linearize easily. Experiments on three image classification benchmark datasets demonstrate that reducing the inference gap can indeed improve the performance consistently.
review:
The paper formulates dropout as a latent-variable model and introduces expectation-linear dropout networks to quantify the mismatch between training-time averaging and test-time weight scaling. It derives bounds showing that small layer operator norms and max-norm constraints reduce the inference gap, then proposes an expectation-linearization regularizer that adds a sampled penalty to standard dropout training. Experiments on three image classification benchmarks reportedly show consistent improvements.

Strengths: The latent-variable view is clean and clarifies parameter sharing. The inference-gap analysis is well motivated and the connection to max-norm regularization provides a useful theoretical explanation for a common practice. The proposed regularizer is simple and claimed to be as efficient as standard dropout, making it practical. The uniform deviation bound and the accuracy trade-off analysis add theoretical depth.

Weaknesses: The empirical validation is limited to three image datasets and largely compares against standard dropout; stronger baselines such as variational dropout, concrete dropout, or max-norm dropout alone are needed. The sensitivity to the regularization coefficient λ and the actual computational overhead are not thoroughly reported. The expectation-linearity condition is strong, and the bounds involve constants that may be loose in deep networks. The paper also does not analyze interaction with batch normalization or modern architectures. Results are summarized rather than showing per-dataset variance.

Overall, this is a solid theoretical and algorithmic contribution. I recommend acceptance with expanded baselines, sensitivity analysis, and clearer empirical reporting.

title: HyperNetworks
abstract: Abstract:###This work explores hypernetworks: an approach of using one network, also known as a hypernetwork, to generate the weights for another network. We apply hypernetworks to generate adaptive weights for recurrent networks. In this case, hypernetworks can be viewed as a relaxed form of weight-sharing across layers. In our implementation, hypernetworks are are trained jointly with the main network in an end-to-end fashion. Our main result is that hypernetworks can generate non-shared weights for LSTM and achieve state-of-the-art results on a variety of sequence modelling tasks including character-level language modelling, handwriting generation and neural machine translation, challenging the weight-sharing paradigm for recurrent networks.
review:
The paper explores hypernetworks, where a smaller network generates weights for a larger main network, trained end-to-end by backpropagation. It introduces static hypernetworks for convolutional filters via layer embeddings and dynamic hypernetworks for recurrent networks, including HyperLSTM with memory-efficient row-wise weight scaling. Experiments cover MNIST, CIFAR-10, character-level Penn Treebank/enwik8, handwriting generation, and NMT.

Strengths: The framing of hypernetworks as relaxed weight sharing is insightful and connects convolutional and recurrent architectures. The static factorization is simple and substantially reduces parameters, and the dynamic row-scaling variant is a practical response to memory constraints. HyperLSTM results on character-level language modeling are competitive with strong LSTM and LayerNorm baselines, and the combination with LayerNorm is promising. The paper is clearly written and covers a useful range of tasks.

Weaknesses: The CIFAR-10 static hypernetwork results are notably worse than the corresponding Wide ResNet baselines despite far fewer parameters, so the efficiency–accuracy trade-off is not compelling for image recognition. Dynamic hypernetwork gains are modest and often comparable to LayerNorm, with limited ablation isolating the contribution of dynamic weight generation. The method adds complexity and hyperparameters (embedding size, hypernetwork hidden size) whose sensitivity is underexplored. Training cost and wall-clock comparisons are not reported. The NMT and handwriting results are only briefly summarized. Theoretical understanding of when hypernetworks help remains limited.

Overall, this is an interesting and practically relevant contribution, but claims of challenging weight sharing need stronger ablations and efficiency analysis. I recommend acceptance with revisions.

title: A Learned Representation For Artistic Style
abstract: Abstract:###The diversity of painting styles represents a rich visual vocabulary for the construction of an image. The degree to which one may learn and parsimoniously capture this visual vocabulary measures our understanding of the higher level features of paintings, if not images in general. In this work we investigate the construction of a single, scalable deep network that can parsimoniously capture the artistic style of a diversity of paintings. We demonstrate that such a network generalizes across a diversity of artistic styles by reducing a painting to a point in an embedding space. Importantly, this model permits a user to explore new painting styles by arbitrarily combining the styles learned from individual paintings. We hope that this work provides a useful step towards building rich models of paintings and offers a window on to the structure of the learned representation of artistic style.
review:
The paper proposes conditional instance normalization for feedforward style transfer, enabling a single network to model many artistic styles by learning style-specific affine parameters after normalization. It shows that only ~0.2% of parameters are style-specific, that an N-style network matches separately trained networks, that new styles can be added cheaply by fine-tuning γ and β, and that convex combinations of these parameters yield smooth style interpolation.

Strengths: The idea is simple, effective, and practically valuable for memory-limited deployment. The parameter-sharing analysis is compelling, and the experiments on Monet and 32 diverse styles support flexibility. The new-style and interpolation experiments demonstrate a useful learned style embedding. The paper is clearly written and well motivated.

Weaknesses: Evaluation is largely qualitative; quantitative style/content metrics and human studies are limited. Comparisons use the same architecture and losses, but no ablations isolate the contribution of mirror padding and upsampling changes. The interpolation evidence is mostly perceptual and a style-loss curve; semantic meaningfulness of convex combinations is not established. Style identity assumes discrete labeled styles, and the method does not address style images at test time. The interpretation of γ/β as an “element of style” vocabulary is speculative. Claims of scalability would benefit from larger style sets and runtime/memory measurements.

Overall, this is a solid and influential applied contribution. I recommend acceptance, with stronger quantitative evaluation and ablations.

title: Hadamard Product for Low-rank Bilinear Pooling
abstract: Abstract:###Bilinear models provide rich representations compared with linear models. They have been applied in various visual tasks, such as object recognition, segmentation, and visual question-answering, to get state-of-the-art performances taking advantage of the expanded representations. However, bilinear representations tend to be high-dimensional, limiting the applicability to computationally complex tasks. We propose low-rank bilinear pooling using Hadamard product for an efficient attention mechanism of multimodal learning. We show that our model outperforms compact bilinear pooling in visual question-answering tasks with the state-of-the-art results on the VQA dataset, having a better parsimonious property.
review:
The paper proposes low-rank bilinear pooling using Hadamard product, factorizing a third-order bilinear weight tensor into three matrices. It applies this to multimodal attention in Visual Question Answering, yielding Multimodal Low-rank Bilinear Attention Networks (MLB). The paper also analyzes full-model biases, nonlinearities, shortcut connections, and connections to MRN.

Strengths: The method is simple, parameter-efficient, and well motivated. It avoids the high-dimensional projections of compact bilinear pooling while retaining multiplicative interactions. The VQA results are strong, with MLB outperforming MCB and prior single models on test-standard, and the ablations over blocks, glimpses, activation placement, answer sampling, shortcuts, and Visual Genome augmentation are useful. The parsimonious property—roughly 52M parameters versus 70M for MCB—is practically relevant.

Weaknesses: The theoretical justification is limited; low-rank approximation quality relative to full bilinear pooling is not analyzed. The comparison with compact bilinear pooling is not fully controlled for parameter count, training setup, and ensemble effects. Ablations are sequential, so interactions among choices are not isolated, and some gains are small. The model still depends on many hyperparameters—rank d, output dimension, number of glimpses, and answer sampling—whose sensitivity is underexplored. The relation to MRN is somewhat incremental, and claims of state-of-the-art are dataset-specific. No failure cases or qualitative error analysis are provided.

Overall, this is a solid applied contribution with an effective and efficient pooling mechanism. I recommend acceptance, with clearer comparisons and sensitivity analysis.

title: Learning Continuous Semantic Representations of Symbolic Expressions
abstract: Abstract:###The question of how procedural knowledge is represented and inferred is a fundamental problem in machine learning and artificial intelligence. Recent work on program induction has proposed neural architectures, based on abstractions like stacks, Turing machines, and interpreters, that operate on abstract computational machines or on execution traces. But the recursive abstraction that is central to procedural knowledge is perhaps most naturally represented by symbolic representations that have syntactic structure, such as logical expressions and source code. Combining abstract, symbolic reasoning with continuous neural reasoning is a grand challenge of representation learning. As a step in this direction, we propose a new architecture, called neural equivalence networks, for the problem of learning continuous semantic representations of mathematical and logical expressions. These networks are trained to represent semantic equivalence, even of expressions that are syntactically very different. The challenge is that semantic representations must be computed in a syntax-directed manner, because semantics is compositional, but at the same time, small changes in syntax can lead to very large changes in semantics, which can be difficult for continuous neural architectures. We perform an exhaustive evaluation on the task of checking equivalence on a highly diverse class of symbolic algebraic and boolean expression types, showing that our model significantly outperforms existing architectures.
review:
The paper addresses learning continuous semantic representations of symbolic expressions, proposing EQNETs: tree-recursive networks with multi-layer residual combination, unit-norm SEMVECs, and a subexpression autoencoder regularizer. It formulates equivalence-class prediction with a max-margin objective and evaluates on generated Boolean and polynomial datasets.

Strengths: The problem is well motivated, and the architecture is thoughtfully designed to balance compositionality with the need for large semantic changes from small syntactic edits. The subexpression autoencoder is an interesting regularizer that encourages abstraction and reversibility. The evaluation is broad across expression types and includes seen and unseen equivalence classes, transfer to larger expressions, and component ablations. EQNETs substantially outperform tf-idf, GRU, stack-RNN, and TreeNN baselines on most datasets, which is encouraging.

Weaknesses: The task is synthetic and reduced to equivalence-class classification; the learned representation is not evaluated on downstream symbolic reasoning, search, or real code/math. The class-embedding classifier may encourage representations tailored to known classes, and the unseen-class evaluation is still drawn from the same generator. Baselines are limited and somewhat dated, with no comparison to graph-based or attention-based models. SUBEXPAE introduces several hyperparameters and an annealing schedule whose sensitivity is not fully analyzed. The kNN metric is reasonable but does not establish semantic compositionality in a strong sense. Results on POLY5 are mixed.

Overall, this is a solid and original contribution. I recommend acceptance with stronger downstream evaluation and broader baselines.

title: Discovering objects and their relations from entangled scene representations
abstract: Abstract:###Our world can be succinctly and compactly described as structured scenes of objects and relations. A typical room, for example, contains salient objects such as tables, chairs and books, and these objects typically relate to each other by virtue of their correlated features, such as position, function and shape. Humans exploit knowledge of objects and their relations for learning a wide spectrum of tasks, and more generally when learning the structure underlying observed data. In this work, we introduce relation networks (RNs) - a general purpose neural network architecture for object-relation reasoning. We show that RNs are capable of learning object relations from scene description data. Furthermore, we show that RNs can act as a bottleneck that induces the factorization of objects from entangled scene description inputs, and from distributed deep representations of scene images provided by a variational autoencoder. The model can also be used in conjunction with differentiable memory mechanisms for implicit relation discovery in one-shot learning tasks. Our results suggest that relation networks are a powerful architecture for solving a variety of problems that require object relation reasoning.
review:
The paper introduces Relation Networks (RNs) for object–relation reasoning, using a shared pairwise MLP over object pairs followed by a permutation-invariant aggregation. It evaluates RNs on synthetic scene-description classification, disentangling objects from permuted inputs and VAE latents, and one-shot relational learning with a MANN.

Strengths: The architecture is simple, well motivated, and clearly captures desirable inductive biases—permutation invariance and shared relational computation. The experiments convincingly show RNs outperform MLPs of comparable size on relation-defined classification, and the generalization to unseen relation classes is a compelling demonstration of compositional learning. Using RNs as a bottleneck to induce object factorization from entangled and pixel-level representations is an interesting and useful idea. The paper is generally clear and the tasks are well designed to control for non-relational shortcuts.

Weaknesses: Evaluation is entirely synthetic, with small object sets and controlled generative graphs; real-world scenes, noisy object detections, and variable object counts are not addressed. The VAE disentangling evidence is mostly indirect, and no quantitative measure of object factorization is provided. The comparison focuses on MLPs; stronger relational or graph-network baselines are missing. One-shot results are only briefly summarized, and the MANN/RN integration is not ablated. The aggregation is fixed to summation, with little analysis of alternatives or failure modes. Scalability to many objects is O(m²) pairs and is not discussed.

Overall, this is a promising workshop contribution with clear conceptual value. I recommend acceptance, with broader baselines, quantitative factorization metrics, and scalability analysis.
